It transcends the distinction of subject and object, the

The absolute of experience is not the absolute of 
language or of logic. The Real to which we belong is 
beyond description in its majesty, power and glory. 
Spiritual humility requires us to look upon the varied 
expressions and interpretations as suggestions of the 
Supreme. By encouraging dogmatism and the use of 
force to spread belief, religions have become discredited. 


The seers affirm that they are one with the Sup- 
reme : ahah brakmdsm. Hallij exclaims . “I am the 
truth ” and was executed for his heterodoxy. 


A well-known Sufi tradition attributes to the pro- 
phet a saying : “He who knows the self knows the 
Lord”. Of Abi Yazid it is recorded that he said: “I 
sloughed off my self as a snake sloughs off its skin; 
then I looked into my self, and lo, I was He”.* Reli- 
gion, it is said, springs from the great ‘I am’ in each 
‘me’, The fountains are within. 


On the pathway to the goal we feel that the 
attainment of the goal is conditioned by the effort of 
the seeker and the grace of God — tapah-prabhdva and 
deva-prasada. 


The seekers look upon the Supreme as a Person 
separate from us, whose commands we obey, whose will 
we accept with reverence. The One beyond sense-per- 
ception, speech and logic is also the Controller, the 
Lord of all, the Creator and Ordainer of all, “ There is 
nothing marvellous in my love for you, O God, you- are 
a mighty being but your love for me a poor slave is 
really marvellous. It is impossible,to know thee and 
not to love thee.” The personal is not a falsification of

The secret of true greatness is love of fellowmen. 
Love of neighbour is not only a moral duty but a wise

PREFACE TO VOLUME V 


The fourth volume of the History of Dharmasdstra 
was published in October 1953, i.e. more than eight 
years ago. This last volume was in the Press for more 
than five years. The delay is due to several causes 
This volume in two parts contains over 1700 pages. It 
is thus far more bulky than any of the previous volumes. 
Nonavailability of sufficient quantity of good printing 
paper was another cause. The third cause was my age 
(1 am now 82 years old) and frequent bad health. 
It is gratifying to my friends and myself that at last 
this undertaking spread over thirty-seven years is 
completed. 


This volume is divided into ten sections. The first 
section deals with Vratas and Utsavas ( religious vows 
and festivals); the second with Kala (time), Muhirta 
( auspicious times), and calendar; the third with 
Santis ( propitiatory rites for averting the wrath of a 
deity, a calamity or unlucky event); the fourth and 
fifth with Puranas and Dharmasgistra and the causes of 
the disappearance of Buddhism from India ; the sixth 
with Taintrik doctrines and Dharmagastra ; the seventh 
with Mimarhsi and Dharmagastra; the eighth with 
Sankhya, Yoga, Tarka and Dharmasistra ; the ninth 
with cosmology, Karma and Punarjanma ; the tenth 
With the fundamental conceptions and characteristics of 


Hindu ( Bharatiya ) culture and civilization, and future 
trends. 


In the Preface to the 2nd volume I have indicated 
the reasons for numerous and lengthy Sanskrit quota- 
tions. In the Preface to the 4th volume I have mentio- 
ned the aim I had in view in bringing together the facts 


vin Hustory of Dharmasastra 


in each branch of DharmaSastra with detachment and 
integrity and without bias. The same aim and mental 
attitude have been kept in view in this volume also. 
But if may be argued that when an author selects 
some of the numerous facts he passes a judgement 
about the importance of facts and his judgement may 
be biased all the same. I do not dispute this argu- 
ment, but will only argue that, facts being numerous 
and there being limitations imposed by the space 
available, the author has a right to pronounce a judge- 
ment as to the importance of the facts he selects. 


As regards volumes two, three and four, I could 
rely on a tower of strength in the person of Parama- 
hamsa क्राणा Kevalananda Sarasvati of Wai. But, 
unfortunately the Svami passed away in March 1955 
before I began to write this last volume, and I 
could not get the benefit of his wise counsel in this fifth 
volume, 


In this last volume I received help from many 
people, either personally or by correspondence. I have 
to thank Mr. M. B. Arte, Dr. R. N. Dandekar, and 
Prof. H. D. Velankar for help in translating impor- 
tant passages from several French and German works, 
Prof. Gode, Curator of the Bhandarkar Oriental Resea- 
rch Institute, Poona, was always ready to render help 
as to manuscripts and books. He had been a close 
friend for nearly forty years and his sudden death has 
meant for me the loss of a learned, sympathetic, and 
ever-obliging friend. Dr. A. D. Pusalker very carefully 
read the chapters on Puranas and indicated several mis- 
prints and some inaccurate statements. Dr. Raghavan 
very kindly brought to my notice the calendars in use 
in Southern India and certain works on Vratas ; Pandit 
Srijiva Nydyatirtha sent me in Sanskrit the Naiyayika

may be later than 1000 ए. C.. Some scholars have

that there is any better proof for any later ‘date

his Calcutta Readership Lectures, p. 20) remarks 
‘it is more probable that this urknown time of the 
Vedic Literature was nearer 2500 B.C. or 2000 
5. ©. than to 1500 or 1200 B.C.’ Both Bloomfield 
and Winternitz frankly confess that they know 
nothing at all about the date of the early Vedic 
Literature. Some Western scholars are rather 
too cocksure or dogmatic than the facts warrant.

Vedic meaning and procedure of Santis 


The word Santi is derived from the root ‘gam *, which has 
several meanings (such as ‘to stop’, ‘to ba appeased’, ‘to Icfll’ 
rarely) and belougs to the 4th conjugation and also to the 9th, 
The word Santi itself doos not oceur in the Reveda, एप it occurs 
in the Atharvaveda and the Vajasaneya Sarhhita. The root 
‘gam’, its several forms and derivatives and the indsclinable 
particle ‘éam” occur hundreds of times even in the Reveda, 
The word ‘gam’ is often conjoined in the Reveda to ‘ yoh’ either 
as ‘Yamyoh’ (Rg. 7. 93.7, 1. 106.5, शा 17.8, I. 18.4, TV. 12.5, 
V. 47.7, V. 53.14, ए. 693, VI. 50.7, VIL 35.1, VIL 69.5, ॐ, 9.4, 
X. 15.4, X. 37.11, XK. 182.1-3) or as ‘gam ca yoSca’ (as in Rg. 
1. 114.2, 189.2, IL 33.13, VILL 39.4, VOL. 71.15). In these places 
the words are generally rendered as ‘ happiness and welfare’ or 
‘health and wealth’ (by Keith in translation of Tai. 8. IL. 6.10.3) 
and these meanings generally suit the context, 8. ह. in Re. 
VL 507 ‘dhata tokaya tanayaya gam yoh’ (confer on our song 
and progeny happiness and welfare ), in Re. X. 182 the words 
‘atha karad-yajamanaya sam yoh’ (may Brhaspati confer happi- 
ness and welfare on the sacrificer) occur as the last quarter 
of all the three verses, ‘Sam’ by itself occurs about 160 times 
in the Reveda and it is somewhat remarkable that in Re. VIL

(68 times in all). Rg. I 114.1183 ‘woe bring these lauds to

water for the sake of Santi; water indeed is (a means of ) Santi 
and then he should touch the material (that has fallen out) 
with his right hand and recite a mantra ( that is specified ) or he 
should recite another rk verso ‘by whose power the worlds ara 
made fixed’, which is addressed to Visnu and Varuna; Visnu 
indeed is the saviour against what is badly sacrificed (1, 6. the 
defects in it), while Varuna profects (i.e prevents obstacles to 
securing the fruit of ) what is well sacrificed; (this latter mantra

The Aitareya-Aranyaka mentions ten dreams viz a person 8998 
a dark man with black teeth and such aman kills him, or a boar 
kills him, or an ape jumps on him, the wind carries him 
swiftly; having swallowed gold, he vomits it; he eats honey ; he 
chews stalks of lotuses; he carries a single (red) lotus; he 
drives with a team of asses or boars; himself wearing a wreath 
of nalada flowers,“® he drives towards the south a black cow 
having 9 black calf. If aman sees any one of these, he should 
fast, cook a dish of rice in milk in a vessel, offer into fira 
oblations thereof with each of the verses of the hymn to Night 
(Rg. X 127, 1-8), feed brahmanas with other food { cooked in the 
house) and should himself eat boiled rice "116+ The same Aranyaka

the sky becoming like madder and prescribes the recital of some 


Revedic verses ( such as 1X. 67, 21-27, VILL 6, 30, LX. 118. 6-11, 
, +. 50. 10).

The preceding discussion with regard to Santis is enough to 
show thafi Santis were prescribed in the Vedic literature, the 
srautasitras, Samavidhana-brahmana and Revidhana, not only 
for appeasing the angry divinities or powers of evil, but also for 
occurrences like bad dreams or of portentous phenomena like the 
fun’s or moon's appearance, the cries of unlucky birds &c, 


This subject about Santis against ali sorts of omens and 
portents was very much elaborated in the post.Vedic literature. 
An extensive literature on Santis exists in the Grhyasiitras, the

(Visnu), Three of the verses are: “Just as the sun shines 
brightly in the heaven, Vayu dwells in the sky and Agni enters 
the earth, so may this Jisnu be firm and unmoving. As the 
rivers day and night pour their sediment (clay or mud carried 
by them) in the sea without fail, similarly may all tribes 
(of gods?) with one mind approach my invocation (or sacri- 
fice) without fail; may the Goddess (Earth) along with all 
deities be firm and unmoving for me and may (the Goddess) 
drive away from us all evil and pierce my enemies that hate 
me.” After having offered oblations with the words ‘ svahd to 
the earth’ he should offer oblations with the verses Atharva VI, 
87. 1, VI 88.1 and with the verses of the anuvitka beginning 


with Atharva XI, 1,1. This is the prayascitti there (in case 
of an earthquake ).

Meamng of adbhuta, utpata and nimitla edt 


“what will happen in future’. Yaska paraphrases ‘adbhuta’ by 
the word ‘abhita’ (that has not taken place) and remarks that 
पष word ‘adbhuta’ in popular speech also means ‘something 
that has nob happened before’. Re. L 25. 11%! says ‘the 
intelligent man expects from ghis (Varuna) all wonders (or 
portentous happenings ), whether already performed or to be 
performed’. Reg. 3. 105. 7 is perhaps a little clearer than the 
preceding. ‘(May Indra reduce our sins) Indra who is golden- 
bearded, who has tawny horses, whose jaw is never broken and 
“who made against the dasyw for easily killing him a thunder- 
bolt like the sky that is wonderful (or full of portents)’. The 

word usually employed in the Grhyastitras is adbhuta and the 
dantig are called ‘ adbhutasantis’. Adbhuta is a word of very 
general import. It includes not only such serious phenomena as 
earth-quakes, eclipses, comets, falling sbars but such compara- 
tively minor yet unexpected or unusual happenings as a cow 
yielding blood-red milk or a cow sucking the udder of another 
cow. The ancient writer Vrddha-Garga defines ‘adbhuta’ as 
any eccurrence that had not occurred before or 2 total change 

_soming over what has occurred before1!® The 67th Atharvana- 
paridista is called Adbhutesanti (pp. 432-485). It distributes 
‘adbhutas’ into seven groups relating to Indra, Varuna, Yama, 
Agni, Kubera, Visou and Vayu and names some adbhutas under 
each such as 2 rainbow at night (relating to Indra), a vulture or 
owl alighting on 9 man’s house or 2 kapota entering it (relating 
to Yama), smoke without fire (relating to Agni), eclipse on the 
naksatra of a man’s birth (relating to Visnu) and prescribes as 
santi the gape of Atharvasiras, making brahmanas say ‘svasti, 
honouring and feeding brahmanas. That parisista is based on 
the Adbhutabrahmana of the Simaveda.

Classification of Utpitas "45 


uttered in the same breath with eclipses. But Garga, 1189 
Paragara, Sabha-parva, Brhatsamhits 45. 2, Matsyapurana 225.5, 
Atharva-parisista LELX (1.2) and other works divide utpatas 
into three classes, viz. diya (arising from heavenly bodies), 
antariksa (springing in the sky or atmospheric region and 
bhauma (that appear on the earth). This classification is ancient 
enough. The Atharvaveda™ expressly refers to the three 
classes of uipatas ‘May the earthly and atmospheric utpatas and 
the planets moving in heaven confer welfare on us’. The 
Brhatsamhita™! says that it isthe king’s business to arrange 
for santis in his kingdom for counteracting (fhe consequences 
of portents). Garga’* declared that those who, when advised 
by brahmanas for performing Sautis, perform auspicious rites 
with faith do not suffer defeat, but that those who having no 
faith or because of atheism or reseniment do not perform rites 
for counteracting (omens) perish in a short time. Garga, the 
Brhatsamhita, Matsya 229. 6~9, Agni 268. 12-13 furnish 
examples of the threa kinds of utpatas, viz, the divya ones are 
concerned with the abnormal conditions of planets and naksatras, 
eclipses, comets: those of atmospheric regions are hurricanes, 
unusual clouds, fall of meteors, twilights, preternatural reddish 
appearances of the quarters, halo, Fata Morgana (appearance of 
illugory town in the air), rainbow and strange rainfall (such as

Individual Santis 


It is now time to turn to indrvidual sintis, mostly post-vedic, 

The first is Vinayaka-santi or Ganapatipija. This 1s performed 
atthe commencement of all samskiras such as «panayana and 
marriage in order that the fruit thereof may be had without obsta- 
-olesorfor averting the evil effects of portents or in order to mitigate 
the adverse effects of the death of a sapinda or the like. When 
it is performed for its own sake 1 should be performed on the 
4th tithi of the bright half, on Thursday and the auspicious 
naksatras Pusya, Sravana, Uttara, Rohini, Hasta, Aévini, Mrga- 
Sirsa, but when performed at the commencement of Upanayans 
or the like, one may, perform it at a time suited to the time of 
the principal rite, The उपपद्य is given below.™% In H. of 
Dh. vol. I pp 213-216 it has baan shown how in the earliest 
stages represented by the Manava-grhya and Baijavape-grhya 
which speak of four Vinayakas, all were evil spirits, how in the 
next stage represented by the Yapiiavallcyasmrti (I, 271-294). 
Viniyaka is not only represented as causing obstacles ( Vighna- 
krt) but also as bringing success in all actions and rites 
(Vighnabrt) and how later on it was prescribed that Ganapati- 
pia must be done first in all rites (Gobhila I-13). Ya, 1, 298 
provides”? that by worshipping Vinayaka in the way pres- 
eribed and also the planets, a person secures success in his 
undertakings and the highest prosperity, The Visnudharmottara 
II, 105. 2-24 borrows the verses of Yay. 1, 271-292, though not 
in the same order and adds a few. The Brahmanda provides™®

The number of santis is legion. They are prescribed for 
Conjuring away the effects of rare natural phenomena such as 
eclipses, earth-quakes, rainfall ( of peculiar kinds, of blood &c. } 
hurricanes, fall of meteors, comets, halos, Fata Morgana; for 
protection against the evil offects of the positions and movements 
of planets and stars for the world and for individuals; for strange 
births among human bemga and animals; for the good of horses 
and elephants; for certain untoward happenings about Indra’s 
banner and about images of gods falling or weeping, the 
eries of birds and beasts, the fall of Hzards and the like ona 


person’s limbs and on certain stated periods or on solemn 
occasions, 


All rites of Santi, Paustika rites and the Mahadanas were 
fo be performed in ordinary fire, since there is no authority to 
prove that they are to be performed in érauta fires or in smarta 
fire. Manu 3. 6Y and Yay, 1. 97 refer only to ceremonies laid down 
in the Grhyastitras, On Yaj, 1, 285-86 the Mitaksara prescribes 


ordinary fire for offerings in Vinayaka-santi. Vide also Santi- 
maytkha p. 4, 


Both Manu वमा and the Visnudharmasitra prescribe that 
homas in which the Sun is the deity worshipped and Santihomas 
should be performed by a householder on the parvans (i.6. on 
Paurnamast and Améavasya). These were Santis at fixed 
periods, Similarly, when a person, male or female, of any caste 
completed sixty years, there was the possibility that he may 
die soon, or that he may lose his mother or father or his wife of 
sons or that various diseases may affect him; for removing this 
danger a éanti is prescribed (and is often performed even now ) 
in order that he may enjoy a long life, be free from all calamities 
and for his complete prosperity. This is called Sastyabdapiirt: 
(completion of sixty years) or Ugrarathaganti12!7

One of the oldest available descriptions of the Ugraratha- 
Santi 1s found 77 the Baudhayanagriyagesa-sitra (V.8.). Tt is 
brief and the main items in it are set out here. It should be 
performed in the month of one’s birth and on the naksatra of 
birth. A ved: as large as a bull's hido should ba made, a jar full 
of water should be placed thereon and on the jar an image of 
Mrtyu (Death ) manufactured with two mskas (i. 6. gold probably 
weighing as much) should be placed in the south-east corner; 
worship should be offered to the image and a japa of each of the 
mantras ‘apaitu mrtyuh’ (‘may Death go away’, Tai. Br, IL 7. 
14 4), ‘param Mrtyo’ (0 Death! follow the path beyond &c,’, 
Tai. Br 11, 7.14.5 and Re. X, 18.1), ‘ma nas-toke’ (O Rudra! 
do not injure our progeny’ &c., Tai. 8. I. 4, 11, 2 and कष्ट. 1 
114 8), and‘ Tryambakam’ (‘we offer sacrifice to Rudra’, Tai. 
§.I 8.6 2and Rg. VIL 59. 12) be made 108 times; he offers 
oblations of cooked food with the puronuvakya (invitatory 
prayer ) ‘ma no mahantam’ (O Rudra! do not destroy our grown 
up ones &c’, Tai S IV 5 10.2 andRg.1114,7) and the Yaya 
(offering prayer) ‘Ma nas-toke’ (Tai. S, IL, 4. 1]. 2and Re. I 114. 
8). Then he makes subsidiary offerings of ghee with each verse of 
the Ghrtastkta #8 Then he sprinkles himself with water from- 
the Jar to the accompaniment of mantras from the Mrtyustkta, 
from the Ayusyasikta and with Paurinika mantras, honours 
the officiating priest, gives daksinag to the brahmanas and 
a dinner.

_ The general rule about the time for Santis is that no definite 
time can be fixed for them, since santi rites are performed with 
the object of removing the evil consequences of men's lapses 
suggested by such indications (or omens) as dreams, the evil 
aspects of planets and the like i. 6. they are to be performed as 
and when omens or portents occur or are observed and one 
should not wait for such times as the northward passage of the 
Sun, bright fortnight and that one may perform sintis even in 
the southward passage of the Sun or even 19 an intercalary

Nirnayasindhu (0, 233) about the question of a rite on the first

prescribed after an elaborate homa and worship and the Maha- 
Santi is explained as consisting of the recitation of Rg J. 8% 
1-10 (beginning with ‘4 no bhadra’), Rg V. 51. 11-15 (beginning 
with ‘svasti no mimitim &c ’) and Rg. VIL 35, 1-15 (begin- 
ning with ‘san-na Indragni’). The Bhavisyottara (143, 2-46) 
describes a Mahasanti to he performed at a king's coronation: 
on his marching out on an invasion, when one has bad dreams 
or inauspicious omens (z:m:ifas), when the planefs are une 
favourable or when there is lightning and the fall of meteors, 
when a Ketu appears, in a hurricane, earthquake, birth on 
a Mila naksatra or Gandanta, on birth of twins, when parasols 
and banners fall on the ground, when a crow, owl or pigeon 
enters a house, when melefic planets are retrograde (especially 
in the naksatra or rasi of birth), when Jupiter, Safurn, 
Mars and the Sun are in the Ist, 4th, 8th or 12th houses 
(in a person’s horoscops), when there is grahayuddha; when 
garments, weapons, horses and cows, or jewels and hair 
are lost, or when rainbow is seen at night in front, when the 
beam on a house pillar is smashed, when a she—mule conceives, 
on eclipses of the Sun and the Moon—on these a Mahasanti 
is commended. The procedure is briefly as follows: Five learned 
and well-conducted brahmanas should officiate in a mandapa 
tan or twelve cubits on each side, in the midst of which there 
should ba a raised platform four cubits on each side and in the 
south-east corner of that platform there should be a Aunda 
(receptacle for fire) Five jars should be placed, four in the four 
intermediate quarters (south-east &c.) and the fifth in the 
middle of the platform and numerous things such as twigs and 
leaves of some plants, jewels, sandalwood, mustard grains, gam 
and durva, kusas and grains of rico should be collected thereon; 
Vedic mantras such as ‘asuh Signo’ (Re. X 103 1) on north- 
wast, ‘184 vasya’ (Vay 8. 40.1) on north-east, were to be recited 
over the jars, worship is to be offered with gandha, flowers, lamps, 
fruits like cocoanut to the jars and fire should be placed in the 
hunda with ‘agnim ditam’ (Rg 1. 12 1), seat (Gsana) should 
be offerred with the mantra ‘hiranya-garbhah’ (Rg X. 121.1 ) 
then payasa should be cooked to the accompaniment of Purusa- 
sukta (Re X. 90), eighteen fuel sticks of इण and seven palasa 
ones should be cast into Agni, seven Ghuts of clarified ghee and 
seven of rice boiled in milk should 78 offered to Agni witha 
mantra ‘Jatavedase’ (Rg I. 99 1), four more with the hymn

‘tarat sa mandi’ (Rg. IX. 58), seven with ‘yamaya’ (Rg. X. 14 
13) and again seven with ‘idam Visnur’ (Reg. 2, 22. 17) and 27 
ahutis to the 2% naksatras, then performance of ‘svistalkrt’ 
home, grahahoma with sesame covered with ghee, then praya- 
geitta; thus ends the homa; then the yajama@na sitting ona

learned in the Veda. On doing this he securas long life, quick 
victory over enemies, even difficult undertakings succeed. 


The huge work Adbhutasigara is mostly concerned with 
tare natural phenomena such as halo, rainbows, hurricanes, 
glowing horizon (d:gdaha), meteors, comets, earthquakes, rain 
without clouds, red rain, shower of fish, Fata Morgama &e. 


A few words must be said about some striking ones out of 
these. First comes earthquake, The Br. S, (32.1-2) puts forth 
four theories of his predecessors about the cause of an earthquake 
viz. ii was caused by huge animals dwelling inside the seas 
(view of Kasyapa ) or according to others (Garga) it was caused 
by the heavy breaths emitted by the elephants of the quarters 
when tired by carrying the weight of the earth: others (like 
Vasistha) said that earthquake noise is caused by the winds 
striking against each ather (in the sky Jand falling on the earth; 
other acaryas (like Vrddhagarga) held that an earthquake was 
caused by adrsta (i, 8. by the sins of the people on the earth 1277), 
Th verses 3-7 of छ, 8. (chap. 32) Varaha narrates the myth 
that mountains had in the dim past wings and the earth being 
much shaken by their movements approached Pitamaha 
(Brahma) and Brahma seeing her sad plight asked Indra to 
discharge his thunderbolt for clipping the wings of mountains 
and for removing the anger (or sorrow) of the earth ; Indra did

It should not be a matter for surprise that ancient and 
medieval Indians regarded earthquakes as punishments sent by 
God for the sins of men. The English poet Cowper gives vent to 
this belief in his poem ‘Timepeace’.1228 The most distinguished 
Indian of modern times viz Mahatma Gandhi, regarded the 
earthquake in Bihar that occurred on January 15, 1934, and 
affected an area of about 30000 square miles and a population 
of about 15 millions and that killed thousands and made 
millions homeless, as God’s punishment for the prevalence of the 
evil system of unfouchability in Hindu’ gocisty. To the 
natural and usual query why God should punish a small country 
or asmall community with frightful earthquakes and overwhelm- 
ing waves when other countries and millions of other people are 
guilty of the same misdeeds, Cowper endeavours to give a reply

in the Ist, 4th, 8th and 12th च्छ from the सदं of birth. The 
view of Garga, was that if an eclipse occurs when the sun or

amavasya, on Vyatipaita-yoga or on Vaidhrti or in an eclipse,

The Aélesa naksatra has a mean measure of 60 ghatis, It 
is to be divided into ten parts in order126* viz, 5, 7%, 2, 3, 4, 
8, 11, 6, 9 and 5; birth of a son in these parts indicates in order 
the loss of kingdom, death of father, death of mother, addiction 
to lovemaking, he has devotion to fathor, has strength, loses pro- 
perty, has proneness to charity, pleasures, wealth, If the naksatra 
be divided into four parts, birth in the first part is auspicious but in 
the other three parts indicates loss of wealth, death of father, death 
of mother. If the child is a girl born on the last three quarters of 
Aslesa indicates the death of the future mother-in-law of the 
girl; if the child be a boy andis born in the last three quarters 
of Aglesi, that indicates death of his future mother-in-law. One 
should perform a santi for birth on any quarter of Aslesa, either 
on the 12th day from birth, or if that be not possible, on the next 
Aélesa or on any auspicious day. On that day he (the father or 
other performer) should make a sankalpa?#?7 as noted below

The birth of a girl after three successive births of boys or of 
aboy after three successive births of girls was supposed to 
indicate unfavourable consequences to the parents and the family 
and death of the eldest, loss of wealth and great sorrow. There- 
fore a Santi was recommended on the 1160 or 12th day from the 
birth of a girl or boy (as the case may be) or on an auspicious day. 
He (the father) should choose acarys (chief officiating priest) and 
other priests, then perform a sacrifice to planets and offer worship 
to the golden images of Brahma, Visnu, Siva and Indra on 
ajar placed on a heap of grains. On a fifth jar he should 
worship Rudra and one brahmana should recite four hymns to 
Rudra eleven times and all Ssantisiktas when homa is being 
performed. The acarya should cast into the fire fuel-sticks, gheo. 
sesame and boiled rica 1005, 108 or 300 times to four deities viz. 
Brahma, Visnu, Mahesa and Indra respectively with the mantras 
‘Brahma jajfianam’ (Tai. 8. IV. 2.8, 2, Vaj. 8. 13.3), ‘idam 
Visour’ (Rg, 1 22.17), ‘Tryamabakam yajamahe’ (Rg. VII. 
59. 12}, ‘Yate Indra bhayamahe’ (Re. VI. 61.13). Then he 
should perform ‘Svistakri’ homa, % then offer bali and 
pirnahu. The family members should be sprinkled with the 
sacred water. The performer should honour the acarya and 
donate some gold and a cow to him and give daksind to the other 
priests, should look into a vessel full of ghee and should make 
the brahmanas recite Santi verses. The images with the addi- 
tions or decorations thereof should be donated to the guru, 
brahmanas, poor and helpless people should be fed according to 
his ability. By doing this ganti all misfortunes are destroyed. 
(Nirnayasindhu p, 248 and Santiratnakara, folio 109 ),

(i) the position of planets and stars, (2) individual horoscopes, 
(3) flight and cries of birds like khafijana and crow, (4) natural 
phenomena (eclipses, meteors &ce ), (5) dreams, (6) voices 
suddenly heard, (7) the physical and mental conditions of men, 
animals &c The first four have already been briefly dealt with. 
Now dreams will be taken up for discussion.

Dharmasindhu on untecky dreams (1) 


The Dharmasindhu (pp. 359-360) collects in one place 
numerous dreams that are lucky or auspicious and that are 
unlucky or inauspicious and then prescribes (p, 861) the rem- 
edies to avert the consequences of unlucky dreams viz worship 
of the Sun with the mantra (Rg IT 28.10, Tai 8, IV. 14-123) 
‘O king Varuna! protect us from the danger which my helper 
or friend declares fo me (fram what I saw) in a dream or from 
the thief or wolf who desires or is about to injure us’; or one 
may recite Inaudibly the verse‘ Adha svapnasya’ (Rg. 1. 120.12) 
or perform a sraddha like fhe one on Amé&ydsy3, or should 
recite the Saptagati in honour of Candi or the thousand names 
of Visnu or recite or listen to the recitation of the Hberation 
of Gajendra in the Bharata or Bhagavata. 


All ancient countries and peoples believed in draams and 
satisfied their curiosity to know the future by interpreting 
them. The Chaldean astrologers and dream-interpreters were in 
high favour at Babylonian and Assyrian courts The Book of 
Daniel (chap 2) tells us how Nebuchadnezzar, a great king of 
Babylon, asked the Chaldeans not only to interpret dreams but 
commanded them on threat of death to make known to him the 
dream which he had forgotten and then to interpret it, Plato, the 
greatest of the Greek philosophers, regards dreams as important 
physical and psychic symptoms while certain dreams ara con- 
caded as of supernatural origin and explains in his Timaous (chap. 
46 and 47) that dreams are prophetic visions received by the 
lower appetitive soul (through the liver ). In JRAS (old series) 
vol. 16 pp. 118-171 N. Bland contributes a long and inter- 
eating article on ‘the Mahomedan science of Tabir or inter- 
pretation of dreams’ There are striking parallels between the 
7188 to be observed by the dreamer and by the interpreter and 


the principles of interpretation (of dreams) by contraries and 


by depandenca upon the religion, country and bodily conditions 
(such as total fast or full stomach) of the dreamer. On p. 141 
of TRAS there is an Interesting account of a dream of Nushirwan 
a Sassanian -king (531-579 A. D. }, who saw a dream that he 
drank , from a golden goblet and that a black hog put its 
head in pe goblet and drank from if. Then we are told 
पाः his minister, whom he consulted, told him it signi. 

ed that his favourite princess had a black slave who was her 
Over and suggested that the women of his harem should be 
द्द to dance undressed in the presence of the king. One of 

hem showing some hesitation in complying and being protected 


by the others was discovered to ba a Hindu male slave and the 


१82 250 of Dharmahistra [ 886. 1, Ch, इदा 


Vazir's interpretation was verified.” The name of the Vazir 
remarkably agrees in sound with fhe name Varahamihira and 
it is not very fantastic to suppose that Varahamihira, probably 
the most famous astrologer and astronomer of early times in 
India, had been patronized by Nushirvan and held a high 
position in his court Chronology is quite in favour of this 
identification since Varahamihira takes gaka 427 (505 A D.} as 
the starting point for finding out the aha? gana. 


In modern’! times many educated people think dreams as 
of no consequence whatever, while there ara others who regard 
dreams as almost infallible indicators of coming events; there is 
also a third class of people who are willing to listen to the argu- 
ments advanced on behalf of the interpreters of dreams and also 
of those who regard thoughts on the use and value of dreams as 
frivolous To those who want to hear arguments on both sides 
and to form a judgment of their own about dreams, I would 
recommend the ‘Fabric of Dreams’ by Catherine Taylor 
Craig (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner, London, 1918 ) ; Freud's 
‘Interpretation of dreams’ is the most important of his works, 
in which he develops his psycho-analytic technique, Then 
there is the work ‘Second sight in daily life’ by W H.W. 
Sabine who has a theory of his own. His work deals with 
precognition (or foreknowledge) which according to him is a sub- 
division of Extra-sensory perception He propounds the theory 
that the mind comprises of not only normal memory appearing to 
derive from physical perception but also ‘anticipatory memory , 
deriving from the Basic Experience which from time to time 
passes to some degree into conscious awareness Time is one and 
0098 not exist except as a verbal convenience and that what wa 
call ‘future’ has already happened but it is not indicated in 
what form it has happened Considerations of space and rele- 
‘vance preclude further discussion of this subject here

provides for Santis for the tithis (from the first onwards) on 
which the fever started, derived from Baudhayana in which the 
presiding deity of each tithi is to be offered worship (puja) and 
homa, for each of which the mantra (of which japa is to be 
made) is different, and the incense, flowers, naivedya also are 
different There are also santis, when a person suffers from 
fever, about the weekday on which the fever started and images 
of the presiding deity of the weekday made of different metals 
according to the name of the day are to ba worshipped with 
different mantras (Madanaratna, folio 123). For example, if 
fever atarted on a Sunday or on a Monday, then the images of 
Rudra (for Sunday ) and Parvati (for Monday ) were to be made 
of gold or silver and the mantras to be recited were respectively 
‘ya te Rudra’ (Tai. S IV. 5.1.1), ‘gaurir-mimaya’ (Rg 1, 164 
41). The gandha, flowers, incense, lamp and nanwedya were

imparted it fo Bhaguri. Most of the above works confine it to 
the king, since the king is the very root of the tree—ths 
“subjects—and since any harm to or welfare of that root (the king) 
results in misfortune or welfare of the people; therefore care 
must be taken for the increase of the king’s welfare As the 
treatment in the Brhatsamhita is the fullest and is among the 
most ancient descriptions, it is briefly set out here. The royal 
astrologer and family priest should perform the rite of Pusya- 
snana for the king, than which there is nothing more holy and 
nothing more destructive of all evil portents, This may be per- 
formed on pusya-naksatra every time, but the Santi on this day 
when the Full Moon is in Pusya-naksatra is the highest and if 
such a sndna is performed without there being Pusya naksatra on 
that day, then it yields only half the fruit. There is no utpata 
which is not averted or mitigated by this sinti and there is 
no other auspicious rite which surpasses this. About Pusya

have followed the Matsya. They all agree that throbbing” of 
the right side of the body is auspicious and of the left inauspi- 
cious in the case of males, while the reverse is true in tho case 
of women. They all set ont fhe consequences indicated by the 
throbbing of the several parts and limbs of the body from the 
top of the head to the soles of the feet. To set out all these in 
detail would occupy much space. A few are mentioned by way 
of illustration. The fruifindicated by the throbbing of the top 
of thea? head is the acquisition of land (or earth), of the 
forehead, the prosperity of the position already occupied; of the 
region between the eyebrows and nose, union with persons dear 
to one; of the region of the eye, death, of the portion near the 
eyo the acquisition of wealth, of the upper arm, union with 
friends; of the hand, the acquisition of wealth; of the back, 
defeat; of the chest, success; of the upper part of the foot, the 
securing of a position; of the soles, journey with gain therein. 
The Matsya-purina ? prescribes that when inauspicious indica- 
tions (by throbbing) occur, brahmanas should be placated with 
the gift of gold,

Throbing of armts and eyes 801 


Kalidasa twice mentions the throbbing of the arm of the hero as 
indicative of good fortune and the throbbing of the right oye of 
Sakuntala as presaging™ misfortune, Shakespeare in “Othello” 
makes Desdemona speak about the itching of her eyes as a bad 
omen, Tho Brhad-yogayatra (दा, 10), Br. 8. (51.10) and 
Vasentaraja declare that the throbbing of moles, boils, marks, 
eruptions (on limbs) are to be deemed to indicate consequences 
similar to the limbs on which they exist2" 


The Brhatsamhita (chap 93 verses 1-14), Brhadyogayatra 
(chap, 21 verses #92 1-21) and Yogayatra (chap. 10 verses 1~75 ) 
dwell at length on the prognostications to be drawn from the 
arrangement of the tusks of elephants, from the marks seen 
when the tusks are cut, from the tired appearance and move- 
ments of elephants, particularly when the king is to march on 
an invasion, since as the Yogayatra says the king’s victory 
depends on elephants.3 These, however, do 20 describe any 
Santi and ara hence passed over here as not relevant to the 
subject of Santis. But the Agnipurana (chap. 291 verses 1-24 ) 
Visnudharmottara (IL 50. 1-98), Baud. grhyaéesasitra I 20 and 
Hemadri (on Vrata, vol. I. pp. 1086-1051) prescribe gantis for 
removing diseases of elephants and therefore a brief note is 
added here from Baud. grhyasesa-siitra, which is probably the 
earliest and simplest description of a Gajaganti.

The Gajasanti in Agnipurana (chap, 291) is entirely differ- 
ent from the above. One should worship on the 5th tithi of the 
bright half Visnu, Laksmi, the Airavata's elephant and the other 
slephants (in all eight) and Brahma, Sankara, Indra, Kubera, 
Yama, the Sun and the Moon, Varuna, Vayu, Agni, the Earth 
and Akasa, The elephants should be sprinkled with éantyudaka 
(propitiatory water). The Agnipurana proposes an elaborate 
worship, on a lotus-shaped diagram drawn on an altar, of several 
gods, several weapons, sages, rivers and mountains &c., elephants 
&c, and provides that an astrologer should ride the principal 
slephant of the king and say into its ear ‘ you are made the 
chief of elephants, the king will honour you with gandha, flowers, 
best food and people at the order of the king will honour you; 
you should protect the king in battle, in his journey and in his 
palace, You should forget that you are a mere beast and revolve 
in your mind that you are divine!’ &c. The king should then 
tide such an elephant and armed warriors should follow and 


various gifts should be made to the elephant keeper, the astrol 
oger, the dcarya &c,

A noticeable feature of Vasantaraja’s work is that mora 
than half of it (781 verses) is devoted to the sounds’#!? made by 
threo birds viz. Syama (400 verses ), crow (187) Pingalika (200) 
and that 312 verses are devoted to the barking, movements and 
howling of dogs (verses 222) and fomale jackals (verses 90), 
Tt is romarkable that among the Saktas it is believed that a 
fomale jackal is a messenger of Kali and is auspicious and on 
hearing its howl in the early morning a person should offer 
salutation and then success is in the hands of the sadhaka. The 
brief contents set out above will show that ho extends the 
meaning of Sakuna so as to include prognostications based on 
the actions of men and beasts, He himself says at the end 
that is gakuna, which in this world is remembered, heard, 
touched or seen or which is declared in dreams, since they all 
yield results. He claims that the system of gakurfas is as 
authoritative as the Vedas, smrtis and puranas, since it never 
fails to convey correct knowledge.444 Some of his interesting 
statements may be briefly set out. If an owl hoot at night on 
the top of a house that portends#5 sorrow and the death of the 
owner's son (VIIL 40). This is in line with modern popular 
belief in India, The cawing of crows is at the head of all 
prognosticatory sounds ‘The barking of dogs is the essence 
among all éekunas. The Brhad-yogayatra™*® provides that

A pecular mode akin to ‘upagruti’ is described in the

Puranas (montioned in verses 51-53) may be employed as 
containing prognosticatory words. The procedure is that a 
maiden more than five years of age and less than ten years or 
any girl who has not attained puberty may be honoured with 
gandha, flowers, incense and other upacaras, she should be made 
fo recite the words ‘speak the truth, speak what is agreeable, 
O blessed Sarasvati'! salutation to you, salutation to you!’ She 
should be given three pairs of dirvaé grass and she should be 
asked fo cast them between two leaves of the book. The varse 
between two leaves would be indicative of success in the under- 
taking. The verse should be carefully considered and its meaning 
sattled and applied to the matter in hand, This is like sortes 
Sanctorum or sortes Vergilianae 2, 8. divination by opening at 
tandom the Scriptures or a book of Virgil or by pricking the 
text with a pin. Thon directions are given as to what should be 
done if the leaves are half burnt or indistinct &c. and it is said 
that one should look upon the verse as sent by fate like the 
words in the upaéruti method12 It is further stated that this 
method should not be resorged to avery day, but rarely and that 
then one should worship the Purana the previous night and in

SECTION IV 
THE PURANAS AND DHARMASASTRA 
CHAPTER XXII 


Origin and development of Purana literature 


The History of Dharmaéastra (vol. I pp. 160-167) has a 
brief chapter on the Puranas. It has been shown therein how 
the Taittirlya Aranyaka, the Chandogya and Brhadadranyaka 
Upanisads mention Itihasa and Purana ( sometimes collectively 
as ‘Itihdsapurdnam' and sometimes separately aa ‘ Itihasah 
Puranam’) and how some of the extant Puranas are much 
earlier than the 6th century AD. It is further pointed out there 
that the number of the principal Purinas has been traditionally 
handed down as eighteen,=% that some puranas such as the 
Matsya, the Visnu, the Vayu and Bhavisya contain much Dharma- 
‘astra material, that the Garuda-purdna and the Agnipurana 
contain several hundred verses each that are identical with verses 
of the Yajfiavalkya smrti, that there is great divergence as to the 
extent of almost all Puranas, that some of the Puranas them- 
selves enumerate minor works called Upapuranas, that the 
Puranas are divided into three groups, viz. sitévika, rdjasa 
and t@masa (as done by Garuda I. 228. 17-20, and Padma 
VI. 263. 81-84). Details were also furnished as to the chapters 
of the Puranas in which the several topics of Dharmaddstra ( such 
a8 GeGra, Ghmka, dana, rajadharma, & Gddha, tirtha) were 
dealt with. 

In the present section it is proposed to trace the great trans- 
formation that took place in the ideas, ideals and practices of the 


ancient Tndian people owing to the influence of the Puranas 
in the first few centuries of the Christian era,

Kumiarilabhatta in his Tantravartika refers in several 
places to the Puranas and their contents. A few interesting 
passages are set out here: On Jaimini I. 3.1 Kumarila says 1344 
“Therefore the authoritativeness of all smrtis is established by 
the purpose which they serve; whatever therein (in smrtis) is 
connected with dharma and moksa (is authoritative), because 
it springs from (is based on ) the Veda; whatever concerns 
wealth (artha) and pleasures is based on the usages of the 
people. In this way ॐ distinction is to be made. This very 
reasoning applies to horfafory passages in the Itihdsa and 
Puranas, The Upakhyanas may be explained by the reasoning 
applicable to arthavadas (1. 6 they have a purpose and authorita- 
tiveness just like the commendatory passages of the Veda). 
Narration of the divisions of the earth serves the purpose of 
distinguishing the regions for undergoing the consequences of 
the (actions that are the) means of dharma and adharma and 
are partly based on personal experience and partly on the Veda. 
The orderly presentation of vaméas ( dynasties) in the Puranas 
is intended to facilitate the knowledge of the brahmana and 
ksatriya castes and their gotras and is based on actual experi- 
ence and traditional knowledge ; countries and measures of time 
are intended to facilitate worldly transactions and astronomical 
needs and are based on actual perception, mathematics, tradition 
and inference. The narration of what will happen in the future 
is based on the Veda, since it conveys knowledge of the variety 
of the ripening of the consequences of (complying with) dharma 
and of adkharma and knowledge of the characteristics of yugas 
that have been in operation from time immemorial.’ It is 
clear from this passage that the Itihdsa and the Puranas that 
Kumirila knew contained stories, geography of the earth, 
dynastic lists, measures of time and description of what will 
happen in the future. These are matters dealt with in the 
extant Puranas, On JaiminiI 3.7 Kumarila observes: ‘In the

The question about the Puranas is further complicated by 
the fact that some of the Puranas themselves mention the names 
of a number of Upapuranas, though others ignore them. For 
example, the Matsya (53. 59-62) names the Narasimha, the

purina, The Kirma ( 7. 1. 16-20 ), Padma (IV. 111, 95-98 ), the 
Devibhagavata (1. 3, 18-16 ) set out the names of eighteen 
Upapurinas. Some of the Upapurdnas bear the same names as

and Naradiya. Prof. Hazra%58 states that the number of Upa-

The Puranas may be classified into several categories, viz. 
(1) encyclopasdic like the Agni, Garuda and Naradiya, (2) 
those mainly dealing with tirthas such as Padma, Skanda and 
Bhavisya, (3) sectarian, such as Linga, Vamana, Markandeya, 
(4) Historical such as Vayu and Brahmanda The Vayu, 
Brahmanda, Matsya and Visnu are probably the oldest among 
extant Puranas, though they too have received substantial 
additions from time to time.

Some remarks on the important conclusions of Pargiter and 
Kirfel are necessary. Pargiter tries to construct history from 
the earliest times to the Bharata war which he holds to have 
taken place about 950 ए, 0. (ATHT, chap. 15 p 182). He 
holds that there were two traditions in ancient India, viz. the 
Ksatriya tradition and the Brahmana, tradition (AIHT, chap. 5 
DD. 58~77). He harps dozens of times on the utter lack of the 
historic senso among the brahmanas in his work (AITHT'), holds 
that the Puranas represent the ksatriya tradition, that there 
were three racial stocks, viz. the Manavas (or Manvas as he 
styles them ), the Ailas and the Saudyumnas, that respectively 
represent the Dravidian, the Aryan and Munda (AIHT chap. 25 
DD. 289-302), that the Puranas are Sanskritizations of works 
in Prakrit (pp. K-XI )of ‘Dynasties of the Kali age’. His 
date for the Mahabharata war has not been accepted by later 
scholars, since his handling of that subject is not judicial, 
objective or straightforward, एप relies too much on his own 
Prejudices and on averages. In his ‘Puraéna texts of the 
dynasties of the Kali age (pp. 58, 74) he appears to favour the 
View that the Bharata war was fought 1050 years before the 
Nandas i.e. about 1475 B,C. The mss. and the printed Puranas

with Pauranika statements and brush them aside as practically 
worthless, Prof. Pradhan takes the kings actually named in the 
three lines, holds that 28 years are the average reign period of 
each and multiplying the number of kings by 28 arrives at the 
conclusion that the Mahabharata war was fought about 1150 B.C, 
Zé is not possible to deal at length with his arguments. 
Buthe ignores the express words of the Puranas that they enu-

scholars like Pargiter who regard 17 or 18 years as the average

the time when the Puranas wero narrated, Then the same 
Purinas (Vayu 99.30, Matsya 271.23 and Brahmanda IIL. 74, 
113) state that in the lime of Jardsandha (ruler of Magadha), 
who was a contemporary of the Pandavas and whose son

was 7th in descent from Sahadeva Those three are described as 
vartamdna kings in the Purinas and all those that came after 
these three are desertbed as bhau:sya. Pargiter first (ATHT 
p. 180) takes the total of the kings of the three dynasties: 
Aiksvika, Paurava and Magadha that are actually named 
(ignoring what the Puranas say viz. that only the principal or 
important kings are named and not all) and the total of the re- 
igns of all these (1408 years), finds that the average of the reign 
of each king in the three lines works out at such large figures a3 
47,50, 31, which he regards as impossible when tested by real 
historical averages But he forgets that the Puranas say that in 
the Aiksvaka, Magadha and Paurava lines and also generally 
only the prominent kings are mentioned and also that the 
extant Puranas ara only fragments left of the originals, since in 
the Brahmanda (ITI, 74) all Paurava and Aiksvika kings are 
altogether lost. ‘Then he takes the total number of kings in ten 
kingdoms up to Mahapadma and arrives at the average of 26 
kings for each kingdom (AIHT 9 181). ‘Then he says that the 
average of fourteen series of kings in Eastern and Western 
countries which he examined comes to 19 years for each reign 
and, holding that the average in eastern countries is less than 
in western countries, he arrives at the average of 18 years for 
each reign (pp. 181-182), which he regards as fair and rather 
liberal. Ho then multiplies the average 18 (of length of reigns) 
by 26 (the average number of kings in ten countries which he 
supposes to be the only kings in those ten) and arrives ati the 
figure 468 years. He adds these to the date which he assigus 
to Mahapadma Nanda 382 B, ¢, and thus arrives at 850 B. ¢, as 
the mean date of the beginning of the reign of AdhisImakrsna, 
Divakara and Senayit, who were .artamina kings. Then be 
takes five as the average of the kings between the vartamana 
kings and Yudhisthira and assigning about 100 years to ५० 
5 kings, arrives at the date 950 B,C, for the Bharata war.

or 6th century A. D. to the 9th cenfury A.D. This represents

The question why the extant Purdnas do nob narrate the 
traditions about the dynasties of the Guptag and their successors 
cannot be satisfactorily answered. One reason may be ४086 the 
original kernel of some Puranas like the extant Matsya were 
compiled before the Guptas rose to power, while others like the 
Vayu and Brahmanda wera compiled while the Gupta rule was 
in its infancy, Another reason may have 09911. that in the 5th 
and following centuries when many of the extant Puranas were 
compiled northern India was very much disburbed by the 
invasions of foreigners like the Hiinas, 158 Toramana and 
Mihirakula, numerous sects and schisms had arisen, Buddhism 
had become powerful and therefore the first task of the intelligent 
and deyout followers of the Veda was held to be fo wean the 
common people away from schisms like that of Buddha, to lay 
down the foundations of a new ideology among the masses and 
toemphasize and assimilate as many of the doctrines of the 
sects and schisms as possible with their ancient traditions 
and practices. Ths intelligent classes, therefore, emphasized 
the importance of such virtues as ahims’, satya, bhakti and of 
vratas, pilgrimages, sriddhas and danas and were probably not 
in a mood to record the names of foreign conquerors or of small 
chieftains fighting with each other and unable fo repel the 
cruel invaders. For the absence of references to the dynasties 
of the Guptas and their successors, Pargiter blames the 
brahmanas in the following characteristic passage (AIHT 
chap. + p.57) ‘the abzolute dearth of traditional history after 
that stage is quite intelligible, both because the compilation of 
the Purana hed set a seal of tradition and because the Purana 
soon passed into the hands of brdhmanas who preserved what 
they had received, buf with tho brahmanic lack of the historic 
sense, added nothing about the later kings’. Supposing for 
argumant that brdhmanas lacked the historic sense, Pargiter’s 
opinion appears to be entirely one-sided, He assigns no reason

of the most plausible is now put forth. The Mahabharata and the

How Vyasa was prociamed as Veda-arranger 861 


The easiest way was to proclaim that Vyasa, the author of the 
great Epic and of the distribution of Puranas into eighteen, was 
also responsible for the division or arrangement of the Veda. 
If all this glorification of Vyasa occurred in the centuries 
immediately precading and following Christ, how could the 
supposed arranger of the Veda be mentioned in the early Vedic 
Literature, which, most scholars agree, was closed some centuries 
before Buddha (ie before the 6th century B.C.)? No body 
claims that the arrangement info mandalas or astakas or kandas 
is eternal. lt 18 only the hymna or mantras that are claimed 
to be eternal. Even the padapatha of the Reveda is declared 
to be non-eternal and is ascrihed to Sakalya whom the Nirukta 
criticises in VI, 28, Visvartipa on Yaj III 242 expressly states 
that the pada and iiama arrangements of the Veda are dus to 
human authors,.8% This theory explains all matters and has 
far better claims to be accepted than Pargiter's bold ascription 
of fraudulent suppression inferred from (a supposed) silence,

Samba between 500 and 800 A. D. (2. 91), the Visnudharma- 
puraina between 200-300 A. D, (p. 143), the Visnudharmottara- 
purana between 400 to 500 A. 9, (ए, 212) and the present 
Narasimha~purina between 400 to 500 A.D. To examina all 
his reasong the present writer would have to write another book. 
Therefore, he proposes to give only a few illustrations of the 
way in which Dr. Hazra arrives at his dates. But beforo this 18 
done 16 is better to mention some of his own findings on the 
Puranas and the four Upapurinas mentioned above. On p. 37 
he observes that the text of the extant Mahipuranas which are 
the results of innumerable changes, modifications and interpols- 
tions mada 26 different times and by different sects is scarcely 
vehable and can be used with great caution and careful 
discrimination. I agree with him. But the game or perhaps worse 
is the case with the Upapurinas. Prof. Hazra himself says 
(‘Studies’ vol. I. p. 23) that after the group of 18 principal 
Puranas had been compiled many sub systems and sects like the 
Saktas and Sauras came into prominence and their adherents 
interpolated chapters in the 18 established Puranas and wrote 
new and independent works styled Puranas in order to propagate 
their own ideas and that some of these latter came to be called 
Upapuranas, The result 1s that, unless wo have critical editions of 
the Puranas and the principal Upapurinas on the model of the 
critical edition of the Mahabharata at the BORI in Poona, all 
chapters and often single verses are suspect, But the task of 
preparing critical editions of even the principal Puranas and 
some of the Upapuranas based upon ancient and medieval mss. 
collected from all parts of India would be far more colossal and 
costly than even the orttical edition of the Mahabharata. 
Therefore, most chronological conclusions about the dates of 
Puranas and Upapuranas and about the borrowings of one 
Purana from another are just tentative at the most and likely 
to be set aside by new evidence as long as critical editions of 
Puranas and Upapuranas are 2100 available.

about Upapuranas are certain, viz that Samba is mentioned

no reliable evidence to hold that the remaining portion of the 
Samba is earlier than 800 A.D or even earlier than 950 A. D.

three sections. The first deals with geography, solar and lunar 
dynasties, astronomy and astrology, gotra and pravara, Sriddhas, 
Manvantaras, Bharata’s fight with Gandharvas and Satrughna’s 
with Lavana, The 2ndsection deals with various aspects of Raja- 
dharma and the third section of the Purana daals with Citrasgutra- 
vidhana and contains several topics such as painting, dancing, 
musio, song, rasas, riddles, dramaturgy, metricg, figures of speech, 
construction of images, building of temples, symptoms of 
approaching death, gifts of various kinds, law and justice, hermits 
and sannyasins. On p. 212 Dr. Hazra places this Purana bet- 
ween 400-500 A.D. Reasons of limitations of space preclude 
any detailed criticism of Prof Hazra’s treatment. In IIT. 351.54 
Buddha is mentioned as an avatira which Prof Hazra says is

So much space had to be devoted to an examination of Prof. 
Hazra’s work on the Upapurdinas for cogent reasons. His 1s 
the latest and most elaborate treatment of Puranas and parti- 
cularly of Upapurainas, on which he has bastowed immense 
labour. His opinions, particularly about the dates of the 
Upapuranas, are likely to be taken as the last word on the 
subject and even his unfounded surmises are likely to be taken 
as well-established conclusions. Modern Sanskrit scholars have 
sad experience about such matters. Max Muller, working back 
from the date of Buddha and assigning arbitrarily two hundred 
years each for three periods viz. the Upanisad period, the 
Brahmana period and the Samhita period, inferred that the 
composition of the Vedas was to be assigned to a period about 
1200 B 0. He no doubt said that his perlods were the 
minimum and that his was a pure surmise. Yet most writers 
who have not themselves made a deep study of the Veda assign 
the Vedas to about 1200 to 1400 B ©, even after the lapse of 
about one hundred years from the time when Max Muller 
launched his surmises, For example, Prof. Toynbes in the table 
of the time spans of the growth phases of civilizations on p. 758 
of volume IX (1954) gives the dates of Epiphany and of 
breakdown of the Indic civilization as 1375 B,C, and 725 B.C. - 
respectively, The present author does not at all agree with the 
dates assigned to the Upapuranas by Prof Hazra and with the 
methods and reasoning adopted for arriving at those dates. He 
had to perform this painful duty even in spite of his regard 
for Prof, Hazra.

probably composed near the rise of the Godavari, since if says 
that that part of the country towards the northern ranges of the

the manvantaras, pupils of Vyasa, the distribution of the Veda 
Sakhas &c, The third section is the longest and after mentioning 
Vaivasvata Manvantara and, after dilating upon the creation of 
gods, asuras, gandharvas, sages and their progeny, is deals at 
length with all aspects of Sraddha (in chap. 9-20 and 879 verses ), 
describes Parasurama’s austerities, his securing of weapons, his 
slaughter of Kartavirya and ksatriyas, filling five lakes with their 
blood (in chap. 21-47 and over 1550 verses): then follow in 
chapters 48-57 the story of Sagara and the bringing down of the 
Ganges by Bhagtratha, the protection of Gokarna from the sea, 
and the story of Stirparaka (chap. 57 and 58), the dynasties of the 
solar and lunar race (chap. 59ff ); then it speaks of Dhanvantari 
receiving from Bharadvaja Ayurveda in eight angas; in part IV. 
it refers to Manus, jiiana, karma, mokea &c.

Vayupurana (Anandagrame ed.), This has 112 chapters 
and 10991 verses. It appears to have been divided like the 
Brahmanda into four pidas, Prakriya (chap. 1-6), Anusanga 
(chap. 7-64), Upodghata (65-99) and Upasamhara (100-112) 
In the first chap, the first versa is the famous one ‘Narayanam 
namaskriya’ andthe 2nd esulogises Vyasa (both these are not 
found in several mss). The third verse refers to bhakts for 
Siva, Chap 104 is not found in many mss and the chapters at 
the end on Gayamahaimya are deemed to be later additions by 
some scholars. There is Saiva bias in several chapters such as 
chap 20. 31-35 (with a prose passage containing Vedic texts), 
24, 91-165 (called Sarvastotra), chap. 55 (Sivastuti put in the 
mouth of Visnu), chap. 101. 215-330. Probably to counter- 
balance this the chapters on Gay& were added and also tha 
praise of Visnu in chap. 98 where Dattatreya, Vyasa, Kalkin are 
said io be avataras of Visnu, but Buddha is not mentioned. 
Chapter 99 is the longest one in the Purana, contains 464 verses 
and is full of legendary material and historical references. 
There are several verses in the Purana that appear also in the 
Mahabharata, Manu and Matsya. For its relation to Brahmanda 
vide pp. 852, 896 above. This Purana, like the Matsya, contains 
much Dharmasgastra material. It is one of the oldest and most 
authoritative Puranas, though it contains some later additions,

Visnupurana 909 


The date of the Visnupurana is a difficult question. There 
is no doubt that it is one of the early Puranas and that its text 
is not very much inflated. Hundreds of verses quoted in the 
three early digests viz. Kalpataru, Apararke, and Smrticandrika 
can be traced in the current text and this leads to the inference 
that the text has remained fixed for at least a thousand years, 
One important fact is that in this Purana Vyasa and the Sita 
do not play a prominent part as in many other Puranas. It 
states as some other Puranas do, that Vyasa had four pupils fo 
whom he imparted the four Vedas and a fifth pupil the Sita 
Romaharsana (IIL chapters 3-7). But the stita does not appear 
anywhere as the narrator of this Purana. In the 4th amsa one 
remarkable matter is the mention of Sakya, Suddhodana and 
Rahula and it is stated that Suddhodana was 23rd in descent 
from Brhad-bala of the Iksvaku line (chap. 22). The possibility 
of interpolations, particularly in the prose passages, would have 
to be admitted. Raéis are referred to in III. 14. 5 (rasisvarke ca 
gacchati) and the words lagna and hora also appear (in a prose 
passage). Vacaspati in his commentary on the Yogabhasya 
2, 32 quotes it by name on yamas and mamas (Visnu VI. 7. 
36-38) anda half verse ‘evam bhadrasanadindm’ etc, Visnu 
Vi. 7, 49 in com. on Yogabhasya IU, 49. Vacaspati wrote his 
Nydyasiicinibandha in vatsara 888 which should be taken as 
Vikvama year as he was a northerner and as the word ‘vatsara’ 
is used (and not saka) i.e. 841 A. D, 


The following may be read on this question. Wilson's Intro, 
to the translation of the Visnu, vol. I. pp. LIX-LXXII ; त. 
‘date of Visnupurana’ in ABORT vol. 18 pp. 265-275 and PRHR 
pp. 19-26 (puts if between 100-350 A. D.); Prof. Dikshitar in 
Pro, of the 13th Indian History Congress pp. 46-50; Jos. Abs in 
Festgabe Jacobi pp. 386-396 (on heterodox systems mentioned 
in different Puranas including the Visnu). Vide above p. 869 
fora Visnupurana of 23000 verses not utilized by the Danasagara. 


It would not be far from the truth to hold that the present Visnu 
was composed between 300 to 500 A. D.

SECTION V 
CHAPTER XXIV 
Influence of Puranas on Dharmagastra 


Literary works and society act and re-act on each other, 
The state of Indian society a few centuries before and after 
Christ, riven as it was by the growing strength and onslaught of 
Buddhism, Jainism and other dissenting seots and disturbed by 
invasions of the Greeks, Sakas, Pahlavas, Hiinas and other 
foreign tribes, gave much food for thought to those who were 
devoted to the Vedic religion and induced them to write works 
setting forth now ideologies and practices and effecting a re- 
statement of the ancient Vedic and Smrti religion. When these 
works attained a position of authority and eminence, the endea- 
vour of the followers of tha Veda was to follow them as far as 
possible and to adapk their practices and religious rites to the 
requirements of the Puranas. We have to see how the Puranas 
sot about their task of re-orientation. We must note that current 
Hindu religious practices, judging from the sankalpa made at 
the heginning of every rita, are meant to confer upon the per- 
former the rewards declared by Sruti (Veda), Smrti and Puranas 
(Sruti-smrti-puranokta-phalapraptyartham ). The task was two- 
fold, viz. (1) to undermine the power and prestige of Buddhism 
and Jainism and the influence of the numerous philosophical?” 
schools that had sprung up and (2) to wean away large sections 
of the masses from the attractive features of Buddhism and to 
convince them that they could secure in the re-orientated Hindu 
faith the same benefits, social and spiritual, as Buddhism 
promised and that the religious principles of the followers of 
Veda coincided with many of the teachings of Buddhism and 
were borrowed by Buddhism from Vedic practices. Ultimately 
Buddhism vanished from the Jand of its origin. The main 
causes of this disappearance of Buddhism from Bharata will be 
stated at the end of this section, but this much may be said 
here at once that the Purdnas played a substantial role in bring-

several passages of the Upanisads austerities, liberality, straight-

to or superior to the actual performance of the ceremonial of 
sacrifice (yajna), vide Chandogya III. 17. 4, Pragna I, 15, 
Mundaka I. 2. 11. 


Though in a few passages of the Upanisads the knowledge 
of the Highest Self 1s put higher than the four Vedas, the Upa- 
nisads generally treat the Vedas as authoritative and quote 
Vedic verses in support of their statements. For example, the 
Ait. Up. II. 5 quotes Reveda IV, 27. 1 (taduktam-rsind-Garbhe 
nu &c,), Pragnop. I, 11 quotes Rg. I. 164. 12 ( paficapidam 
pitaram ), Br, Up. II. 5.15,17 and 19 quote respectively Reg. 1. 
116, 12, I. 117. 22, VI. 47 18 (rapam ripam pratiripo). The 
Upanisads further emphasize? that brahmavidya is to be 
imparted only to those who are sroir:ya (who have studied the 
Veda), who engage in their duties and who have properly per- 
formed Sirovrata. The 27.468 Up, shows that Veda study, 
sacrifices, charity &c. are preparations for the knowledge of 
brahma: ‘ Brahmanas (and others) desire to know this (great 
Self) by study of the Veda, by sacrifices, gifts, tapas, fasting’, 
These passages make it clear that study of the Veda and per- 
formance of sacrifices enjoined by it are accepted by the Upa- 
nisads as preparatory and as cleansing the mind of its lowet 
passions and as making a person worthy of receiving the know-

ig not accepted for women, sidras and brahmanas in name only 
and Puranas are compiled for the purpose of benefitting them’. 
From this it follows that in the case of stidras the listening to 
the Bharata was deemed fo bring about the same results that 
the Veda does for dujas and that even the Sidra may acquire 
the knowledge of the Self (and moksa) from the Bharata, 


Though the brahmanas in the 5th and following centuries 
A.D wanted to placate the Siidras who were probably a majority 
of the whole people and to wean them away from Buddhism, they 
still kept a distinction between दणड and sidras and the only 
concessions made were that the stidras could worship in the 
same way as dvijas did and that they could have mantras 
(Pauranika) in their rites and caremonies, For oxample, in 
allowing bhasma-sn@na (smeaiing ashes on the body ) the Padma 
(IV, 110. 286-289 ) provides Vedic mantras for men of the three 
varnas buf Pauranika, mantras only (Padma IV. 110. 290-293) 
for gidras. The Padma further provides that stidras could 
not perform pranayama, or utter the sacred syllable ‘om’ but that 
they should substitute dhyana in place of pranayama and ‘Siva 
in place of ‘om’.

or Paficaratras and (on p 15) he says the same about the con- 
secration of temples,47! images and the like

matter of fact we find that some Puranas like Agni, Matsya, 
Visnudharmottara are encyclopaedia and include treatises on 
politics and government, on law, medicine, astronomy, astro- 
logy, poetry, music, sculpture &c. They illustrate India’s life and 
character 28 a country and exemplify Bharata’s achievements, 
weaknesses and shortcomings. Two questions that arise are: 
(1) could the Puranas including the Vedic mantras quoted 
therein be read by the siidras themselves; (2) supposing that 
‘Vedic mantras equld not be read by the sidras, could they, if 
they wera able to do so, by themselves read the puranas without 
& brahmana's help, All writers of digests and commentaries 
were agread that Sidras could not read or listen to the Vedic 
mantras contained in the Puranas (which being meant for the 
benefit of all varnas contained Vedic mantras also), but only 
those that belonged fo the three upper classes, Some writers, 
however, were agreeable to Sadras reciting Pauranike mantras in 
religious rites, relying on a passage of the Padmapurana. But 
others like Kamalakarabhatia, author of the Nirnayasindhu and 
Stdrakamalakara, held relying on verses of the Bhavisya that 
Pauranika mantras alone were to be used by a brahmana in a 
religious rite for a siidra, that the Stidra was only to listen to the 
reading of a purana by 2 brahmana reader. There was a third 
view held by Sridatta and others that a Sidra could recite a 
paurénika mantra, but he should not himself read the Puranas 
aud should only listen to the reading of Puranas by a brahmana, 
In the times of the Dharmastiiras the only mantras employed 
were mostly Vedic and therefore in the case of sidras 
Gautama '477 provided that the sidras were allowed the alter- 
native of saying ‘namah’ in place of a Vedic mantra. In the 
centuries preceding Christ the siidras would naturally have been 
attracted to Buddha's teaching as it was addressed fo all 
including sgidras Comparatively early orthodox writers like

The relation of Sruti, Smrti and Puranas and their spheres of 
application are summed up in the Naradiyapurana as follows:— 
“The Veda exists In different forms; there is tha Veda which 
has the performances of sacrificial rites (as its sphere); smrtis ara 
the Veda for the householder’s staga; both those are centered in 
{or supporied by) the Puranas. Just as this wonderful world 
sprang from the ancient Being (God), there is no doubt that all 
this literature arose from the Puranas. I hold that the meaning 
(or purpose) of the Puranas is more extensive (or superior to) 
than the meaning (or purpose) of the Veda. All tha Vedas 
always rest on the Puranas; the Veda is afraid of the man of 
little learning (with the thought that) that man may harm it. 
The Veda does not deal with the movements of the planets, nor 
does it contain correct calculations about the proper times (for 
religious acts), nor does it deal with the gthewrddhz or titheksaya, 
nor with the determination of the parzans (ama&vasy4, piunima 
&c.) or eclipses, Determinations about these were formerly 
made in Itihdsa and Puranas. What is not seen in the Vedas 
is all noticed in the Smrtis; what is not seen in hoth is declared 
in the Puranas. What is declared by the Vedas and what is 
declared by the auxiliary lores—it is Veda that is declared by 
Smrtis and Puranas. The person who looks upon Puranas in 
any other light would be born as a lower animal’.™ Tho

The Puranas introduced several striking changes in fhe 
religious rites, practices and ideals of the people. The most 
characteristic thought and the keynote of the Puranas is to 
declare how great rewards and results could be secured with 
little effort The Visnupurana (VI. 2) narrates how sages 
approached Vyasa with the question ‘in what age does a little 
dharma yield very great rewards’? Vyasa was bathing in the 
Ganges; he came out, uttered ‘Sidra is good and Kali is good’ 
and then again plunged into the river; then he again came out 
and said ‘well done, O Sidra! yon are blessed’; he again 
plunged into the river, came out and said ‘women are good and 
blessed; who is more blessed than they’. When he finished his 
bath and performed his morning rites, the sages asked him to 
explain what he meant’by calling Kali, Stidras and women good 
and blessed. He replied: ‘a man secures in asingle day and 
night in Kali age as much reward of fapas, celibacy and japa as 
is obtained in ten years in Krta age,in one year in Treta and 
in a month in Dvapara; therefore, I spoke of Kali as good; in 
Kali age a man secures merely by the glorification or incessant 
repetition of the name of Keéava what he would secure by daep 
meditation in Krta, by sacrifices in Treta, and by worship in 
Dvapara; I am pleased with Kali because a man secures great 
eminence of dharma with a little effort Persons of the three 
higher varnas have to study the Vedas after observing many 
strict rules, then they have to peiform sacrifices which require 
wealth, they incur sin if they do not perform thoir duties 
properly; they cannot eat and drink as they 10168899 but are 
dependent on the observance of many rules as to food &e.; 
dvijas secure higher worlds after great trouble; the 801४ 
secures his worlds by serving the three varnas, he has the right 
to offer the p@kayajfas (without mantras) and therefore he is 
more blessed than a dvija He has nof to observe strict rules

As a consequence of the abovementioned dominating 
principle the Puranas strongly recommend dana (gifts, parti- 
cularly of food), pilgrimages and baths in sacred waters, vratas, 
ahimea, bhakti, repetition of the name of god, sraddhas &e, 
These will be briefly illustrated below, 


The Puranas institute a comparison between solemn Vedic 
sacrifices on the one hand and pilgrimages and baths at sacred 
places on the other, The Vanaparva™® contrasts the two as 
follows, “the solemn sacrifices promulgated by fhe sages cannot 
be accomplished by a poor man; sacrifices require many imploe- 
ments and a collection of various materials, which are secured 
by kings or sometimes by rich men, but not by poor men who 
have to rely on themselves alone, who have no helpers and who 
do not possess means. Going to holy places confers merit and 
surpasses sacrifices. One does not secure that reward by such 
sacrifices as Agnistoma, in which profuse fees are distributed, 
which is secured by repairing to sacred places.” Vide H. of Dh. 
vol. IV pp. 561-564 for further encomiums of sacred places and 
the virtues to be cultivated for reaping the full merit of 
pilgrimages.

Then as to gifts to brahmanas. In tho first place, if muat 
be remembered that all brahmanas were not priests and are 20 
priests in modern times, Similarly, all priests in all Indian 
temples and shrines are not brahmanas Temple priests are 
comparatively a later institution and in olden times they were 
looked down upon and are regarded as inferior brahmanas even 
in modern times, Manu (IDL. 152) states that a devalaka (a 
brahmana who performed for remuneration service before the 
image in a temple) was unfit to be invited at a sraddha or to 
officiate in a sacrifice to gods, if he continuously served for three 
years in that capacity. The ideal set before brahmanas from 
very ancient times waa of poverty, of plain living and igh 
thinking, of abandoning the active pursuit of riches, of devotion 
to the study of the Veda and Sastras, of cherishing a high 
cultura and of handing down literature and cultural outlook. 
Smrtis like Yay 1. 213 recommend that even if a brahmana be 
fit for receiving a religious gift he should refuse gifts and 
thereby he secures the same worlds that habitual donors secure. 
It was for preserving such high ideals among brihmanas that 
Yay 1. 333 prescribes that a king should make gifts of cows, 
gold and land and should bestow on learned brahmanas houses 
and requisites for marriage (maidens, expenses of marriages 
&e }. Vide H. of Dh, vol. IL. pp. 856-858 where references are 
given to inscriptions containing donations to brahmanas of 
houses and marriage expenses. In these days every body talks 
of the high culture and literary traditions of ancient India, But 
who cultivated the vast Vedic and other Sanskrit literature, 
preserved it and propagated it for several millenia? The answer 
would have to be that 16 was mostly due to some of the 
brélmanas who stuck to the ancient ideal for thousands of years, 
Ifthe Rgveda can be put forward in these days as the most 
ancient of the literary monuments in any Aryan language, who 
preserved ifs more than ten thousand verses with unparalleled 
care by oral transmission without hardly any variant readings. 
The reply will again have to be that the brahmanas did it by a 


~ Self-denial by many br&ihmanas 937 


golf-denying ordinance. The Brahmanas had to study the Veda 
with auxiliary lores without®* an eye to any ulterior motive, 
but simply as a duty and to understand the meaning thereof, 
they were to teach the Veda and other lores without demanding 
beforehand a fee, they had to bring up their own families, per- 
form sacrifices and make gifts themselves, The only substantial 
sources of income were officiating at sacrifices and religious 
rites and receiving gifts. These sources must always have been 
variable, fitful and precarious The brahmanas had no power fo 
tax people as in the case of fithes in the West. Nor had they 
arogularty paid hierarchy of deacons, priests, bishops and 
archbishops as in the Anglican Church Therefore, the 
prahmanas are advised to approach the king or a rich person for 
their livelihood (vide Gautama IX 63 ‘Yogaksemaxtham-{svaram 
adhigaccet), It should be noted that before Buddhism spread 
far and wide the stiras and amrtis emphasized that religious 
gifta should be made only to a worthy brahmana, learned and 
well-conducted, For example, Apastamba® prescribes “one 
should invite for dinner in all religious acts brahmanas that are 
pure, that have studied the Veda and that one should distribute 
gifts aba proper time and place, on occasions of purificatory 
sites and when there is a worthy recipient.’ To the same effect

As Buddhism grew in popularity and secured also royal 
support, the brahmanas had to tackle several tasks, They had 
to keep the number of brahmanas at a high level, they had to 
find maintenance for those devoted to the deep study of the 
Veda and they had to make accommodation with prevalent 
Buddhist thoughts by assimilating as many of them az possible 
in their own writings. Every brahmana could not possess the 
memory, the intelligence and the persistent endeavour for long 
years required for memorizing and mastering even his own Veda 
and its subsidiary Literature. If one hundred brahmana families 
were patronized, hardly ten percent of them could have been 
mastera of their own Veda, but there was always the possibility 
that those who ware nof themselves good Vedio scholars might 
have sons, some of whom might furn out to be profound students 
of the Veda, Therefore, the number of brahmanas was to be 
increased and they had to be fed and nof to ba allowed to fritter 
away energy and time in working for their bread 10 is mainly 
due to these factors that some of the Puranas contain incessant 
and frantic appeals for gifts to brahmanas.

At the time when most of the Puranas were composed, the 
brahmanas were hemmed in by great difficulties and hostile 
forces, From about the 3rd century B.C. to the 7th century 
A.D. Buddhism enjoyed royal patronaga under such great 
kings as Agoka, Kaniska and Harga, Buddhism was not really 
a tevolt against caste, bui against the sacrificial system, against 
the Veda and its authority to show the way to salvation. 
Buddha did not found a new religion, but he was a greafi re-~ 
former of Hinduism. He laid sole stress on moral effort, ahimed, 
satya &c, which had already been integrated info Hinduism 
and were part of if and which continue fo this day to ba part of 
Hinduism. Buddha in his first sermon in the deer-park near 
Banaras preached that one who renounced the world should shun 
two extremes viz, the pursuit of pleasures and the practice of 
useless austerities, that it is the course discovered by him that 
led to wisdom and १४६ एकाद. He expounded the four noble 
Axioms or Truths (Aryasatyani) viz. suffering (duhkha), the 
cause of suffering 5 viz. tanh@ i.e. trend (duhkha-samudaya), 
the suppression of suffering (duhkha-nirodha), and the way that 
leads to the suppression of suffering ( duhkha-nirodhagamini 
patipads). This last is the Noble Hight-fold path (astangilco 51

Because the doctrine of karma was deeply rooted in the popular 
mind at the time of Buddha, Buddhism took over that doctrine, 
which, {0 men who are not Buddhists, appears to be contradic- 
tory of the denial of the existence of a soul, The word ‘Dhamma’ 
is used in thres senses in the Pali ‘Dhammapada’ ( which being
