The latter verses explain how the Cakra is to be drawn with the 
bindu in a small triangle. The bindu represents Sakti or Mila- 
prakrii solidified In published works on Tantra the Sricakra 
is represented in colours (asin Saundaryalahari published by 
Ganesh & Co. Madras, 1957, facing the title page ), while others 
represent if only by means of plain uncoloured lines (as on the 
outer caver of the above edition of Saundaryalahari or on the 
cover of the Kamakalavilasa ed by A Avalon and published 
by Ganesh and Co. 1953). In some works the figure of Sricakra 
shows no gates as on the cover in ‘Principles of Tantra’ by 
A. Avalon or on the cover of Kaimakalavilasa, while gates are 
shown in other works (asin the above edition of Saundaryala- 
hati before the Sanskrit text). There are nine triangles, five 
of which have their apex pointing downwards and these represent 
Sakti and four (representing Siva) have an apex pointing up- 
wards, The bindu is situated in the smallest triangle pointing 
downwards. Then there are two pairs of ten triangles ( shown 
in some books as blue and red respectively), then fourteen 
triangles (coloured blue in some works ), then sight-petalled 
lotus (sometimes coloured red ), 16 petalled lotus (coloured blue), 
then three circles, then three boundary ines with four gates, 
these éwo latter being the outer sections of the yantra and the 
fotuses of 8 and 16 petals being the inner section of the yantra, 


There are in all 43 angles (some works make 44 ). The part of 


the Cakra within the boundary lines is called bAiipura. The 
worship of yantra is एवते

nature of upisana and not of the nature of bhakt: and that this 
upasana is of two sorts, one consisting of the recitation of the

the yantra'®55 (or cakra). Verses 126-204 of the Nitydsodasi- 
karnava detail the different items in the worship of the Sricakra.

may secure whatever he desires 1687

buried near the house of one’s enemy for the latter's destruction.

Yantras for cruel or zmmoral objects 1139 


In XXIV. 17-18 and 19-21 two yantras for the destruction of 
an enemy are described. Vide above p 1105 for Prapajficasira 
(34. 33 ) providing 9 yanira for creating passion in a woman and 
making her run to the person practising magic. 


The Tantrarijatantra provides (8th Patala, verses 30-32 ) 
that yantras that yield all desired objects should be engraved, 
painted or drawn on pieces of gold, silver or copper or on cloth 
or birch leaf with paste of sandalwood, agalochum, camphor, 
musk or saffron and should be worn on the head or the arms or 
neck, waisé or wrist or one should worship them after placing 
them somewhere (on the ground &c.); vide also Prapaficasara- 
tantra XT. 46 for similar provisions, 


At the end of this chapter on Tantrik doctrines and practices 
reference must be made to a remarkable circumstance, The 
Sarvadarsanasamgraha of Séyana-Madhava (14th century A.D), 
that deals with 15 Darsanas (points of view or philosophical 
views}, has not a word to say about Tantras, though it devotes 
considerable space to the atheistic Carvska-dargana and the 
unorthodox Bauddha and Jaina systems It is impossible to 
believe that the most learned brothers Sayana and Madhava were 
unaware of the works on Tantra. The silence must be dua to 
some special reason, If one may make a conjecture, it appears 
that Tantrik doctrines were discarded for the same reasons that 
induced the Bengal king Ballélasona in his Danasigara to 
exclude the Devipurana from the authorities on which he meant 
to rely. Af the tine when Sayana and Madhava flourished 
(about middle of 14th century A. D. ) Tantrik doctrines and 
practices had come into great disrepute. Therefore, Tantrik 


doctrines were probably passed over in si ~ 
Madhava, silence by Ssyana—

stitras and over 900 adhikaranas (called ny@yas or conclusions

canyarthadarsanam” (that occurs abouf 24 times). An adhi- 
karana is described as having five constituents, viz (1) the 
topic for discussion, (2) the doubt about it, (3) the prema face 
view, (4) the refutation of the prima facie view, (5) the final 
conclusion.475 A sifra (aphorism) shovld be concise 926 
(contain afew letters), butclear in its meaning, substantial, 
of wide application (lit. facing all directions), should be without 
pauses or interjected letters and should be faultless, A bhasya

Baving declared in the first siitra that after a person has

dharma ™8 18. The 2nd siitra, therefore, defines ‘dharma 
as an act conducive to a man's highest good, that is chara- 
cterized by an exhortative (vedic) text.’ Sabara explains that 
‘codanai’ means a sentence that urges or exhorts a person 
fo doan act, So this conveys fhat the means of knowledge 
(pramana) as regards dharma are vedic sentences and it 
also means that what is characterized or indicated by codand is 
dharma i, e. the nature (svarfipa) of Dharma is made manifest, 
The word ‘artha’ is putin to exclude acts (from being design- 
ated dharma) that may be mentioned in the veda but the result 
of doing which is evil, such as the sentence ‘one practising 
black magic (to harm a person ) may perform the Syena sacrifice.’ 
This is not dharma, but adharma, since the practica of black 
magic is condemned as sinful, This vedic sentence १088 not 
say that one should inflict injury, २४ only says that syenayaga

relation of Dharma fo the Veda and the Parvamimamsa-sastra 
is clearly and succinctly brought out ina verseof Kuméarila 
himself as follows: 93 "When discussion about the correct 
knowledge of Dharma is being carried on, Veda being the means 
of such knowledge, mimamsa will supply complete information 
about the subject of the procedure or method’ Just as even if 
a man has good sight he cannot perceive anything unless there 
is light, so unless a man knows the methods laid down by PMS 
he cannot correctly judge what Dharma is, Jaimini then exa- 
mines the means of knowledge ( pramanas) and holds that except 
gabda (i, the Veda) there is no means of knowledge about 
Dharme, One cannot perceive directly what Dharma is i.e, 
Dharma is not pratyaksa. All the other pramanas except sabda 
are based on pratyaksa and therefore they cannot define or 
explain what Dharma is According to Kumirile there are six 
pramanas, pratyaksa (direct perception), anumana (inference), 
upamana (analogy), sabda, arthapatti and abhava (non-exis- 
tence) Prabhakara does not accept the last as a pramana,

lost ground and the Bhatta school of Kumarila has been most 
predominant for several centuries. The present writer holds

CHAPTER XXIX 
Some Fundamental Doctrines of Pirvamimamsa 


Some of the characteristic fundamental doctrines of the 
Parvamimamsa will now be set out with some references and a 
few remarks as to some of them, the views of Prabhakara and 
his followers being also rarely referred to. 


(1) Veda is oternal, self-existent, not composed by any 
author, human or divine, and is infallible. This 1s the core of 
the P.M. system. Vide ए, M.S I 1, 27-32 and Sabara on J, 1. 5 
(p. 53) and Slokavartika (Valkyadhikerana, verses? 366- 
368). The argument briefly is, Veda is learnt at prasent and 
was studied in the past also by students from teachers, that 
there is no evidence about the person who first composed it or 
who first studied it. If it be argued that such a reasoning may 
be put forward as regards the Mahabharata, the reply is that 
people know that Vyasa isthe author of it, Similarly, the 
passages in Smrtis and Puranas that Prajapati created the Veda 
are merely arthavadas (laudatory) not based on any evidence 
or perception and are meant only to convey the absolute autho- 
ritativeness of the Veda. Ifthe connection between word and 
sense is eternal and not brought about by any person, the same 
reasoning holds good as to the Veda, This view is opposed to 
the view of the Naiydyikas who hold that God is the author of 
the Veda or the interpretation of V 8. 1 3 (Sastrayonttvat) 
by Sankaracirya based on Br Up 7. 4. 10. Manu I. 21 (stating 
that Brahma created from the words of the Veda the names and 
appropriate duties of all) seems to suggest that (according to

Sabara. The Prakaranapaficiki also states that there is no

When the Veda says ‘one desirous of heaven should perform 
a sacrifice’, three Gkanksis (expectancies) arise, The first is 
‘what is to be brought about’; this is satisfied by the word 
svarqa, stating the reward or the purpose. The 2nd is ‘by what 
means’ 38 the first tobe brought about. That is satisfied by the 
meaning of the root ‘yay*(i 6 by yaga), the thirdis ‘what is 
the procedure or in what manner’, that is satisfied by the esta- 
blishment of the sacred fires and other rites that are described in 
the context of the passage ‘svargakamo yajeta’. Itis learnt 
from this passage that the reward or purpose (svarga) springs 
from (is brought about by} yaga and net by the devata, 1%2

6. The doctrine of apirza (invisible mysterious or subtle 
potency ). The Veda lays down that one desirous of heaven 
should perform a sacrifice. But the reward heaven comes off 
only after a long time, while the sacrifice lasts only for a short 
time. There would thus be no direct connection between the 
sacrifice (the cause) and heaven (the reward) or purpose It 
must be presumed from the Vedic injunction that there is some 
connecting link between the activity of man to perform a yaga 
and the reward. Before the principal and subordinate acts in 
2 88071068 are performed men have no capacity for svarga and 
sacrifices ( described in the texts) are also incapable of producing 
the effect ‘svarga’. The principal and subsidiary acts in a sacri- 
fice when carried out remove the incapacity and produce a _ 
certain capacity or potency for svarga. This must be admitted 
by all Unless such a capacity exists there would be the unac- 
ceptable conclusion thaf not doing the acts and doing them are 
on the same level. This capacity or potency either residing m 
the man (agent) or arising from the sacrifice that 1s performed 
is called api va in this sastra It is true that this capacity 
cannot be proved by direct perception or other means of know- 
ledge except by srut@th@patt:. When we are fold that a man

%. Svatah-pramanya (self-validity of cognition). It has 
already been stated that the praméinas are six (five according to 
Prabhakara), The P.M. system postulates that all cognitions 
as cognitions are intrinsically valid in themselves, do not 
require any extraneous help to establish their validity but in- 
validity of cognitions is (paratuh) established cxtraneously by 
showing that there was defect in the organ that produced the 
cognition or it is established later on that a particular cognition 
waa wrong.?? Prabhakara goes much further and holds that 
every experience as such is valid and no experience can be said 


to be wrong or illusory.

~ 168-171 for descriptions of the joys of heaven in 
the स titerature, the Epic and the Puranas. From considera- 
tions of space the remarks will have to be brief. In Rg. 0X, 118. 
2-11 the sage prays to Soma to place him in that immortal world 
where there is continuous light, where all desires are fulfilled, 
where there are joys of various grades Heaven was deemed to 
be the place whera the souls of valiant men that fought battles 
and sacrificed their lives went (Rg. VI. 46.12) and in Re. X, 
154, 2-4 the soul of the dead is asked to join those departed men 
that had become invincible by great tapas, that had died in 
battle, that had made gifts of a thousand cows, that had led 
a life of right and virtue and that were wise sages 


The Atharvaveda IV, 34.2 and 5-6 say that in heaven 
there are many women, they get edible plants and flowers of 
various kinds, there are streams of ghee, honey and wine (sur), 
milk, curds and there are lotus ponds all round. The Satapatha 
Br. (XIV. 7.1. 32-33) states that the joys of heaven are 100 
times greater than those on earth. Vide Macdonnell’s ‘Vedic 
Mythology’ pp 167-168 and A ए. Keith's ‘Religion and philo- 
sophy of the Veda’ etc, pp. 403-406 (1924). Even the Upanisads 
refer to the joys of heaven e.g. Chan, VIL. 5 3, speaks of two 
lakes in the world of Brahma, asvattha tree showering down 
Soma and the city of Brahma calld Aparajita; the Kausitaki Up, 
(व. 3 and 4) elaborates this and adds that five hundred Apsarases 
80 out to meet him (who reaches heaven ), one hundred with 
garlands in their hands, one hundred with ointments, ons 
hundred with perfumes, one hundred with garments and one 
hundred with fruits. Poets lika Kalidasa love to dwell upon the 
instantaneous arrival of the soul of the warrior whose head was 
cut off in battle and who was at ones joined by an apsaras in 
heaven (vide Raghuvaméa VIL 51 ' Vamangasamsaktasuran- 
ganah svam ortyat-kabandham samara dadarsa’) Tha Puranas 
furnish graphic descriptions of the joys of heaven. Vide Brahma- 
purdns 225. 6, Padma II, 95 2-5, Markandeya 10. 93-95, which 
enumerate Nandana garden, aerial cars with bevies of Apsarases, 
golden beds and seats, absence of sorrows, all pleasure &c, 
Sabara on P, M. ३, छ. 1. 1 refers to two popular views about 
svarga; one is, whatever gives pleasure to a person such as 
silken garments of fina texture, sandalwood, damsels sixteen 
Years old is designated siarga. Another popular view ig that 
Starqa isa certain place where there is no heat nor cold, no 
hunger nor thirat, no dissatisfaction, no tiredness, 


1214 History of Dharmasastra | See, ए, Ch. XXIX 


Sabara and Kumarila say that popular 1968 ideas about svarga 
are invalid, that the Mahabharata and Puranas, being composed 
by men, need not be considered and that the Vedic descriptions 
of svarga are mere arthavadas for praise, 


P.M. 8. 7४. 3 15. provides that svarga 2% is the reward of 
all religious acts (such as V iavajit ) for which no exprass reward 
is provided by the texts. Sabara states ‘happiness is svarga 
and all seek that’; an old verse says ‘that state of happiness in 
which there is no mixing of pain, which 28 not immediately 
overwhelmed by pain, that comes to one when one desires if, is 
called by the word svar (svarga )’. 


Medhatithi remarks that smrtis sometimes state” that 
the gift of a single cow yields all rewards and relieves from sins 
with the resulé that fruits of great religious acts and of slight 
ones would be deemed fo be the same but it should be under- 
stood that the rewards differ in their duration; otherwise, no one 
would engage in great or difficult rites. 


Some Vedic rites expressly declare fruits of sacrifices that 
are other than svarga. For example, the Tai. 8. provides ‘one 
desirous of (plenty of) cattle should offer the cérd sacrifica’ (I. 

4,6. 1.) or ‘one desirous of (leadership or control over) a village 
should offer the Isti called Sangrahant’ (Tai. 8. IL 3.9.2).

Sabara says the Veda does not say that the result of such 
sacrifices cannot be had in thia very life. This the Tuptika म 
expands in an interesting note, The remedy declared by the 
Veda for securing desired objects (son's birth and the like) is 
bound to yield the resuli in this 118 or in the next. Ifa man 
has committed evil deeds in a previous life he has to undergo the 
effects of those sins and while he is undergoing the éffects of 
sius the fruits of sacrifices are postponed. But if the effects of 
sins have been extremely reduced ha secures the fruits of A@myz 
rites in this very life The words of the Veda laying down an 
injunction state only so much that the fruit of the rite performed 
doss come about but they de not say that the fruit follows 
immediately (after the rite is performed), Therefore, there is no 
definiteness (about the time when the fruit will follow). But 
svarga is to be enjoyed only in another life (as a fmit of rites 
performed 17 this hfe), It (svarga) means unequalled happiness 
and is achieved in a degree proportionate to the actions, but it 
cannot be enjoyed in this life, since men experience in this world 
every Moment both happiness and misery. Every happiness is 
not the fruit of Jyotistoma and every being does not perform 
Jyotistoma. But some happiness does come to a man. Therefore, 
it (happiness) is natural The existence, however, of another 
body has to be imagined for the experience of unequalled happi- 
ness, there being no other reasonable explanation. That 
unequalled happiness does not come to a man unless he dies; 
therefore svarga is to be enjoyed in another life. ॑

Doctrines of early 2. M. writers are startling 1217 


knowledge of the Self would lead to Moksa. For example, 1974 
the Br. Y.Y. affirms that both knowledge and actions lead to 
Liberation, that fo say that knowledge alone leads to liberation 
is a sign of indolence, that out of the fear of bodily labour 
ignorant men do not want to engage in actions. 


The doctrines of the early and principal writers on Piirva- 
mimamsa are rather quaint and startling. Their arguments 
about the eternality and self-existence of the Veda are fallacious 
and wera not accepted even by other ancient Indian systems. 
Both Prabhakara and Kumarila have in their scheme no place for 
God as the dispenser of rewards or as the ruler of man’s destiny, 
as being pleased with men’s prayers. They do not expressly 
deny the existence of God, but they assign to God or the deities 
mentioned in the Vedic texts a secondary role or rather practi- 
cally xo role at all. They raise yajiia to the position of God 
and their dogmas about yajfia seem to be based upon a sort of 
commercial or business-like system, 195 viz, one should do 80 
many acts, dispense gifts to priests, offer certain offerings, 
observe certain ethical rules,and other rules of conduct (such as 
not eating flesh, subsisting on milk)19% and then the reward 
would follow without the intervention of God. There is hardly 
any appeal to religious emotions, there is no omniscient Being, 
no Creator and no creation of the world. The Pairvamimamsa 
no doubf lays emphasis on (the rights and) duties of man in 
life. The other darganas are far more concerned with the ques- 
tion of escaping permanently from the world and with man’s 
destiny after death, The P M.S , Sabara and Kuméarila, how- 
ever, make substantial contributions to the exegesis of Vedic

It is remarkable that great doaryas like Sankara and Ramanuja 
never claimed in their own works that they wera the avatiras 
of some deity. It was left to their disciples to say so, if at all. 


Having established that Veda is eternal and self-existont the 
Mimamsakas give free rein to their Ingenuity, powers of reason- 
ing and logic. They have a logic of their own which governed 
not only the interpretation of Vedie passages but also of the 
Smrtis and the medieval works on Dharmasastra ( including law 
and procedure), As Colebrooke, one of the most accurate and 
level-headed of Western scholars of Sanskrit, said more than 130 
years ago ‘the disquisitions on the mimamsa bear therefore a 
certain resemblance to juridical questions; and in fact, the 
Hindu law being blended with the religion of the people, the 
same modes of reasoning are applicable and are applied to the 
one as to the other. The logic of the Mimansa is the logic of the 
law; the rule of interpretation of civil and religious ordinances, 
Bach case is examined and determinod upon and from the cases 
decided the principles may be collected. A well-ordered arrange- 
ment of them would constitute the philosoply of law and this is 
in truth what has been atiompted in the Mimanga’ (Miscolla- 
neous Essays, Vol. I. pp. 316-317, Madras ed. of 1887 ).

Sabara also quotes two varses summarising under ten heads the 
characteristics of Brahmana texts, points out that all this is 
only illustrative and that the characteristics mentioned by the 
Vrttikara sometimes occur in mantras also, such as ‘iti’ in Re. 
क. 119. 1, ‘ityaha'in Rg, VIL 41. 2, ‘akhyayika’ asin Re. 1. 
116. 3, reason (7९) in Rg. 1. 2, 4. The Reveda alone contains 
over ten thousand mantras. Hardly one-third of them are 
employed in all the Vedic rites. The rest are employed in japa. 
Besides, the other Vedas also have thousands of mantras. 
Therefore, no formal definition of mantra is attempted and all 
that is stated is that mantras are those which have been 
recognised as such by the 1% learned, 

Brahmanas are attached to each Veda, such as the Ailtareya 
and Kausitaki Brahmanas to the Reveda, tho Taittiriya to the 
Krsna Yajurveda, the Satapatha to the Sukla Yajurveda, the 
Tandya to the Samaveda and Gopatha to the Yajurveda. The 
Brahmanas contain the oldest known specimens of prose in 
Indo-European languages, though prose formulas (probably 
earlier in date than those in the Brahmanas) are found in the 
Krsna and Sukla Yajurveda Sambitas. They are the primary 
source of information about sacrifices, ritual and priests. They 
contain numerous myths and legends put forward for Wustrating 
ritual and sacrifices. They often mention contests between 
gods and asuras (titans) and abound in etymologies. Their 
contents can be divided into two broad classes, viz. injunctive 
(hortatory) passages (vidhis) and explanatory (or laudatory) 
passages (arthavadas), The scope and purpose of arthavadas 
will be explained later on, But one important point to be noted 
is that the Mimamsakas are strongly opposed éo holding that any 
part of the Veda, aven the smallest, is useless or meaningless. 

It is now time to see how the Mimamsakas deal with the 
contents of the Veda. The extant Vedic literature is of

becomes of infallible authority. The Veda being the only means 
of knowing Dharma, the Mimimsakas had to accept that whatever 
the Veda says was authoritative and binding on them, as 
Sabara ता admits, But many Vedic texts ara apparently in 
conflict with each other and often are in conflict with ordinary 
experience, A few striking instances may be given to show 
how difficulties arose. The Tai. 8 ए. 2.7 and Mai. 8 state ‘one 
should not pile the fire altar on (bare) earth, nor in the sky, nor 
in heaven’. #8 No one can build a fire altar in the sky, nor in 
heaven, The Veda apparently prohibits something which is 
quite impossible and therefora this prohibition seems at first 
sight senseless, The Tai. Br, (TIT 8, 10, 5) states that by offering 
the Pirnahuti the performer secures all desired objects, If 
Ptirnahuti yields all objects, then one nead not perform any 
further rifes of Agnihotra &c Does the Veda mean this? The 
Veda contains stories and legends about individuals 8. g. Tai. ६. 
mentions Babara Pravahani who desired to ba an eloquent 
speaker and therefore performed a sacrifice called Pafcaratra 
and secured his object. The Veda would then be later in time 
than this Babara and this would forfeit the claim of being 
eternal &c, Therefore, Sabara states that a story that never 
happened is described for the sake of praise, This may be an 
escape from a tight corner but the explanation does not redound

The collection of vidhis in the Vedic texts forms the core of 
the Veda and refers to many specific rites The central element 
in a vidhi is the verb or verbal form, which will be analysed 
later on. The question is: how is one to recognize a vidhi. 
Sabara quotes a verse which those who know the propositions 
about the meanings of words and sentences declare traditionally, 
viz. in all the Vedas tho fixed (or definite) sign of a vidhi is the 
words ‘one shall do’, ‘it should be done’, ‘it ought to be done’, 
+ i§ should be so’, it ought to be so’. *? From this it follows that 
a yvidhi is ordinarily couched in the optative form (called vidhi- 
ling in Sanskrit), and that a verb in the present tense cannot 
ordinarily be taken as laying down a vidhi 5 But sometimes 
a vidhi may be inferred even-from a text in which the verb ig In 
the present tense ‘For example, there is a vedio text occurring 
in the Mahapitryajtia which states “he should follow holding the

Another classification of vidhis , 1229 


Another and an important classification is aptirva-vidhi 
(insunction of something quite new and not otherwise establish- 
ed as in ‘svargakamo yajeta’), niyamavidhi (a restrictive 
injunction) asin ‘he pounds the rice’ and parisankhyavidhi 
(an injunction in form where two alternatives being simul- 
taneously possible one is precluded), The Tantravartika defines 
these three in a well-known verse,” Fora sacrifice a plot of 
land is required which may be quite flat or may have ups and 
downs. Hera there are two alternatives only and both cannot 
be availed of at the same time (i.¢.amagn cannot perform a 
sacrifice at the same time on even as well as on uneven ground ). 
Therefore, ‘same dese yajeta’ (one should offer a sacrifice on an 
even spot) is‘a myama (it restricts the performance to ‘lat 
land only ) and excludes the use of uneven land for a sacrifice. 
‘Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten’. This is a 
parisankhya This sentence is not a vidhi, as eating flesh is 
already established by men’s appetites. Nor is i& a niyama, 
since one can eat the flesh of five-nailed animals as well as of 
other animals at the same time. Tt is a parisankhya. i.e. it 
prohibits the eating of the flesh of animals other than of five 
five-nailed animals. In form the sentence is a vidhi (as it 
employs the word ‘bhaksyah’ (which is optative or potential 
passive participle), but in substance it is a prohibition of eating 
the flesh of animals other than the five five-nailed ones. The

securing the reward of happiness, while kratvartha is that which 
helps in the accomplishment of purtsirtha and does not itself

purusartha and not kratvartha. 78 It may be noted that the

Before proceeding further it is necessary to analyse the 
notions underlying the word ‘yajeta’ used in such Vedic 
sentences as ‘one desiring heaven should offer a sacrifice’ 
(svargakamo yajeta). In the word ‘yajeta’°? there are two 
parts viz. the root ‘yaj’ (to sacrifice) and the termination (of 
injunctive third person singular). In the termination algo 
there are two parts (elements) viz. general verbal nature and 
injunctiveness (or injunctive forces). Generel verbal nature is 
found in the ten Jaa ag { verbal forms in fen moods and tenses ) 
but injunotiveness is found only in the injunctive form. Both 
general verbal nature and injunctiveness express only dhivana 
(force that brings into being something, efficient force). 
Bhavané (lit ) means a particular operation or activity of an 
agent which conduces to the coming into being of the resulf (lit. 
which is to come into being). And this bhavand is of two 
kinds, éabdi (word force) and Grthi (result-producing force ), 


It has been already stated that vidhis are the very core of 
the Veda, The doctrine of bhavana is the very heart of vidhis 


and is therefore one of the most important doctrines of the 
mimamsi, 


In ordinary life when a person says to another ‘this should 
be done by you’, the prompting 10 do something comes from a 
person. But Veda has according to the Mimamsa no author, 
human or divine, Therefore, in a Vedic vidhi the promp- 
ting arises from the injunctive or tha optative form of the word: 
there is no Person, human of divine, behind the injunction; 
hence the bhavana is said to be षता (i. 9. based on the word 
itself and not on the will or diraction of a person). There-

We must now turn to the 2nd great division of Vedio texts, 
viz, Arthavadas. They are dealt with in P. M. 8, firat adhyaya, 
2nd pada. There ara numerous Vedio passages such as ‘he 
roared; because he roared he came to be called Rudra’ (Tai. 8, 1, 
5. 1.1.), ‘Prajapati out out his own fat’ (Tai, 8. IL. 1,1. 4), ‘the 
gods, having reached tho sacrificial ground, did not know the 
directions’ (Tai S VI. 1. 5. 1.); ‘who knows whether one lives in 
the other world or not ‘(Tai. 8, VI. I. 1.1.); ‘there should ba no 
piling of fire altar on the earth nor in the sky nor in heaven’ 
(Tai, 8. V 2.7.1). The objector says ‘you have yourself declared 
that enjoining religious rites is the purpose of the Veda’ (P.M. 
8. 1. 1. 2). The above and similar passages do not serve any 
purpose in the matter of religious acts, they are therefore useless 
and are non-eternal (or do not refer to any permanent matter). 
The reply is that these passages form one syntactical or 
connected whole with hortatory passages of the Veda and they 
serve the purpose of commending (or glorifying) the hortatory 
passages, Sabara cites on I. 2.7 the passage ‘one desiring 
prosperity should sacrifice a white animal in honour of Vayu;

It would have been noticed that every Vedic passage is not 
of the nature of a vidhi (of an injunctive or exhortatory 
character), Thera ara numerous Vedic passages that ara 
commendatory of a vidhi, condemn an act that is prohibited, 
give an illustration of some one having performed the vidhi in 
the past or pnt forward an easily understood reason for the 
specific act which is enjoined, These commendatory, condemne~ 
tory and illustrative passages are not to be treated as unnecessary 
or purposeless, but are to be taken along with the uzdh: passages 
to Complete their full import, This doctrine of arthavadas saves 


a huge portion of Vedic texts from being neglected or treated as 
unnhe cesgary.

Tantravartika makes 2019 8 general statement that arthavada

Tho 3rd class of Vedic texts are mantras. They have already 
been treated above (vide p. 1220, nofes 1979 ff). Some mantras 
also lay down an injunction as in Re क, 117.5 ‘prniyad-in- 
hadhamanaya-tavyan’ (the strong must bestow wealth on one 
who begs), also the mantra ‘vasantiya kapifijalanalabhate'’ 
(Vaj 8, 24, 20) cited above on p, 1221. But generally manttas 
are only expressive or assertive and call to mind things that are 
connected with the acts onjoined by vidhi-vikyas (injunctive 
passages). The Tantravartika 2०2 notes that it is definitely 
understood that religious acts that are performed with mantras 
that recall to the mind the things enjoined lead to prosperity (or 
to svarga). The reader would notice how the Parvamimamsd 
system came fo relegate mantras to a secondary place and made 
them play a passive role in the sacrificial system. The Reveds

When the particle ‘na" is employedina sentence, it is 
either a prohibition or a paryudasa or an arthavaida, These 
three have to be clearly distinguished. In Darsapirnamiasa 
the two a@yabhigas are an anga (P M.S IV.4 30) and a 
passage states that the two ajyabhagas are the eyes of the 
Daréapiirnamiasa sacrifice 9 In connection with this the Veda 
says ‘these two are not performed im an animal sacrifice nor in 
@ Soma sacrifice’. The question is; is this a prohibition or a 
paryudase or an arthavada. A pratisedha occurs only when 
there is the possibility of what is prohibited following as a 
matter of course. As the Gyabliaigas are prescribed in Dargapii- 
roamasa there is no possibility of these two being required in 
a Somayaga and there is no real prohibition, Nor is there 
paryudasa, for if it be a paryudisa there would be no proper 
connection, since in paryudisa one would have to say ‘there are 
ajyabhagas त except in somayags’, which 
would be absurd. Therefore, these words ‘na tau pagau karoti 
ne some’ contain an arthavada. A true 2030 prohibition would 
occur only when something is first prescribed and then 
prohibited. The stock example is of the Sodasin cup; there are 
two Vedic sentences of equal authority 'he takes the sodasin cup 
in Atiratra * and ‘he does not take the Sodasin cup in atirdtra’ ; 
owing fo this conflict an option is allowed, Similarly, there is 
a Vedio passage ‘Vrihibhir yayeta yavairva’ (one shall offer a 
sacrifice with grains of rice or with yavas) Therefore, in the 
above two cases where the two texts are irreconcilable, there is

There is one more word, that must be explained, viz,

Vikalpas (options) are grouped under three heads viz. 
those indicated by logic or reasoning, (2) those due to express 
words and (3) those dependent on the will of the performer. An 
example of the first kind is the option about rice grains and 
barley grains (yavair vrihibhir-va yajeta). The 2nd may be 
exemplified from Manu IIL, 267, which says that the Manes 
derive satisfaction for a month when offerings are made of 
sesame or of rice or of barley or of masa pulse or of water or of 
fruits and roots.

Long period of the composition ० smrizs 1267 


As shown above smrtis had been composed before 500 ए. C, 
and they continued to be compiled till about 900 or 1000 A. D 
i, 8, for over 1500 years, Yaj (7. 4-5). mentions 19 smrtis 
including his own. Vide H. of Dh, Vol L pp, 132-135 for the 
enumeration of different numbers of smrtis in different works, 
At least a hundred smrtis if not more can be named. During 
the long period of over 1500 years vast changes in the religious 
and social ideas of the Indian people, in their customs and 
usages had occurred. Buddhism arose, flourished and disappea- 
red from India, the caste system became rigid in the matter of 
food, marriage and social behaviour; Vedic rites, divinities 
worshipped and language underwent great transformations, 
animal sacrifices, though occasionally performed, had ceased to 
be looked upon as meritorious. The religious literature had 
therefore to be recast fo suit new ideals, new worship and new 
patrons (viz. the common people who had ceased to follow 
ancient ritual and worship). Smrtis reflected the changes in 
idess, beliefs, worship and usages that occurred: from tima to 
time and naturally gave rise to great conflicts among them- 
selves, At last it appears that the learned men of the 10th and 
following centuries of the Christian era hit upon the plan of 
providing that certain customs and practices, though formerly 
allowed and practised, were harmful in the:Kali age, A theory 
was put forward that great sages cama together at the beginning 
of the Kali age and declared that certain rites, customs and 
usages, though allowed in past ages, should be prohibited in the 
Kali age.2%5 The actions prohibited or to 18 avoided in the 
Kali age (about 55 in number and therefore called Kalivarjya ) 
have been 58६ out and discussed at length in H of Dh, vol, IIL 
pp 926-967. It is clear from Medhatithi’s bhasya on Manu

Were writers who had condemned govadha (in Madhuparka &c. ), 


muyoga and the giving of a larger share to the eldest son and 


expressed the view that those practices were only allowed in 
bygone ages,

that therefore the path (to be followed ) isthe one followad by

We are here concerned with the attitude of Jaimini and 
his early commentators like Sabara and Kumarila towards 
Smrtis, The established conclusion arrived at by Jaimini (in 
२. 3. 2) is that in case of conflict with the Veda Smrti is to be 
discarded, but if thera be no conflict (of Smrti with Veda), it 
may he inferred (that Smrti is based on some Vedic text), 


This amounts to saying that there 15 always a presumption 
thai अपाह are based on Veda, if their prescriptions are not 
directly in conflict with the Veda, Smrtis prescribe the obser- 
vance of Astaka Sraddhas, the digging of tanks, following and 
obeying a teacher, These are authoritative because they do nat 
conflict with any Vedic text of opposite import, The Smrtis do 
claim that they are based on the Veda, Gautama says so (in XT, 
19 in note 2042) and Manu states (II. 7) ‘whatever Dharma is 
prociaimed by Manu for anybody has all been (already } declared 
in the Veda, since Veda possesses all knowledge’.

taught in the Veda and Smrti, such practices can be understood to 
be authoritative but if there is contradiction between what 18 
taught by Veda and by Smrti and by usages, then their authori- 
tativeness would be opposed (i 6 would be lost) and further 
that 25 srrti is more authoritative because it is based directly

CHAPTER XXX . , 
On Mimamsa principles and rales of interpretation 
in relation to Dharmasastra 


The Parvamimamsa evolved a method of its own and a set 
of principles for the interpretation of Vedic texts, It is now 
time to 89 down and explain some of these principles and rules 
and point out how they have been employed by Dharmaéastra 
writers for solving their own difficulties. 


The Mimamea principles and rules of interpretation fall into 
several groups, There are rules that are concerned only with 
the details of Vedic sacrifices and their inter-relations, The 
most important rule in this field is this that only Vidhis proper- 
ly so called have absolute authority and binding foree, while 
what are called arthaviidas have authority in so far only as they 
form one syntactical whole with the vidhis and as they are 
Meant fo praise the vidhis. (P.M.8 1.2.7) Vidhis and 
Arthavidas are not discussed consecutively, but they are 
scattered over the several chapters of the P.M 8. For example, 
arthavadas are first dealt with in I. 2, 1-18 (the arthavadadhi- 
karana), but in many other places thera is a discussion about 
arthavidas as in III, 4 1-9, ना 4, 10, I 4. 11, IV. 3. 1-3, V0 7, 
26-30, X. 8.5, क, 8, ¶ and 8, 


Tt should not be forgotten that the Mimamsa is not concer. 
ned with legislation by the king or a sovereign popular assembly, 
It promises to convey correct knowledge of Dharma (meaning 
religious rites and matters connected therewith) andthe means 
of arriving at that knowldga is the Veda itself and the main 
purpose of the Mimimsa is to tegulate the procedure (2८7८

first place, statutes are man-made, they express the will of the 
enacting authority, have mostly secular purposos, may be 
amended or even repealed and have to be expounded according 
to the intent of those thai made them. But the Mimimsa 18 
concerned with the Veda that is deemed eternal and self-existent 
(and not man-made ), that deals with religious matters, cannot 
be amended or repealed and is to be expounded according to the 
intent of the Vedic words, Therefore, though some rules of the 
interpretation of Vedic texts evolvad by the Pirvamimimss are 
identical with or resemble the rules of the interpretation of 
statutes developed in such works as Maxwell’s on ‘ interpretation 
of statutes’, the author will not enter into any detailed treat- 
mont showing the parallelisms between Mimamss rules and 
Maswell’s rules. This task was attempted over fiffy years ago 
by Mr. Kishorilal Sarkar in his Tagore Law Lectures published 
in 1909. It would appear ungracious on the part of the present 
author to offer criticisms against a predecessor in the same field 
who wrote more than half a century ago when Mimamsa studies 
by modern educated Indians were in their infancy. Bué the 
author cannot help stating that Mr. Sarkar was obsesed by the 
notion that he must show somehow or other that Jaimini’s rules 
of interpretation were not inferior to those of Maxwell's and 
agreed closely with him. For this purpose he relies often on 
far-fetched analogies and employs obscure explanations. In 
several cases it appears that he had not been able to grasp 
correctly what Jaimini and Sabara meant, 2095 


Tn this work the author is concerned only with the question 
of the influence on Dharmasastra of Pirvamimamsé doctrines 
and rules of interpretation. He has already shown how many 
of the doctrines arid technica] expressions of the Mimamsa have 
dominated Dharmaéastra He would now turn to the mules of 


interpretation.

The Mimazhs’ rules of interpretation fall into different 
classes from different standpoints, Some rules are general and 
some are special, Some rules have to do with the proper proce- 
dure to be followed when several texts Jaying down matters 
relating to the same subject are in conflict by means of the 
application of the technical words éruti, linga, vakya, prakar- 
ana, sthina and samakhya (IIL 3, 14) and there are rules about 
adhikara, atidega, tha, badha, tantra and prasanga, 


Some examples of general rules may first be cited. That 
vidhis alone have special obligatory authority and that artha- 
vadas are authoritative oly in so far as they form one 
syntactical whole with the vidhis is a general rule. The rules 
distinguishing between wdias (properly so called), nama 
vidhis and narisankhya are general,

A word is to be understood in that shade of its meaning 
that is appropriate to the act in hand, For example, éruti says 
“he cuts off with sruva, he cuts off with a knife, he cuts off with 
the hand’ (the same verb ‘avadyati’ being used for all the acts ). 
The question is whether one is to cut all offerings, whether liquid 
or solid, whether of flesh or other substances, with sruva ladle or 
whether he is to employ the method or implement appropriate 
for each i.e, clarified butter should be taken from a pot and 
offered by means of a sruva ladle, flesh should be cut off with a 
knife and offered, and hard or thick things (like fuel sticks) 
should be offered with the hand. The conclusion is that one is 
to offer in tha way most appropriate to each kind of offering. 
This is called ‘simarthyadhikarana’ (PMS. ग" ब, 4.25). The न, 
M. relies on this when dealing with the homa prescribed by 
Pitamaha for all ordeals in the words ‘ homa should be offered in 
the four directions with clarified butter, boiled rica and fuel 
sticks &c’ and declares that the homa of clarified butter should 
be made with sruva ladle, of havis (1, 8. ‘boiled ries &c" ) with 
srue ond of fuel sticks with the (right) hand, on account of the 
fitness (simarthya) of these for the various offerings and sharply 
criticizes Raghunandana who in his Dayatattva provided that 
० homa should ba made of all three together (and not separate- 
¥). A similar rule is applied to the ten sacrificial implements

Another rule (PMS 7. 3.10) about words is that 2" words, 
though of foreign origin, that are in vogue in Sanskrit, are to 
be understood in the sense which they have in the foreign 
language and one should not think of an attempt to derive them 
with the help of Nirukta and grammar. Sabara cites four such 
words viz pika (cuckoo), nema (half), tamarase (lotus), sata 
(circular wooden vessel ).

Lat us now turn to the interpretation of va@kya { sentence ). 
The Reveda and the Samaveda are metrical and therefore there 
is generally no difficulty in arriving at what constitutes in 
them one syntactical unit (vakya). But much of the Krsna 
Yajurveda is in prose Therefore, PMS (71. 1. 46) defines ०५०८ 
what makes one vikya by stating that when a number of words 
serve a single purpose, but if one or a few of those words are 
separated from the rest, the latter words are incomplete in 
effecting a purpose and stand in need of the words separated, 
then all these words make one vakya. An example is the 
mantra ‘I offer thee, that art dear to Agni, af the command of 
God Savitr with the arms of Aévins, with the hands of Pasan’. 
This is one sentence, the purpose of which is nirvapa { offering ). 
For other definitions of vakya, vide the author's uotes on 
Sabityadarpana (U1. 1) ए, 34, For constituting words into a 
sentence with an understandable meaning expectancy 74 
(akainksi), compatibility (yogyata) and proximity (sannidhi) 
are required, particularly the frst. For example, Sankaracarya 
on ए, 8.7. 4 3 says that without akauksa there is no cognition

Let us now turn to the interpretation of कठेन (sentence). 

The Reveda and the Samaveda are metrical and therefora there 
is generally no difficulty in arriving at what constitutes in 
them one syntactical unit (vakya), But much of the Krsna 
Yajurveda is in prose Therefore, PMS (161.46) defines 2122 
what makes one vakya by stating that when a number of words 
serve a single purpose, but if one or afew of those words are 
separated from the rest, the latter words are incomplete in 
effecting a purpose and stand in need of the words separated, 
then all these words make one vikya. An example is the 
mantra ‘I offer thee, that art dear to Agni, at the command of 
Gad Savitr with the arms of Aévins, with the hands of Pisan’, 
This is one sentence, the purpose of which is nirvapa ( offering ). 
For other definitions of vaiya, vide the author's notes on 
Sihityadarpana (Tl. 1) p, 34. For constituting words into a 
sentence with an understandable meaning expectancy 2123 
(akanks3), compatibility (yogyaté) and proximity (sannidh! )} 
are required, particularly the first, For example, Sankaracarya 
on ४. 8. 4 8 says that without akankss thera is no cognition

that the words form a धत, The word ekavaiyati occurs in 
V. 8. TUL 4.24 and conveys that there is a twofold akanksa viz, 
grammatical as well as psychological. It is tha listener or 
reader who has, on hearing or reading a word, a desire to know 
another idea or word to get a complete sense. When several 
sentences, each conveying its own sense as far as it goes, are 
brought together having regard to the fact that one of them may 
be principal and the others auxiliary, they form one syntactical 
whole. This shows that sentences are of two kinds, valryas and 
mahavakyas, as the Sabityadarpana puts it, 

It follows from the definition and the bhasya thereon that, 
in order to constitute a vakya, three conditions are necessary 
viz, (1) there must be a number of words uftered or put down 
together (padasamtha), (2) the words must have an expact- 
ancy for each other (i.e. if a word in the collection is dropped 
no complete sense can be had), (3) all the words must serve 
0116 purpose or convey together one meaning ( arthaikatva, acc, 
to another view). It is not absolutely necessary that the words 
in order to form a vakya must be in close proximity. Even if 
some words intervene there may be a sentence, provided there 
is akinksa between the words, Sabara on PMS IV. 3.11 illus- 
trates this well as stated in the note.?4 In the verse quoted 
^ pasyasi’ is to be connected with ‘jaradgavam’, though several 
other words intervene. Though there is proximity (sannidhi) 
between ‘pinaksi’ and ‘jaradgavam’ they do not form a sentence 
as there is no capacify as also akanks& between the two. The 
upshot is that sannidhi (proximity) of words is genorally 
required to form a sentence, though not necessarily required in 
every Case.

The doctrine of Vakyabheda plays a very important parb 
in Mimarhsi as well as in Dharmasasira. Vakyabheda literally

independent and one sentence does not require or expeck words 
from the other sentence to complete it, they should be treated as 
separate sentences, This is one sense of ‘ Vakyabheda,’ Another 
and more frequent sense of Vakyabheda is as follows: The under- 
lying principle of vakyabheda is that one and the same text 
cannot be construed as laying down two separate o:dius {pres- 
eriptiong) or that when a certain matter has already been 
proscribed and then several ausiliary matters are to be prescri-

give rise to the faulé of vakyabheda (syntactical split of 
sentence). In Tai. 5 there is the following passage ‘ the sacri- 
ficial post is to be of udumbara tree, the udumbara (trea) is 
vigour, cattle is vigour; he obtains for him ( the sacrificer) by 
means of vigour पय (i.e. by udumbara post) vigour (3. 8. cattle) 
for the attainment of vigour’. This is one syntactical whole 
(vakya). If 16 be said that there is a vidhi prescribing the use 
of udumbara postina sacrifice and that there is also another 
vidhi about the fruit viz securing vigour (i e. cattle); this would 
give riseto vakyabheda Therefore there are no two vidhis 
in the sentence but only a vidhi and an arthavada (praise). 2” 
Sankaracarya on V. 8. 10.3 57 remarks ‘ekam hidam vakyam 
Vaisvanaravidyavisayam paurvaparyadlocandt pratiyate ... eka- 
vakyatavagatau satyam vakyabheda-kalpanasyanyayyatvat.’ 
This is said with reference to the first aspect of the idea of 
Vakyabheda. 


The basic idea underlying the latter sense of vakyabheda 
is this. Tf an act or a substance ora secondary matter has 
already been the subject of a vidhi and if concerning the act 
(or substances &c ) a number of other matters (actions, subs- 
tances &c.) are enjoined in one sentence, there would be 
vakyabheda (i.e there would have to ba a separate vidhi 
for each of the other matters relating to what has already 
been the subject of a vidh:) On the other hand, if an action, 
substance or a guna is enjoined for the first time along with 
several secondary matters in one sentence, there would be no 
fault of vakyabheda i. 6. in a single vakya however long or 
containing many matters, if there is a single vidhi there is no 
fault. If, in the passage quoted on p. 1258 above 29 ‘one dasir- 
ing prosperity should offer in sacrifice a white animal to Vayu’, 
one were to hold that first there is to be a wdhz about prosperity 
as the fruit or reward, there would be two vidhis and so fhe fault 
of vakyabheda, but if one holds that the vidhi is only concerned 
with offering a white animal and what follows ‘vayurvai ksepis- 
+ha......bhitim gamayati’ is merely an arthavada (praise of the 
preceding vidhi), there is no vakyabheds. The fault of vakya-

A few examples must be cited to illustrate the principle of 
valyabheda. A simple example is ‘graham sammarsti’, If one 
ware to interpret this as meaning ‘he is fo clean the cup’ and also 
as Meaning that only a single cup is fo be cleaned there would 
be vikyabheda, Therefore, it was decided that the singular 
number in ‘graham’ is not to be insisted upon and cleaning of 
all cups was to be resorted to; otherwise there would be two 
vidhis viz. ‘graham sammrjyat’ and ‘ekam-eva sammurjyat’. 
Sabara quotes (on PMS 13.3) a grut: ‘one who has a son and 
whose hair is dark should consecrate the vedic fires’. Agnyadhina 
is laid down by éruti texts such as Tai. Br. I. 1.2.6, Sat If 1. 2. 
Therefore, the above text only lays down certain subsidiary 
matters about it A man may have dark hair but no son or he 
may have a son when his hair is turning grey. Therefore, if 
that sentence is meant to prescribe both attributes (having a gon 
and also having dark hair}, there would be two distinct vidhig 
in the same zitkya, that is, there would be the fault of vakya- 
bheda, which has to be avoided, Therefore, thafi sentence must 
ba understood as indicating a certain age viz. he must 0 be a 
mere boy (at the time of agnyadhana) but of an age to bear a= 
son, nor very old (when hair turns gray ). १, 8.06 must be neither

through affection with them (or any of them) is said to be 
re-united with them (or him)’. According fo the Mit, a reunion 
is possible only with father, brother and paternal uncle and with 
no one else, since no ons else is mentioned in the text of 
Brhaspati. The V. M. does not approve of this limitation and 
says that a re-union fs possible with all or any of those that 
participated in the partition and that the three persons, father, 
brother and uncle are mentioned only by way of illustration 
(i. 8. there 18 Jaksanz). A man may separate not only from the 
three named persons but also from his paternal grand-father, the 
grandson of his brother and the son of his paternal uncle and 
several other persons and therefore the construction of the text 
of Brhaspati by the Mit. is liable to the faulé of yakyabheda, 
since on that interpretation there would ba two separate proposi- 
tions viz. (1) that man is to be called re-united who having 
become separate again stays together with the one from whom he 
separated, (2) one can re-unite only with the father, brother, or 
paternal uncle, Thus there would be two distinct prescriptions 
in one sentence. Therefore, one should have recourse to lakgana 
viz. that the three named parsons indicate a class of persons 
from whom one may have separated but with whom he then 
stayed together. The Viramitrodaya (on Vyavahara), V. R.

There is another principle about sentences called ' anusanga' 
(elliptical extension) or fhe extension of a word, phrase 
or clauses from a sentence to another or other sentences, 
provided all those sentences are of the same type or form. 
This is one typo of anusarga. Anothér type is where 
each of two or more sentences appears fo be complete by itself, 
but there are certain words of a subordinate character in the last 
sentence of a passage which have to be taken up or understood 
in the preceding sentences, This latter is also called anukarsa, 
In the three wpesads of Jyotistoma, the first23* is in honour of 
Agni in which the mantra is ‘ya to Agne ayisayii tantir-varsistha 
gavharesthogram vaco apaivadhim tvesam vaco apaivadhim 
svaha"; the other two Upasads have the two mantras ‘ya fe Agne 
rajasaya’ and ‘ya te Agne haragayi,’ which are incomplete and 
in need of complementary words {0 complete the sentences, The 
conclusion is that the words ‘ Varsisthd ... svaha’ are to be sup- 
plied from the first sentence and not other words from the popular 
language that one may choose. Another passage of the Tai, अय 
8, 18 ‘ cit-patistva punatu, vakpatis-tva pundtu, devas-tva saviti 
punatvacchidrena pavitrena vasoh siiryasya ragmibhih'. Here 
the first two clauses appear to be prima facie complete, but when 
we look to the last clause where the word ‘pundtu’ is parti- 
cularised by certain other words, we ab once feel that the first 
two clauses also should be connected with the words ‘acchidrena... 
ragmibhih’ and that then they would be quite complete.

Veda enjoins many acts such as performing a एद, casting 
an oblation into firo, making a gift, milking a cow, melting 
clarified butter &c, but all are not on the same level. Some are 
pradhane (primary 7 or principal), while others are guna- 
bhita (subsidiary). The acts denoted by words such ag 
Prayajas by which some substance is not embellished or not 
made fit or is not produced are primary, while those which 
produce a substance or make it fit (such as pounding in the case 
of grains of paddy ) are subsidiary, Acts are further classified into 
various groups such as nilya, narmitteka or k&mya or as kratvartha 
and purusittha. These have already been explained. Thera 
are six means 744! by which is ascertained the difference or non- 
difference among acts viz. (1) Sabdantara (different words, 
such as yajati, juhoti, dadati, i.e. yaga, homa, dana are different 
acts); abhyasa 2142 (repetition) as in ‘samidho yajati, tanina- 
patam yajati’ &o, (Tai. 8.0. 6. 1. 1-2), where the word yajali is 
repeated five times and therefore there are five different acts 
prescribed; (3) sankhya (number ) as in ‘he sacrifices seventeen 
animals to Prajapati’ (Tai. Br, 13.4 3), which are seventeon 
distinct acts; (4) guna (an accessory detail such as the deity

Some examples of anga and angin may have tobe given

the sprinkling (proksana) isan anga (stands in a subsidiary 
relation to) of rica grains as directly shown by the objective 
dase (yrihin). The proksana (is motivated by) has the purpose 
of contributing to the transcendental reault (the api va), sinco 
what is meant is that if, without the sprinkling of water on the 
tice grains, a sacrifice (yaga) were performed, apiirva would not 
be brought about, To take another example, 2447 ‘he tales hold 
of the bridle of the horse with (the mantra beginning with ) ‘they

assertion (éruti) shown by the objective casa in ‘ragandm’ 
shows that that mantra stands in a subordinate relation to (is an 
anga of ) the bridle of the horse, since the utterance of it when 
taking hold of the bridle of the horse effects a samskara in the 
bridle and taking hold is also an anga of the horse bridle (which 
is in the objective case), just ag proksana 28 an anga of rice 
grains,

be four cages of conflict between linga and vakya or each of the 
three ones (of the means) that follow vakya in the इद्त, in the 
same way vakya may be in conflict with prakarana and the 
other two (ia all three cases), prakarana may be in conflict 
with sthana or samakhya (i. ९, two cases) and sthina may be in 
conflict with samakhya. So that there are in all fifteen cases of 
conflici of the six means among themselves. We need net

In PMS ४. { 16 it is decided that the order expressed in 
mantras should be followed in preference to the order contained 
in Brahmana texts.?465 The Darsapiirnamdsa sacrifice is made 
up of three component sacrifices, Agneya, Upameu and the Agui- 
somiya. In Tai 8.10.5 2.3, the Agnisomiya sacrifice is first

‘adhikari is the owner (or master) who stands above all actions 
(yiga).’ Another more elaborate definition is given as ‘ adhikart 
is one who desires some reward (such as heaven or happiness), 
who is possessed of the capacitiy to perform the act prescribed, 
who has learning and who is not excluded from performing a 
sacrifice (by Sruti)’. Even lower animals desire happiness ; hence 
to exclude them the words ‘possessed of the capacity’ &o, ara 
added. A man may be totally ignorant and so the word ‘ vidvan’ 
is added; a Sidra may desire happiness, may have capacity and 
be also learned but he is excluded by the vedic text, ‘ Therefore 
the Sidra is not fit (or ordained ) for sacrifice’. 


In VL 1. 39-40 it is established 2455 that every man belong- 
ing to one of the three higher classes has a right to perform 
Vadic sacrifices A. man though at one time devoid of wealth 
may acquire wealth by various means, Similarly, it is said in 
VI 1. 41 that one who is defective in a limb is just like one who 
is devoid of wealth i, e. such a man has a right to offer Vedie 
sacrifices provided he takes steps to remove the weakness, In 
VI,1 42 it is further provided that if the defect is congential 
and incurabla, the person who suffers from such a defeot is not 
entitled to perform Vedic sacrifices,

Exclusion from inheritance 1319 


The ancient and medieval Hindu law of inheritance and 
succession was modelled on this. Vide Yaj. Il 140, Manu IX. 
201 and Narada (diyabhaga, verses 21-22) Yaj II. 140 declares 
that the impotent, the outcast and his son, a lame man, a 
lunatic, an idiot, a blind man and a person afflicted with an 
incurable diseasa are not entitled to a share, buf are entitled to 
recaive maintenance. This subject has been dealt with in H. of 
Dh. Vol. आ pp 610-612 The Mit. on Yaj. II. 140 provides that 
the grounds of disqualification apply to males and females 
alike. But the recent Hindu Succession Act (No. 32 of 1956) 
sweeps away all these grounds of disqualification by providing 
that no person shall be disqualified from succeeding to any pro- 
perty on the ground of any disease, defact or deformity or, save as 
provided in this act, on any other ground whatever (section 28).

process or method by which the details preseribed in connection 
with one rite are taken beyond that rife and transferred to 
another, Sabara quotes from some ancient author a éloka defin- 
ing atidesa. The sacrifice from which details are transferred is 
called prakri: (model or Archetype) and the sacrifice to which 
details are transferred or extended is called vikrti (or Ectype). 
Atidega may be provided for by vacana (Vedio text) or by the 
name The first is of two kinds viz. by a direct statement or by 
an inferential process, For example, as regards a magic 
sacrifice called Isu the text says, after speaking of some details, 
that the rest are the same as in 2274 Syena. An instance of an 
inferential vacana is the extension to the Saurya sacrifice of the 
details of the Agneya in DarSapirnamasa, because both are very 
closely connected and because no details are prescribed by the 
text about ‘Sauryayaga’ (PMS VIL 4.1), The name also is 
two-fold, viz. name of a rite and name of 2a samshia. Tho 
Masagnihotra prescribed (vide PMS II, 3.24) in Kundapayl- 
nam-ayana is a different rite from the obligatory Agnihotra (as 
in ‘y&vayivam-agnihotram juhuyat*) as proved above, but the 
name ‘agnihotra’ being common to both, the details of the usual 
Agnihotra (such as milking the cow, offering curds or milk, 
using a Khadira fuel stick &c.) are to be extended to M&signi- 
hotra (Jai. VII. 3 1-4). Extension due to samskara name ig 
instanced in Jai.VIL 3 12-15. In the Varunapraghasa (one of 
the caturmasyas), Avabhrtha ( bath) is prescribed, but no details 
are added and therefore the requisite details are to be taken from 
the rules about the Avabhrtha in Somayaga. 7275

combination) occurs when even after we have the knowledge 
that certain matters are to ba extended to the vikrii there is the

vikrti.

This change is brought ous briefly in Tantravartika on HI, 5, 26.

The preceding pages are enough to exhibit the main 
doctrines and some of the principal Mimaimsa rules of interpreta- 
tion and the great influence that the Mimamsa exercised for 
over two thousand years on Dharmagastra works from the 
Apastambadharmasitra to late medieval works like the Smrti- 
tattva, Nirnayasindhu and Vyavaharamaytikha. An exhaustive 
treatment of the numerous technical terms, topics and principles 
of the mimamsa would easily cover a thousand pages, would 
enormously add to the extent of this work and has to be given 
up here for reasons of space, if for no other reason. 


The Mimamsi rules have been of considerable help to 
Dharmasistra writers. But it should not be supposed that 
application of the Mimamsa rules is easy or that the rules always 
enable scholars to arrive at agreed or cerfain and definite 
conclusions, Apart from the schism between the Pribhikara and 
Bhatia schools already referred to above (on p. 1189) there are 
many circumstances which militate against the certainty and 
usefulness of mimamaa conclusions. There are variant readings 
in the sitras themselves (8, £, on 1, 2.9 there are three readings 
according to Tantravartika p. 123, on I. 2. 14 two readings acc. 
to Tantrav pp. 128-129). Sabara omitted the sutra IL 4. 17 
(vakyasamevayat) and the Tantravartika notes (pp. 895-897 ) 
that Sabara omits six sitras after II.4.9. Sabara frequently 
mentions a predecessor called Vrttikara with great respect but 
differs from him in some cases (6, छ, on 1. 1, 3-5), does not like 
his way of dealing with sitras like I. 1, 32,33 and VII. 1.2. 
Sabara gives alternative explanations of the same siitra (6. g. of 
I. 3. 4, VIL 4,13, जा, 1.39). Sometimes he treats two or more 
sifras as forming one adiikarana and alternatively freats 0116 
of them as forming a separate adhikarana (as in 1, 3. 3-4, 
II, 2, 23-24), He proposes more than two explanations of the 
same sitra viz. IV. 1.2. He puts forward two or more explana- 
tions of the same adhtkarana (as in IV. 3, 27-28, VIIL 3. 14-15

Mimamsa lore, differ on numerous points, some of which ara:—

the Dayabhaga denies it and says it is on the death of the previ- 
oug owner or by partition, (2) superior right to inherit depends 
on religious efficacy according to the Dayabhiga, while nearness 
of blood relation is the determining factor according to the Mit.; 
(3) Members of ajoint family hold family property in quas!- 
severalty and can dispose of their shares even before partition 
according to the Dayabhaga; the Mit. 0068 not say 80; (4) 800, 
to Diyabhage even in a joint family a widow succeeds to hor 
husband's share on his death without male issue, while the Mit. 
does not accept this view.

In passing it may bs stated that to call the Act ‘ Hindu 
Adoptions Act’ is a travesty and misnomer. It should have 
simply been called the Law of Adoptions in India and should 
have retained the ancient Hindu rules for Hindus as developed by 
the courts and should have been of a permissive character for all 
Indians like the English Statute (of 1926) on the adoption of 
children. The general Hindu law of adoption as developed in the 
authoritative smrtis and commentaries and the case law did not 
contemplate the adoption of a daughter (except when she was 
made in ancient times a zutr:kit) and to allow the adoption of a 
daughter when 4 son was living throws to the winds the basic 
priniciple of the Hindu Law that asonless man should adopt a 
male as a son for the sake of the presentation of pindas and water 
(to the Manes} and for continuance of the family name 
(sections 7 and 11 of the Act). The Act allows a woman (even 
if not married ) to adopt to herself a son or daughter or both and 
under it a woman, if married, can adopt a daughter even if she 
has a son but a married woman cannot adopt a daughter if she 
has already a daughter or a gon's daughter living at the time of 
adoption (sections 8 and 11) The Act does not recognize 
dvyamusyayana adoptions which were recognized by Sanskri¢ 
texta and also by judicial decisions The ministers in the Govern- 
ment and their followers ( most of the latter hardly know what 


Hindu Law was and has been ) were carried away by enthu- 
siasm for equality of tights for 


both men and women. As 
the Indien Union is now a welfare State and it is professed that 
laws ara to be made keeping in view a socialistic pattern, Govt, 
should have disallowed adoptions altogether or at least put great 
curbs on indiscriminate adoptions. Instead, they extended the 
scope of adoption among Hindus by allowing a man to adopt a 
daughter oven when he had a son or sons and by allowing even 
ummnamied Women to adopt a son or daughter or both This ig 
against 8 socialistic pattern, 1 adoptions had been disallowed 
entirely or allowed within narrow limits cases of escheat to 
Government for want of heirs would have been many and to that 

RD १६५ 


1338 History of Dharmastisira | Seo, VII,Oh, XXX 


extent a socialistic pattern would haye been advanced, There ig 
no evidence to show that women were keen on the right to adopt 
& son or daughter even when they were unmarried. The first 
principle of introducing reforms in the existing law is that only 
strictly necessary changes should be put forward, Reformers 
and legislators should take to heart fhe advice of Mr. Aldous 
Huxley (in ‘ Ends and Means,’ p. 30) that change as suck is more 
or less distressing to most human beings, that man’s conser- 
vatism is a fact in any historical situation and that social refor- 
mers should abstain from making unnecessary changes or 
changes that are of startling magnitude, Legislators should 
not forget that when they introduce far-reaching changes to 
lessen hardships, real or supposed, deomed to be caused by exist- 
ing social conditions, they very often create new problema for 
the immediate future, To take a simple example, under the old 
Hindu Law all girls were to be married before puberty, though 
Manu (IX, 90 ) provided that a girl should wait for three years 
thereafter during which, her parents or relatives might select a 
bridegroom for her, but that if they failed to do so she may 
herself choose her partner. This was not a bad provision. 
People however went in for child marriages for girls and tho 
problem of spinsters never arose. Then over thirty years ago 
came the Child Marriage Restraint Act (XIX of 1929) whereby 
the legally allowed marriageable age for girls was fixed at 14, 
By subsequent amendments and by the Hindu Marriage Act 
(25 of 1955 ) the lowest marriageable age for girls is now fixed 
at 15. This Act of 1929 originally wont a long way in raising 
the minimum age for the marriage of girls. Then, after the 
second world war, owing to economic stringency, and other 
factors, the tendency of marrying at a late age increased and 
now the problem of spinsters among Hindus has emerged and 
great difficulties about the marriages of grown-up women im 
middle class families are baing experienced.

1348 History of Dharmaéistra { Sec, VII, Ch, XXX 


and Pavamina offerings and 1६ 1s stated that one of these 18 subordinate 
to tbe other Both subserve the same purpose, viz. being employed in 
Darsapiitnamasa and other sacrifices. A Vedic text states that vessels 
made of Varana and Vaikankata wood are fit for sacrifices, but a vessel 
of Varana wood 18 not to be used for homa while one of Vaikanhata may 
be used. Both classes of vessels are subsidiary to sacrifices, but the 
text about not using Varana vessel in homa 15 of a general character, 
Therefore, one of the two clauses 1s uot subordinate to the other, 
Hence Vaikankata vessels are to be used in yagas 1n which homa 1s 
requisite, but Varana vessels are not to be used in such yagas.

Dharmasastra and Sankhya, 


Sankhya is one of the well-known six darganas (philoso- 
phical points of view) 


2 


Sankaracdrya in his bhasya 723 on V. 8, IL 2.17 says that 
Manu and others who were deeply versed in the Veda took up 
to some extent in their works the doctrine of 2 adhina being the 
cause of the world with the idea of relying on that part of its 
doctrine viz. the effect is (already) oxistent in the cause. 
Similarly, on ए, 8. I. 4. 28 he says that great effort was made by 
the Sititrak’ra and himself for refuting the doctrines of the 
Sankhya system (and not for the refutation of the theory of 
atoms being the cause of the world), since the Sankhya system 
ig near to the Vedanta as it accepts the view of the non-differ- 
ence of cause and effect and as some Dharmasttra writers like 
Devala have had resort to it in their works, on प. 9. 7. 1.8 
Sankarécarya remarks that, though there are many smrtis 
dealing with metaphysical topics, great effort was made for the 
refutation of Sdnkhya and Yoga only, since the two systems are 
well-known in the world as means of securing the highest goal 
of man, as they have been accepted by srstas ( respectable and 
learned people) and are supported by Vedic indications in their 
favour (as in Svetaévatara Up. ‘tat-karanam sankhyayogabhi- 
pannam’ VI.13). It would be shown later on that Manu and 
Devala rely on and propound (some) Sankhya doctrines.

Origin and development of Sankhya 1353 


1६ would not be irrelevant to say a few words about the 
origin and development cf the Sankhya system. This ( rise of 
Sankhya) is one of the most difficult problems in Indian philo- 
sophy. A good many works and papers have been written on 
the Sankhya system.2™ As to whaf the original Sankhya 
teaching revised in the Sinkhyakarika of Isvarakrsna was, no 
generally accepted answer can be given, From the 5th century 
A.D at least the Sinkhyakarika of fsvarakrsna has been re- 
garded as the foremost exponent of the Sankhya. The Sankhya- 
karika and a commentary on it were translated into Chinese 
about 546 A D by Paramartha, originally a brahmana of 
Bhiradvaja gotra and a Sramana from Uyayini {vide BEFHO, 
1904, p 60). Sankaracarya on V.S I. 4. 11 quotes the whole of 
the 3rd verse of the Sankbyakarika and the first quarter of it on 
V.8.1 4. 8. But the Sinkbya system, it appears, went through 
saveral phases, Chinese sources say that there were eighteen 
Sinkbya 8000018 (ए 2 of Johnston’s “Karly Sankhya,” quoting 
Takakusu in BEF EO, 1904, p. 58).

attributed to Kapila (published with two commentaries viz that 
of Aniruddha and parts of the Tika of Vedantin Mahadeva edited 
by Garbe in B I. Series 1881). This is a late work composed 
about 1400 A.D as shown by Garbe in his Introduction and by

Fundamental conceptions of Sankhya 1857 


verses, Kapila-muni is here said fo be the first promulgator of 
the Sankhya. 


Before proceeding further the most characteristic and 
fundamental conceptions of the standard Sankhya must be sef 
out. The most fundamental conception is that there are two 
entirely distinct essences existing from eternity, viz. piakrt: (1.6, 
nature or matter) also called pradhing and avyakta, and pur usa 
(soul or spirit, the knowing subject). The 2nd fundamental 
conception is that purusas are many. Another most characteri- 
stic feature of the Sankhya system is the doctrine of three 2215 
gunas (factors) called sattva (light, intelligent), rajas (energetic, 
active, domineering), famas (coarse, inert, enveloping, dark). 
Pradhava or prakrti or avyakta is said to be constituted by the 
three gunas (trigunitmaka) when they are in equilibrium 
(Sativarejastamasim simyavastha). The Sankhya analysed 
all physical and mental phenomena. The lowest factor is the 
heavy Impenetrable matter and coarse foolish impulses, They 
are called famas (described as guru, heavy and 2aranaka, 
enveloping}. Then there is the factor of constant change in the 
physical world as well as in the mental. This is called 78188 
(cala, changing and upastambhaha, exciting, as the S, Karika 
puts 1). The third factor or element in the world is the varied 
operation of consciousness that leads to knowledge and experi- 
ence, which is called Saftza (laghu, light as opposed to the coarae, 
merely material objects and prakdsaka, luminous, as contrasted 
with tamas). These three factors or elements combine in 
various proportions and make up the evolving universe, The 
three are called gunas from several points of view viz they are 
qualities, they also bind as with a Tope the Purusa to samsiira. 
The basis of the universe is to be found inthe gunas. Pradhana

is not different from the gunas, but it is only the name of the

a theory of cosmic evolution which is practically as reasonable 
as any modern theory of evolution. It is probably the earliest 
attempt tio furnish an answer from reason alone to the questions 
about the origin of the world, about the nature of man and hia 
relation to the physica] world and man's future destiny. In the 
nineteenth century mind and matter were held to be entirely dif. 
6190४ and atoms were supposed tio be indivisible. Modern physics 
has reduced matter fo energy but the nature of this last also is a 
mystery. Under the Sinkhya system, purusa or prakrt: or both 
serve no religious purpose. There is no definite or convincing 
answer asto why purusa becomes entangled in the web of prakrti, 
The Sankhya simply says that aa a result of non-discrimination 
purusa somehow becomes entangled. The Vedantasiitra refers 
to pradh@na as amarta in I. 2.19 and as‘ inumdinika' in 1. 4. 1.

rapa ) and on the other hand manas (mind) and the ten indryas 
(sense organs). From the five subtle elements are evolved the 
five great elements, earth, water, tejas, vayu and akaéa (ether).

In the Bhagavatapurana (1. 3, 10) Kapila is said to be 
ets avatra of Visnu, is called s:ddhega { the lord of siddhas } 
and the teacher of Asuri in Sinkhya that had bacome decaden fi 
(by lapse of time). The Gita also (X. 26 ‘siddhanadm Kapilo 
munih’) mentions Kapila as a munz and the most eminent 
among siddhas, The 8. Karika also refers to him as muni. The 
Karmapurana (UL पर, ए) echoes the very words of the Gita 
(‘ siddhinam Kapilo munih >} 


In the cages in Br, Up. 0.6.3 and VI. 5, 2-3, in which 
succession lists of teachers and pupils differing from one another 
occur, Asuri is said to be disciple of Bharadvaja in the first and 
the pupil of Yajfiavalkya in the second. Hach list contains at 
least 60 teachers from Brahma downwards. In the first place, 
it is difficult to hold that these lists are authentic and there is no 
evidence to establish that the Asuri mentioned in both is the 
same ag the pupil of Kapila. 


Paficagsikha’s is a great name in the Sankhya system. His 
systematic work on that system was called Sastitantra. The 
5. Karika (70, 72) refers to him as the author of the Sastitantra 
containing great details, illustrative tales and discussions of 
others’ views. It was called Sastitantra because if expounded 
sixty topics and it contained sixty thousand gathas,223 The 
Yogastifrabhisya (IV. 13) quotes a verse which is ascribed to 
Sastitantra by Vacaspati on Yogasiitrabhasya IV. 13. The 
present writer cannot agree with Keith 7, 69 that the reference 
to Sastitantra in S. Karika (verse 72) is not to a work but toa 
philosophy of sixty topics. The arya 72 had a Sanskrit commen- 
tary which was translated into Chinese in 546 A.D, in which it 
was stated that the work contained six thousand giihas, 229 but 
the Bhamatl (by Vacaspati) on V. S. 1. 1,3 ascribes it to 
Varsaganya. It may bea slip on the part of Vacaspati or it is 
possible that he regarded Paficasikha and Varsaganya as the 
names of the same person, the first being a nickname and tha 
latter a gotra name. On Yogasiitra I. 4, 25, 36, IL $, 6, 13, 17,

philosophy has to be considered. ‘Sankhya’ means ‘number ',

twenty-five tattvas and as the Sastitantra of Paficasikha dealt 
with sixty topics, it is likely that the philosophy came to be 
called Sinkhya. The Sv, Up. I 4 is full of numbers, 2258 ‘Verse

philosophic system which postulates twentyfive tattvas, Prakrti, 
Purusa and others, This is the sense in which the word is used 
once even in the Gita (18.13, Sankhya krtante proktani &c ), 
The Matsyapurana also emphasizes this aspect of the Sankhya 
system, 


The word ‘Sankhy&’ has another sense as the Amarakoga 
states (‘carci sankhya vicairana ) viz, ‘rational examination’ or 
* discornment’; and the word Sinkhya may be derived from it in 
the sense of ‘system of rational examination’ and in the sense 
of ‘philosopher’ (masculine) according to ‘tadadhite tadveda’ 
(Pan, IV. 2.59) meaning ‘Sinkhyam veda’,259 The Bhamati 
explains the word in the second sense, Sankhya in a general 
sense means tattvajiiana ( knowledge of ultimate reality, includ- 
ing Vedanta) or a ‘person who knows the ultimate reality.’ The 
word Sainkhya, is frequently used in the Bhagavadgita in the 
sense णा fativazAGna (as in 11, 39, V.5, XIII. 24) and in the sense 
of a person knowing ultimate reality (in IIL 3, V. 5). 


Some comparatively early Sanskrit works that disclose tenets 
similar to the standard Sankhya of the Karika may be briefly 
noticed here, The Buddhacarita of A’vaghosa (in chap. XIII. 17) 
mentions a dialogue between Ardada and Gautama (the future 
Buddha ) in which occur prafrii, five elements, ahankara, buddhi, 
the indriyas, objects of sense, mind, ksetrajiia as Atman and 
states that Kapila with his pupil was enlightened as to 1688 
that nescience, actions and desires are the causes of samsara; 
that avidy@ has five aspects ( verses 33-37) which are defined, 
speaks of brakmacarya, and mukt. Though the tattvas 876 
mentioned here the rest of the doctrines bear very little 
resemblance to the official Sankhya.

the note below. 1 will be noticed that after enumerating the

Puranas contain lengthy disquisitions on the Sankhya 
doctrines. For example, the Visnupurana 1. £. 19-23, 25-62, 
VI 4, 13-15, 17, 32-40 (in all about 66 verses) are full of Sankhya 
doctrines and are all quoted in the Krtyakaipataru (Moksakanda 
pp. 102-108). But that Purana emphasizes that Paramatman 
(called Visnu) is the support of all tattvas, In Visnupurana 
J, 2, 29-23 it is asserted26 that brahmavidyns who are proficient 
in Vedic doctrines recite (a verse) that expounds pradhina, 
(and state) ‘there was then (before creation) neither day nor 
night, no sky nor earth, neither darkness nor light, there was 
only one male brahma that was evolved as pradhina and that 
could not be apprehended by the ear (and other indriyas) or by 
buddhs. Verses 39-40 (of Visnupurana VI. 4) assert that both?* 
prakrti and purusa become dissolved in the Highest Self who is 
called Visnu in Vedas and Vedantas ( Upanisads ). 


Many other Puranas devote a great deal of space to the
