CHAPTER XXXII 
Yoga and Dharmasastra 


Sankhya and Yoga often go together in the Upanisads as 
well as in the Mahabharata, the Bhagavadgita and the Puranas 
and their relationship to one another is the same in all these 
In Sv. Up. VI.13, Vanaparva 2 15, Santiparva 2270 228. 28, 289. 1, 
306, 65, 308, 25, 326. 100, 336. 69, Anuéasana 14. 323, Bhagavad- 
gita प, 4-5, Padma purana (Patalakhanda, 85.11 # ), the two 
are mentioned together. 


Though Sankhya greatly influenced all works dealing with 
the evolution of the world in its various aspects, it did not enjoy 
that great esteem among all sorts of people in India that the 
Yoga system enjoyed and still enjoys. The word yoga is derived 
from the root ‘yuj’ to join or to unite ( of rudhad: class }. The 
germs of yoga can be traced back to the Rgveda. Reveda V. 
81. 1 (a verse in praise of Savitr) reads ‘wise men, priests and 
sacrificers concentrate their minds and join their prayers to the 
wise, the greai (Savitr), who knows all {prayers)’, Another 
Vedic या verse also speaks of concentrating the mind. The 
word ‘yoga’ occurs frequently in the Reveda in several shades 
of meaning. Sayana in many passages takes ‘yoga’ to mean 
‘acquiring what is not already possessed’ (as in Re. I 5. 3). 
In Rg. 7, 18. ¶ God Sadasaspati (Agni) is said to pervade the 
prayers (or thoughts) of sacrificers, In Rg. 1, 34 9 it means 
‘yoking’ (kada yogo vajino Yasabhasya yena yajiam nasatyo- 
payathah ’, The word ‘ yoga’ is often used with the word इक 
(separately as in Re. VIT, 54, 3, VII. 86.8) or as a compound

Even if it be held that the authors of the Yogasttra and of 
the Mahabhasya are different persons, there are hardly any 
reasons for definitely assigning the author of the Yogasitra to 3 
date later than the 2nd or 3rd century A D, The date of the 
Yogabhasya of Vyasa is of considerable importance in arriving 
at the probable date of the Yogasiifra. But the question of the 
dats of the Yogabhasya ig also debatable, The Vyisa who 
composed the Yogabhasya would have tobe held as different 

from Vedavyasa, the reputed author of the Mahabharata. 


The author of the Yogasiitra is, according to the tradition 
embodied in such comparatively early commentaries as that of 
Vacaspatimigra, said ta be Patafifali. Important questions arise 
ag fio his age and his identity with Patafijali, the author of the 
famous Mahabbasya on Panini’s grammar and the Vartikas 
thereon. The grammarian Patafijali is generally held to have 
flourished about 150 ए. © Therefore, the question of identity 
becomes important for the date of the Yogastitra, Some scholars 


like Prof. ठ. Liebich, Dr. Hater (ए. 98 of the work of 1932) and 


Prof. Das Gupta favour the identity of the two, but several 
others such as Jacobi, Keith, Woods, Renou are against it, 
Prof. _Renow (inl त. 0. vol, XVI pp. 586-591} examines the 
question from the grammatical point of view, points out that 


cartain words like Pratyahara, Upasarga, Pratyaya are used in 


the Yogasitra in senses entirely different from the senses of 


these words in the Mahabhasya. But as the subjects of the two 
works are entirely different, the same words may have acquired 
different senses. Similarly, Prof. Renou relies on breaches of 
grammatical rules ( in the Yogasiitra 1. 34 ), while he says that 
Pataiijali in the Mahabhasya is very strict in following Panini's 
rules though Panini himself is rarely not strict in observing his 
own Tules: a3 in ‘tat-prayojako hetngca’ (1. 4 55) which is 
against his own इश्क ‘ trjakabhydm kartari’ {7 2,15); bug

Patafijali also employs such an expressions as ‘aviravikanyaya' 2 
( which should be avyavikanyayena) for which Pataiijali is 
criticized in the long Parvapaksa on Vyakarana contained in 
the Tantravartike and which is not explained away in the reply 
to the Pirvapaksa, It cannot be supposed that the Yogasitra 
for the first time settled the technical terms of Yoga. Yoga 
terms had been evolving from Upanisad times and Pataijali 
only used them in the sense which they had acquired in the 
course of centuries, Prof. Renou arrives at the conclusion that 
the Yogasttra is later by several centuries than the Mahabhasya. 
Jacobi in his paper on ‘the dates of the philosophical siitras of 
the Brahmanas’ (in JAOS, vol. 31 pp. 1-29 ) holds (p. 29) that 
the Yogasttra must be later that the 5th century A.D. and, 
following Garbe, thinks that it is not improbable that the 
Vyasabhasya was composed in fhe 7th century A.D, The views 
of Jacobi are strongly criticized by Jwala Prasad in J. 2, A. 8. 
for 1930 pp. 365-375, The present author disagrees with Jacobi 
and Prof, Renou.

Thera is also striking similarity betwean the Bhagavadgita

Similarly, the seat and posture { asana) in which a yogin is to 
practise must be stable ( this refers to, the seat) and comfortable

VL 35 ) that the mind is certainly restless and difficult to control,

४. 8. (112) speaks of the same two means, The Gita (in V. 4-5 )

mitted to one of these secures the fruit held out by both and that

means (sannyasa) ‘renunciation’ and Yoga means ‘ Karma- 
yoga’,

The place of Tiara in Yogasiitia 1408 


Y. 8, nowhere expressly says that Isvara is the creator of the 
world and all that it says about Him is that in him omniscience 
१8 at its highest, that He was the teacher of primal sages and 
that by repetition of the mystic syllable ‘om’ and reflection on 
it the yogin attains correct knowledge of the real nature of the 
self. In the next place, though fhe stmmum bonum in both 
systems is called Aavalya (8 Karika 64, 68 and Y.S UI. 50, 
55, IV. 34), yet the Sankhya does not sef out any elaborate 
discipline for attaining it except correct knowledge, that is, it is 
metaphysical and rational, while the Y. 8, gives an elaborate 
treatment on mind discipline, insists on effort rather than inere 
jfiana, attaches great importance to pranayama and meditation 
( 0728} and is psychological. 


The Sankhya postulated that an intellectual understanding 
of the nature of purusa and of ग (or guras) and of the 
diffarence hatween the two was sufficient for the emancipation of 
the individual self from the liability to rebirth, while yoga, on 
the other hand, was not content with this philosophic easy-going 
mental frame and emphasized systematic training of the will 
and emotions In both Sankhya and Yoga each individual soul 
is eternal and his destiny is to become free from the influence of 
Prakrti and its svolutes and to remain for ever the same ( viz. 
pure intelligence), Herein they differ from the Advaita Vadanta, 
according to which the final destiny of the self is to become 
absorbed in and one with brahig.

whether a work attributed to Yaj which makes Garg! the wife

ig supposed to have composed the Ya3 smrti This one circums-

Diwanji} as a fabrication sought to be passed off as an ancient 
work, If identity was really meant the verse could easily have 
been read as ‘Maitreyyakhya mahabhags’ without any metrical 
fault. Therefore, it is not possible to hold that Yogayajfiavalkya 
is the Yogasdstra composed by Yajiiavalkya before the Smrti 
going under his name was composed. A few other decisive 
grounds may also be urged. The work edited by Mr. Diwan 
mentions Tantras (in V. 10) and Tantrikas (in VIII. 4 and 25). 
Tho Ya). smrti nowhere mentions these two and is free from the 
peculiar Tantrik words or technique. Therefore, the present 
Yogayajfiavalkya edited by Mr. Diwanyi was composed long after 
the Yaj. smrti and probably in the 8th century or after when 
Tantrik rites and works had become common, One more 
important matter may be adverted to, The Yaj. smrti and the 
Yoga-Yajfiavalkya (ed, by Mr. Diwanj) both enumerate ten 
yamas and ten myamas. But the two diverge materially in the 
ten names as the note below will show 2308 The number of yamas 
and niyamas differs in different works, but if the Yay. smrii and 
Voga-Yajfiavalkya were the works of the same author, the 
differences in the ten names would not have occurred at all. 
Therefore, the author of the Ya, smrti is quite different from 
the author of the Y. ¥. There is no evidence for holding that 
the latter flourished before the Sth or 9th century A. D,

The Yogavisistha is an extensive work in 32000 Slokas 
(one sloka meaning 32 syllables) printed in two volumes with a 
commentary by Anandabodha by the Nirn. Press. It is really an 
eclectic work embodying" the tenets of the Gita on anisahit, 
the tenets of the Trika aystem of Kashmir, of Advaita Vedanta 
&c Its text appears to have been added to from time to time, 
Controversies have raged about its date and its contribution to 
Indian philosophy. The present writer holds on reading the 
contributions that the extant Yogavasistha is a late work 
and was composed some time between the 1110 and 13th 
century A. D. 


Ié is now necessary to furnish a brief outline of the maia 
teachings of ¥. 8. Though the work is comparatively small, its 
rendering in English requires to be amplified in order that it 
may be understandable. Only the most important and instruc 
tive mafiters are set out here.

The Patafijalasitra (in 1 19-23) divides yogius for 
asamprajfiafa-samadhi into various categories (vine in all), 
which are passed over here. Patafijali says that asamprajfidta- 
samadhi in the case of yogins (who are not gode or not thoso 
whase bodies are resolved into primary matter) follows upon that 
practice which effects fhe cessation of all vrttis and which com- 
prises only subliminal consciousness and is preceded by faith, 
perfect repose or serenity, energy, mindfulness and discrimino- 
tory insight (into what is real) due to passionlessness, Jt would 
be noticed that so far Patafijali asks the aspirant for Yoga fo 
rely on his own efforts, practice &c. He does nob mention Goi 
or his grace anywhere so far. From this it follows thai any man 
or woman and even one who 18 an agnostic may pursue yogis 
practices and attain fo asamprayfidta-samadhi and liberation 
without devotion to God or without God’s grace. But Pataiali 
as a keen psychologist knew the help that faith affords. Thorefore, 
he provides that, if you believe in God, He will help you in the 
practice of Yoga and from that point of view he assigns fo

devotion to Isvara ( igvara-pranidhana ) who is a special 1.76 
who is untouched by hindrances, by har ma (good or evil) or by

limited by time, is the teacher of even the ancient teachers. The 
mystic syllable (Om) is exprassive of (i. 8. representative or 
symbol of ) God and japa of that syllable and constant reflection 
upon the meaning of ‘om’ (i 9. on Tévara ) leads to one-pointed-

practitioner attainment of right knowledge of the nature of ths 
soul and the absence of hindrances (antaraya ) that distract the 
mind (1.29) These hindrances are nine such as 7170688, langour, 
doubt &c and they are also called Vogamala (taints or blemishes 
of Yoga), the enemies ( prutzpaksa) of Yoga. These hindrances 
are accompanied by pain, mental distress, tremor of the limbs, 
irregular inhalation and exhalation (7. 31). These distractions 
and their accompaniments that are the foes of samad/a may be 
prevented or mastered in various ways such as practice of con- 
centration on one entity (Igvara or the like), by the practice 
of such attitudes of mind as friendliness, compassion, cheerful- 
ness and indifference respectively towards the happy or the 
distressed, the good and the evil (I. 33) or by the expulsion and 
retention of breath (bhasya uses the word ‘ pranayama +}, When

order than what is obtained from scripture or inference and ths 
subliminal impression made in this samadhi is hostile to all 
other impressions and when this Jast impression also is suppr- 
essed or removed, then results the seedless samadhi (i. 8. agampr-

task) and the yogin’s soul! abides in itself, shines forth in its

himsi, asatya &c ), and are therefore called bahkzratiga ( external, 
indirect) sadhanas (means) of Yoga, while dharana, dhyana 
and samadhi are said to be anitaranga to Yoga (ए, 8. U1. ए, 
‘trayam-antarangam ptrvebhyah’. The last three are dealt 
with in the 8rd pada. It is these stitras in the 2nd p@da that 
are emphasized and elaborated in Dharmasastra works. Therefore 
some detailed treatment of these matters is needed here, 


In some works, such asthe Goraksasamhita the angas of 
yoga are said to be only six (omitting yama and niyama 
or omitting some others). The Maitrayani Up. (VI 18), 
the Dhyanabindu Up. the Atri-smrti XI. 6, Daksa VIL 34, 
Skandapurana, Kagsikhanda, 41. 59 and Buddhists say ths 
same, Manu 7 provides (IV. 204) ‘a wise man should always 
practise yamas bué not the myamas always, one who only 
practises niyamas and does not practise yamas incurs sin 
(or falls into hell)’. This १०७३ not mean that niyamas are 
forbidden buf it means only this that yamas are far more im- 
portant than niyamas. The words ‘yama’ and‘ niyama’ both 
occur in the Santiparva (cr. ed. 326. 15 and 339 16 of Ch. ed.). 
Some Smrtis omit them from the angas of yoga probably 
because they are prescribed for all persons in general by Manu, 
ठ], and others. Manu does not enumerate yamas and niyamas, 
but Yaj (quoted on p 1406, 2. 2808 above) snumerates ten 
yamas and ten niyamas, The five yamas="8 of the Y.S. are

while the word dsana (in Yoga) means bodily posture. It should 
be noticed that the Yogasifra does not expressly prescribe any 
of the numerous dasanas mentioned and defined in the Hatha- 
yogapradipika and other works on Hathayoga and indicates 
that those dsanas are not necessary in the practice of the 
Patafijala Yoga and that any posture which is easy, stable and 
comfortable would be enough for the yogin. The Y.S. here 
follows the Sv, Up. (IL. 8 and 10) and not the works on Hatha- 
yoga, if any existed in ifs times, In order to secure the posture 
described above fhe yogin should relax the usual physical 
movements of the body ( prayatnagaithilya) and bring the mind 
to reflech on the Infinite (bratma). As a result of pertect 
mastery over posture, he is not overwhelmed (or overcome) 
by the pairs of opposites (such as heat and cold, hunger 
and thirst ).

nen-ma papma mrtyur-adpnavad-iti ) ‘therefore 008 must 
observe only one vow, he should inhale and exhale with the 
(fearful) thought that otherwise, the Evil one, Death, might seiza 
me’. Here it appoara that we have the germ of the theory of the 
importance of pranayama, In Chan. Up. भ. 18-24 it is stated 
that the five Guts are offered to prana, vyina, apana, samana 
and udana (in the words ‘Praindya svaha’ &c ) at the time of 
ameal and that one who knows the true meaning of Agnihotra 
and offerings offers it in all worlds, in all beings and in all selves, 
Even now these ahutis are takan before meals by brahmanas, only 
the order of the five differs, Pragna 11, 18 says :-— All this that is 
established in the three worlds is under the dominance of Prana,’ 
In Chan. Up IV. 3. 3 Prana is again given five names on 
account of its working in the different paris of the human body 
viz, prana, apana, vydna, samana and udana (all five being 
named in the Tai. §,). 7६ follows that some distinction among. 
the operation of the five pranas must have been made at least 
a thousand years before the Christian era.

In the Yoga system (which is based on the Upanieads) prana 
implies more than mere breath, 1 means vital energy, powers 
such as speech, eye, ear, manas in the hody as well as in different 
forms in the universe. Its most perceptible manifestation in the 
human body is the movement of the lungs. The Y.S. inculeates 
on the yogic student the doctrine that by scientific control (as 
laid down in it) of prana in the body it is possible to obfain 
control over the deep-seated (and ordinarily imperceptible ) 
forces in human consciousness as well as in the external world.

The above examples show that in the times of tho Siitras

act independent of any theory about its being one of the cight 
angas of yoga.

Prantyina explumed in yoga-siitra 1487 


It is now proper to sea how the ए, 8, defines and explains 
praniyama, ‘When the stability of posfure has been assured 
{or secured) prindyadma is the pause (lit. cutting off) in the 
movements of inhalation and exhalation’. The bhasya explains 
‘svasa’ as ‘drawing in of the air which is outside one’s body’ 
and ‘ prasvasa’ as the expelling of the air in the trunk (or chest)" 
and the absence of both these is pranayama. This shows that 
the chief element in pranayama is the absence of both inhalation 
and exhalation 3, 8, Awmbhaka in the technical language of yoga 
works The next stifra states that pranayama {the pause in 
movement) is of three kinds, viz. external, internal and 
suppressed, The idea is that Kumbhaka (stopping or pause) 
may be done after one has taken in air from outside (first kind) 
or after one has expelled air from the trank (2nd kind } or when 
one is in a normal condition (i. 8, neither making an effort to 
fill his chest with air or emptying it of air) one may make a 
pause (3rd kind), Each of these may be regulated and considerad 
from the point of the units of space, time (measurement by 
kalds or matras) and numbers, Pranayama is called mydu (mild) 
when pause is kept up for 36 matras, then moderate one when 
kept up for 72 matras and keen (éiura) when kept up for 108 
matras. When practised for days, fortnights and months, it is 


ealled protracted and when performed with great skill it is called 
stksma (subtle ), 


In connection with pranayama we must look to Y. 8, 7. 34 
also, That sitra leys down that for securing the undisturbed 
calm of the mind one remedy is the expulsion and retention of 
the breath, 360 ६ appears from that sutra and its bhasya that 
ridhtiaya (retention of breath, i. ¢. Kumbhaka) is pranayama.

and satihhya in relation to pranayama. Ordinarily a healthy 
grown-up man breathes in and out in about four seconds i. 9, 
ahout 15 times a minute {21600 times in one day and night }).

of finger-breadths As regards time several units of time are

1446 History of Dharmagastra | Sec. VII, Ch. कद Xi 


Dharana, dhyana and samadhi are said to be the direct 
auxiliaries of Yoga and are three successive stages, the preceding 
one Jeading to the next. Dharan& 1s the holding of the mind to 
a certain spot or point 2377 or object. The bhasya explains that 
the mind is to be held down to such spots (in one’s body ) as the 
navel, the heart-lotus, the head, the light (in the eye), the tip 
of the nose, the fip of the tongue and the like or on external 
objects (such as images of gods in various forms), In this 
stage attention has to ba firmly held upon the chosen object for 
a period of time determined by the will of the yoga aspirant. 
In this stage there ara three elements, the subject, the object and 
the act of concentration. The next stage is dhyana, which will 
be described immediately below. The Markandeya Purana

is put forword in IV. 34 from two points of view. When 2 
purnsa ceases to be affected in any way by the gunas (that 
constitute prakrti) because he has become entirely , passionless, 
prakrti bacomes aloof (kevala) so far as that purusa is concerned. 
When purusa has thorough knowledge and ceases to be affected 
by gunas he temains as bare consciousness (citisakti) and 
remains aloof (kevala) and that is the 2nd point of view about 
karvalya. In that state of kaivalya or moksa we cannot 
Predicate any happiness or bliss about him but we can only 
say about him that he is in a state of bare consciousness 
(नधि, The Upanisads declare? that in such a state the 
liberated soul has neither joy nor sorrow, that happiness or its 
opposite does not touch such an one, since he has risen above 
identifying the body with himself, The ideal of Yoga is to be 
jivan-mukta (i e. to reject Life and Personality, to die to this 
world though the body may persist for some time ).

The last chapter in Dr, Behanan’s book on ‘Yoga, a sciontific 
evaluation’ is interesting and important, He makes an appraisal 
of several aspeots of Yoga by means of experiments which he 
carried out on himself after spending ons year under the 
guidance of Swami Kuvalayanand of Lonavla and after he had 
three years of experience in Yogic breathing. It is not possible 
for reasons of spaca to give here a summary of his appraisal of 
several aspects of Yoga but reference may be made to a few of 
his findings. He finds that by yogic practices the mind is turned 
inward and detached from the external world (p, 232), it seems 
fo him very probable that the pranaiyamic breathing induces a 
state of relaxation, thereby inducing the mind to take an inward 
course (p. 234), that taking normal breathing as o basis of 
comparison it was found that oxygen consumption increased 
24, 8 per cent in Uyjiyi, 18.5 per cant in dhasiisa and 12 per 
cant in Kapalabhati; that the nasal gaze in a meditative posture 
is an aid to checking the wandering propensities of the mind 
(ए, 242), that Yogic practices lead to an emotional stability and 
that watching at close range for o year the daily 14९७ of more 
than half a dozen practitioners of yoga Dr. Behanan concluded 
that they were the happiest personalities that he had known and 
that their serenity was contagious (p. 245 ).

firat santence of which opens with tha words ‘The methods and 
techniques of the yoga, particularly those of the Rajayoga, 
contain in themselves nearly all fhe sound techniques of modern 
paycho- analysis, psychotherapy, psycho-drama, moral education, 
and education of character,’

Patafijali says that Om is the symbol of Tévara and thet repebi- 
tion thereof and reflection on its meaning is a means of attain. 
ing ekagrata, but thera is no explanation why Om is expressiv- 
of Isvara nor is any reference made to the Upanisads &c, abou! 
the importance of Om or how japa is to be performed. This is 
probably due to the agelong tradition that spiritual knowledge 
should be kept secret, should not be taught to all and sundry, 
but only to a disciple possessing certain qualifications, Already 
on pp. 1071-72 notes 1733, 1734 it has bean shown from a few 
Upanisad quotations how esoteric knowledge was imparted only 
by a guru to adisciple In the dialogue of Yayfiavalkya and 
Artabhiaga (Br. Up, HI 2. 13), when the latter asked, after 
saying ‘after a man's death his speech enters fire, his breath 
enters info wind, his eye into the sun, his body into the sarth' 
‘where does then the man remain?’ Yajfiavalkya replied 
take my hand, on this matter we two alone must come to some 
understanding, but not here in the midst of company.’ Then the 
two went aside and conferred with one another. That shows that 
the knowledge about what happens after death was nof held to be 
a matter proper for being discussed in an assembly of people. The 
Chandogya Up. (Ti. 11.5) states ‘therefore a father may tell 
that doctrine of Brahma to his eldest son or to a worthy pupil

Riyayoga holds the supreme goal to be liberation from 
Nature (prakrti) or May& ot the Advaita) and its altitude 
towards the world of senses and our empirical life is that of 
shunning these. Mukti means absorption into brakma for the 
Vedantist or Kaivalya ( ieolation of the Individual self from the 
bonds of birth and death and from prakrti according fo pure 
Yoga). Tor the vast majority of men and women the path and 
final goal of Patafijala Yoga or of the Advaita Vedanta ara 
almost inaccessible and unattainable, as the Gita itrolf states 
(217. 5} “Those whose mind is set on the Unmanifosted 
encounter greater difficulties (than those who worship a personal 
God), since the goal of the unmanifested is hard to reach by 
embodied beings’. The path of _Karmayoga (performing good 
deeds and acts prescribed by Sastra without hankering for 
rewards) and #hakliyoga (wherein there is deep devotion to God 
and self-surrender) appear to be more suitable and practical for 
ordinary human beings. The Gita in chap. XTIL (verses 13-17) 
contains one of the best descriptions of God as tranncondent and 
immanent and verse 18 adds that the devoteo of God who under- 
stands this reaches God.

and all higher religions. Rationalism accepts the postulates 
which science finds convenient and useful. Though these 
postulates work well up to certain limits, it must be said that 
those limits are very narrow. Science aims at establishing 
general rules or laws, From those laws we know only the 
behaviour of nature and how man can utilize natural forces for 
realizing human aims, but sciences does not fell us what those 
aims should be, it is amoral and not concerned with morals or 
spirituality. Rationalism appears to smother many experiences 
of the human mind which are beyond the present machinery of 
science, When the scientific method is adopted in social studies, 
there is little to show that it leads to increased wisdom about 
the values that should be pursued. Rationalism insists that all 
our beliefs ought ultimately to be based on tangible and definite 
grounds and that modern scientific method is the only reliable 
method for acquiring knowledge of all kinds. But there are 
sub-conscious and non-rational impulses, beliefs and intuitions 
in men that are held by men to be truer or of a higher order 
than what is on the rationalistic level (vide W. James' ° Varieties 
of religious experience’ 2. 74, ed. of 1920). It should be the 
endeavour of leaders of thought in each generation to find out 
what is essential and vital in tradition { without believing in

It has been mentioned above (p. 483) how Galileo was per- 
secuted for espousing the Copernican theory in astronomy. Not 
much difference is made to religion whether the Sun revolves 
round the earth or the earth round the sun, In this connection 
it may be pointed out that Aryabhata (born in 476 A. D.) 
appears to have held the view that the stars did not revolve 
round the earth, but the latter revolved round itself and gave 
the illustration of a man sitting in a moving boat feeling that 
it is the stationary objects on the banks that rueh past in the 
opposite direction.?5 The Paficasiddhantika (18. 6) of 
Varahamihira refers to this view and rejects it, not on the 
ground that it is opposed to the Veda, but on the ground that, 
if that view wero corract, hawks and other birds flying high up 
in the sky would not be able to come back to their nests without 
fail. He did not know that the atmosphere also goes with the 
earth. This was more than eleven hundred years before Galileo 
and there is nothing to show that Aryabhata suffered in the 
least for his views For Aryabhata’s view vide ‘ Aryabhatiyam’ 
by W. E, Clark (Chicago, 1930) p 64, As observed by Archibald

mien care nothing at all about the happiness of others, Moral

All writers on Dharmasastra are agread on the existence of 
God. They rarely enter upon the task of adducing arguments 
for the existence of God. Christian theologians for hundreds of 
years put forward various arguments pointing to the existence 
of God. They are briefly summarised in Wiliam James 
* Varieties of religious experience’ क. 437 (ed. of 1980), The 
cosmological argument reasons from the ordered universe to a 
First Cause which must be conceived ag God who must at least 
possess whatever perfection the universe itself contains Thea 
argument from purpose or design (teleological argument) bases 
itself on the evidence of purpose or design in Nature and 
concludes that the First Cause (God) must be a creative intellect 
or mind, Then there are other arguments also such as the 
‘moral argument’ (viz, the moral Jaw presupposes a law-giver), 
the argument ex consensu gentiium (viz. there is widespread 
belief in God all over the world and it should carry weight ). 24

The Upanisads speak of the Absolute braiman as the creator, 
preserver and destroyer of the bhitas (beings or elements or 
both). For example, the Tai, Up, IN. 1 ( Bhrgu?™? is instructed 
by his father Varuna) ‘desire to know that from which all 
bhittas spring, by which, after beg created, they live (are 
sustained) and to which they return and are absorbed therein; 
that is brahma’. This is the basic text on which V.8, 1 1.2 
(janmadyasya yatah) is based. This meana ‘from which the 
creation (sustenance and dissolution) of this (world) proceed’ 
(that is brahma), Another passage of the Tai. Up. (11. 1) states

Vayu Agni, from Agni waters, from waters the earth, from earth 
plants, from plants food, from food man’. A passage of the 
Chan. Up. states?! ‘all this, indeed, is brahma; 2 man, 
cultivating restraint of the mind, should meditate on that (world) 
as springing from, ending in and breathing on account of that 
(brahma)’. This is the basis of V. 8. 1. 2.1 (sarvatra prasiddho- 
padesat). Hera the threa attributes of brahma are creator, 
preserver and destroyer of the universe.

philosophers oscillate between the doctrine of the Firsi Principle

creator and is transcendent. The Reveda and Upanisads appear

enters into it when it craates the Universe (Tai, Up. IL 6 ‘tat 
srsivi tad-evinupravigat’), Chan. Up. VI. 2.1, VI 3.2, Br, 
Up. 1. 4.10. They also speak of God as ruling the Universe 
(antaryamin ) as in Br. Up. LIT 7. Kausttaki Up, प्रा. 8, At that 
time there was no atomic theory. Early Greek thought also 
wavered between the two doctrines. Later on came the rival 
theory of cosmology in which atoms played a great part, that 
was sdumbrated by Democritus (died about 370 8. 0, acc. to 
William James in ‘Some Problema’, and explained by Lucretius. 
In India also the Vaiéesikas put forward the theory that the 
world is paramanus (atoms), Kanida or Kanabhuk (lit, one who 
agsumes or subsists on kanas, very subtle particles) is the reputed 
founder of the Vaisesika system. He does not expressly say 
anything about God. But later medieval writers on Nyiya- 
Vaigesikn combined the two doctrines of God and atoms, .As the 
Tarkadipika?6 puts the theory it is as follows: when God desires 
to create, activity is produced among the atoms, two atoms join, 
dvyanuka (dyad) is produced, tryanuka is produced from three 
dvyanukas and in the end the great earth is produced; of things 
created when God desires to bring about dissolution an activity 
is produced in the atoms, The atoms are eternal and infinite 
tn number,

hhon-being ) nor ‘sat’ (what is); there was no sky nor the 
heaven which is beyond; what was it that covered all? Where

abyss of waters?; (2) There was no death, hence nothing 
immortal; there was no consciousness (distinction) of night and

being any air, really nothing other than that existed ; ( 4 ) desire 
came into being, that was the first flow (seed, offspring) of the

the highest heaven, he indeed knows or even he does not know ? 


It would be noticed that the sage, who was a post and 
philosopher , proclaimed that there waa that one Being, raised 
high above ali gods, conditions and limitations; he, the sage, 
gives expression to what he conceived to be the state before the . 
creation of the universe, Night and day, death and immorta- 
lity are opposites These exist only when there is manifesi- 
ness or creation and therefore he says ‘there was no death » nor 
anything immortal’ The hymn does not say that there was 
non-being out of which being grew. What he means is that 
That One alone breathed, the opposites, being and non-being, did 
not exist. For translations and remarks on this hymn, vide 
Max-Miller’s ‘ History of ancient Sanskrit Literature’ (1859) 
pp. 539-566, and ‘Six systems of Indian Philosophy’ (1919 ed.) pp. 
49-52, Dr. Radhakrishnan's ‘Indian Philosophy’ (1923), vol I. pp, 
100-104 Prof Whitney (Proceedings of American Oriental Society 
Vol. XI p. ORL), in his characteristic supercilions manner 
referred to above on p 512, remarked that the praises bestowed 
on this hymn were nauseating. Deussen, long after Whitney’s 
diatribe, said ‘in its noble simplicity, in the loftiness of its 
philosophic vision, it is possibly the most admirable bit of the 
philosophy of olden fimes' and that ‘no translation can ever do 
justice to the beauty of the original’ (vide Bloomfield’s ‘The 
religion of the Veda,’ p. 234, ed. of 1908), Vide Keith's ‘ Reli- 
gion and philosophy of tha Veda and Upanisads,’ Vol. आ. pp,

The creation hymns refer to a stage when there was no 
generally accepted theory about the origin of the world. But 
this much is clear that in the most ancient times, at least some 
of the Vedic sages had arrived at the theory that thero was only 
one Principle or Spirit, though called by various names and that 
it willed to create the world and created it from itself.

and also creation of other things. In Rg. X 89. 4 Indra is said

The Vedic Samhitis and Brahmanas show that the popular 
belief about the individual self was fhat by good deeds the soul 
reaches heaven, becomes immortal and enjoys various joys and 
pleasures, Vide Rg, IX 113. 7-11, I. 125. 4-6, Atharva IV. 34, 
2 and 5, ५1. 120. 3. There was also the idea of retribution and 
recompense for evil or harmful acts done by one person to 
another. For example, the Sat Br. says (XII. 9. 1. 1) ‘for what- 
ever food a man eats in this world, by the very same is he eaten 
again in the other world.’ Videalso Sat. Br XI 6.1 But when 
we come to the Upanisads, the whole intellectual atmosphere is 
changed The Upanisads frequently assert that Atman is the 
only reality, that there is nothing else and that the Atman can 
only be described as ‘ not this-not this’ i. 8. the Atman is un- 
knowable. This is the firat and foremost aspect of Vedanta, 
But this lofty metaphysical conception clashed with the ideas 
of common people who thought that a real universe existed apart 
from the Creator. The higher philosophic minds had to conceds 
the szeality of the universe for common people. They were 
prepared to say that the universe exists, in truth, however, it 
is nothing but the Atman entered into the universe. They said 
that the world was phenomenal, not false or nothing, but the 
world had the Atman behind it This was the good aspect of 
the Vedanta viz. thai the universe evolved from the first 
principle, b) aha. They distinguished between saguna (quali- 
fied ) by ahman that was for prayer and worship (upasana), and 
for practical purposes ( vyavaharavastha) and ni guna (un- 
qualified) brahina, But the higher thought also insisted that 
the highest truth ( piramérthikasatya ) 18 that brahman is one,

wealth, progeny and higher worlds and beg for alms as long as 
the body lasts. As no other course of conducé for the sannyasin 
is specified here, it would have to be deemed that the Upanigad 
teaches only this mods of life for the sannyasin. This view jis 
farther strengthened by other passages of the Upanisads, where it 
is said that the liberated are beyond sukria (good deads and their 
consequences ) and duskrka (evil deeds and their consaquencas ), 
The Chandgoya says 2 * the self is a bank (a dike or ridge) so 
that these worlds are kept asunder and are not confounded, day 
and night do not pass beyond (over) bank, nor old age, death 
and misery, neither good deeds nor evil deeds; all evil deads turn 


away from him, for the world of bratma is free from all evil’. 
Similarly, the Kausitali Up. says “being freed from good 
actions and from evil ones,

Tn classical Sanskrit several words are employed to describe 
the state of liberation. ‘The Amarakosa regards mukti, kaivalya, 
nirvane, éreyas, nihgreyasa, amrta, moksa and apavarga 
as synonyms. Mukti, moksa, and amrta (or amrtatva) are 
frequently employed in the Upanisads and the Gita, They refer 
to the state of Salvation or Liberation from different points of 
view. Man is liable to have hankerings and to birth and death, 
therefore when the soul becomes free from that cycle and realizes 
brahma it is said that he becomes immortal or secures immor- 
tality. Vide Br. Up. VL 4.7 and 14, V. 15-17 ( Vidyayamrtam- 
aénute), Chan. Up. IL, 23, 2 (he who is firmly grounded in 
brahme attains immortality), Katha Up. VL 2 and 9, Svet. Up.

The Visnupurana in Chapters 2, 4, 5, 7 of the first aga deals 
with several kinds of creation. Chapter 2 starts with Visnu 
and asserts that Pradhana and Purusa are his forms and in verses 
34.50 proclaims the details of the Sankhya system and verse 
54 refers to the production of the egg by Mahat and other 
tattvas. Chap. 3 deals with the question how brakman, which 
is 768 from gunas, inconceivable, pure and untainted, is the 
author of creation, the reply being that there are natural powers 
(Saktia) in all things thaé are inconceivable and so brahman 
has the power of creating the universe, Chap. 5 deals with nine 
kinds of creationa viz. of Mabat, Tanmatras, bhiitas, (elements), 
Vaikarika (i.e, Aindriyaka ), Mukhya (i. ©. of immovable objects), 
of lower animals, of irdhvaretas (2. ९ divine beings), of human 
beings, of Kumaras (1, 6. Sanatkuméra and others). 


The Markandeya-purina in Chap. 42 speaks of the creation 
of Pradhana, Mabat, Ahankara, Tanmatras under the aegis of 
Brahma, Chap, 44 speaks of the nine kinds of creation as in 
Visnu, Ohapters 45, 46, 47 deal with the creations of Gods, 
pitrs, human beings, the four varnas, beasts, birds, trees and 
plants &c, Passages from other Puranas need not and cannot be 
quoted as they are in the same strain a above and as limita- 
tions of space preclude further elaboration.

CHAPTER XXXV 


The doctrine of Karma and Punarjanma 
(transmigration or metempsychosis ) 


This is one of the most fundamental doctrines of the 
Indian system of religion and philosophy, is an endeavour fo 
answer the question that occurs to all thoughtful porsons, viz, 
what happens to man after the death of the body and has 
influenced for thousands of yeara or at least from the times of 
the Upanisads all Indian thought and all Hindus, Jains and 
Buddhists, Thies is a vast subject and has during the last 
few decades attracted the minds of numeroura writers in the 
West, Thera is now a voluminous literature in the West 
on reincarnation. 747 Several countries in historical times 
believed in transmigration, Herodotus 745” states that some of 
the Greeks (whose names he knew but did not disclose) had 
used that doctrine as their own, but that the Egyptians were 
the first to teach that the human soul was immortal and that at 
the time of the death of the body it entered into some other living 
thing then coming to birth, Pythagoras appears to havo 
believed in if and there are controversies whether he derived it 
from India, Prof. A. ए, Keith(in J. BR. A. 8, for 1909 np. 569- 
606) ‘after a lengthy discussion holds that Pythagoras did not 
borrow it from India, The present writer does nob expresé any 
opinion on that subject as it is irrelevant for the purpose of 
this volume. Hopkins and Macdonnell accept the theory of 
Indian Influence on Pythagoras, but Oldenberg and Keith 
do not. 


Not only Pythagoras, but Empedocles (who ia reported to 
have said that he was a boy, a girl, a bush, a bird and & fish) 
and Plato believed in the pre-existence and post-existence ५ 
the soul, in the idea that the podies which will accompany ९ 
goul in several births would hear simjlitude to the Lives

Piato’s Phaedon on this subject and pp. 29-31 for a long 
quotation from Hume's Dialogues concernig Natural Religion 
on the miseries and migration of the soul from body to body. 
Gough on p 25 of the above work opines that since in the Vedic 
literature prior to the Upanisads there is no reference to the 
belief in the passage of the soul into plants and human bodies, 
it is reasonable to suppose that the Hindus borrowed this 
doctrine from the indigenes 17 the course of their absorption 
of indigenous blood Vide also ‘Studies in honour of Bloom- 
field’ pp. 76-88 for ©. W. Brown's views to the same 
effect. This is a most gratuitous assumption, itis a pure con- 
jecture and without any evidence whatever. If belief in trans- 
migration could exist among Egyptians and many primitive 
tribes, there is no reason to assume that Indians did not them- 
selves arrive af the doctrine, particularly when there exists 
nowhere else in the whole world any theory of Karma and 
transmigration so detailed, so influential and so thorough as 
in Sanskrit Literature. One may dismiss the conjectures of 
Gough and G. W Brown as verbiage (the latter conjectures on 
pp. 87-88 that even the words Yoga, Sankhya and Upanisad are 
coined from similar words in some Dravidian tongue now lost). 
All Scholars ( particularly Western ones when writing about the 
Hast) should lay to heart the words of Mallinatha ‘namilam 
likhyate kificit’, The present writer is not against conjectures 
at all but they must not be bold and must always be treated 
as such. But the danger is that the conjectures of former scholars 
or men are often treated as valid conclusions by later writers, 
All scholars must bear in mind Acton’s warning ‘Guard against 
the prestige of great names; no trusting without testing '.

this doctrine and the vicissitudes and modifications of it and 
the objections raised against if in modern times. It is 8 
remarkable circumstance that, though the several daréanas 
(such as Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisesika, Pirvamimams’ and 
Vedanta) severely criticize some doctrines of cach other, the 
doctrine of Karma and transmigration received almost un- 
animous support except among materialists (like Oarvaka), 
Prof, Wilson in‘ Religion of the Hindus’ (London, ed, of 1862) 
vol, 1. p.112 remarks ‘metempsychosis is not only the one 
point on which all are agreed, it is tha one point which none 
have ever disputed’. The Buddhists and Jains, though they 
differed on many matters from Vedic and Smrti literature, 
adopted this doctrine in their own way. There are some 
suppositions antecedent to all beliefa in Karma and fraux 
migration viz. (1) man has a soul, eternal and separate from the 
physical body, (2) that other organisms, animals, plants and 
probably inanimate objects possess souls, (3) that the souls of 
men and lower animals can pass from one kind of physical 
organism to another, (4) that the soul is both dosr and sufferer. 


It has already been shown at some length (in Vol. TV. pp. 
154-171) how ideas of Heaven and Hell were developed from 
ancient Vedic times and it has been stated (on p. 158 of that 
volume) that the doctrine of Karma and transmigration 
modified the doctrine of Heaven and Hell.

whether it be good or evil, And whosoever knows this mounts 
the balance even in this world and escapes being placed on the 


balance in yonder world, for it is good deed that rises and not 
his evil dead’,

it with a hundred years; he who strikes him (shall atone) with 
a thousand years; he who sheds the blood of a brahmana would

This sublime passage is preceded and followed by 7195

The gist of these two passages jis that works and conduct 
done in this life fashion a man's future life and that the present 
birth of a man depends on his actions and conduct in 8 past 
life or lives, But works and conduct are the result of volition 
or will and this last is due to desires, A man may have several 
desires, ha may curb some of them, but may make a resolve to 
consummate some of his desires. Therefore, desires (kama) are 
the root of volition, of works and conduct and ultimately of the 
cycle of birth and deaths (that is called ‘samsara’). Hence 
Sankaracirya, following the idea of the verse ‘yad& ssrve 
pramucyante kama’ (in Br. Up. IV. 5.7) says ‘Kamo milan 
samsirasya’ (Kama is the root of sarhsira ).

The above Upanisad passages are enough to show how the 
doctrine of transmigration was being moulded in the Upanisad 
period. The Rgeveda knows the two paths of Devayana and 
Pitrydna and also that in heaven there were joys and delights 
but the Reveda does not say how long the joys of Heaven were 
to last and makes no clear and definite statement on the doctrine 
of transmigration, In the Brahmana period the two paths were 
often referred to and the conception had dawned upon the minds 
of thinkers that man might have to pass through death several 
times (punarmrtyu) But even then there is hardly any definite 
theory of punarjanma based on good or bad deeds. The claarest 
statements ( and probably earliest) of the origin of the doctrine 
of transmigration are the two Passages (Br. Up. Dl. 3. 13 
and iv 4. 5-7} in which Yajfiavalkys is concerned and 
is the instructor and emphasizes that it is man’s own works 
and conduct that lead a man to new birthe. In hoth those 
passages the Devayana and Pitryana paths are not mention-~ 
ed aot all, But the Br Up. VI 2,16 and Chan, Up. ए. 10 
relate the two paths to transmigration and speak of a thira 
place for those born as worms and flies, This is an addition to 
the doctrine of the two paths, but they make a further departure 
The Chin, Up. ४, 10. 3 states that those that perform sacrifices,

Chan, Up. on conduct moulding future 1557 


One of the most important passages in the Upanisads on 
conduct fashioning the life that would follow is the Chan. Up. V. 
10. 7-8 which may be rendered as follows: Those whose 
conduct has been good will quickly attain some good birth, the 
birth of a brahmana, of a ksatriya or of a vaisya But those 
whose conduct has been evil will quikly attain an evil birth, the 
birth of a dog or a hog or a ष्ठा. Those that do not go by 
either of the two paths become those small creatures (worms, 
flies &c) that are continually refurning and whose destiny may 
be said to be 'to live and die” Theirs is a third place (apart 
from the two paths), Therefore the yonder world dovs not become 
full. Hence one should be disgusted (with this Samsara). 


It may be stated here that the Bhagavadgita (VILL 23-27) 
also rafere to the two paths following one of which a yogin doses 
not return to this world and following the other of which he 
returns to this world. These are called gukla (bright) and 
krsna (dark) gat: (in VIII. 26) and arti (in VIII, 27 ). The 
former is fire, light52* day, the bright half of the month, the six 
months of the northern path of the sun ; those men who have 
realized brahman when going from this world go to brahman 
(the absolute)’. The latter path is ‘ smoke, night, the dark half 
(of the month ), the six months of the southern path of the Sun; 
the yogin reaching the moon-light by that path सला to 
this world. The Santiparva253 of the Mahabharata refers to the 
northern and southern paths, the latter of which is attained by 
gifts, study of Veda and sacrifices (asin Br. Up VL 2.16 and 
Chin Up. V.10.8). The Yajfiavalkys-snarti2526 also refers to those

The Vedantasiitra frequently refers to the doctrine of trans- 
migration, bu owing to the limits imposed by available space 
only a few important stitras and their explanations will be set 
out here. The three sitras of V.8 7. 1. 34-367527 are of great 
importance for the theory of transmigration. An objector says 
‘to hold that God is the cause of the world does not stand to 
reason, for, if it be so, God would be liable to the charges of un- 
equal treatment (or dispensation) and cruelty. He creates 
some that enjoy extreme happiness (like gods and others), some 
lead an extremely miserable life such as beasts (of burden &o. ) 
and some like mon, who enjoy an intermediate position, secure 
2 modicum of enjoyment. So God may be charged with acting 
through hatred and love (like ordinary men ). God also 
produces misery and finally destroys all persons, This aspect 
(of great cruelty ) appears abhorrent even to evil men, To this 
the reply is: if god had created inequality ia the world at his 
sweet will and without regard fio any other matter, he might 
have been liable to the two charges of unequal treatment and 
cruelty. But God has regard to the righteousness (merit) or other- 
wise of beings when he produces inequalities among creatures, 
The position of God should be looked upon like that of rai, 
which is the common cause (or factor) in the production of crops 
of rice and barley, but the difference (in quality) bebween rice 
and batley is due to the varying potentiahties of the seeds. 
God is the common cause in the creation of beasts, men and 
gods but the inequalities in these are due to the special poten- 
tialities of each. Sankaracarya relies expressly on two पथ 
nisad passages viz Kaus. Up. 1,8 and Br. Up. I, हक

Principle of doctrine af Karma 1561 


after a long time because it ig hampered by the results of an 
avil deed and quotes a smrti ( Mababharata ) in support?5! 


The principle of the doctrine of Karma is that every act, 
whether good or bad, produces & certain result or return which 
cannot be escaped, In the physical world there is the universal 
law of causation. The doctrine of Karma extends this inexorable 
law of causality to the mental and moral sphere, The doctrine of 
Karma is not a mechanical law; it is rather a moral or a spiri- 
tual necessity. It cannot, however, be said that this doctrine is an 
induction from observed facts nor can it be asserted that it is €~ 
perimentally verifiable, but it is only a hypothesis or supposition ई 
it is, however, far batter than other naive and childlike theories, 
In the absense of the theory of karma and rebirth it would have 
to be assumed that the world is arbitrary, that the Creator is nof 
bound to regard the nature of men’s actions but may distribute 
rewards as he pleases or by caprice. This doctrine of Karma em- 
phasizes three things, firstly it regards an existence as a sort of 
expiation for the doings of a previous existence or existences ; 
secondly, an evil deed cannot be expiated by works of merit but its 
punishment must be borne; thirdly, the punishment for Wrong 
ig automatic and personal. Under the doctrine of Karma thera 
is no such thing as chance or luck. When we use those words 
they correspond to no reality and are a tacit confession of on 
ignorance or inability to state the cause or causes of what has 
happened. This doctrine of Karma leads on to the doctrine of 
transmigration. The results of a man's actions may not happen 
at once or in the present life, The Adiparva and Manu say2532 
‘an evil deed does not yield its retribution immediately Hke a 
a cow (that yields plenty of milk immediately after she is well 
fed ) but returning slowly it cuts off the very roots of the perpe.

Many questions naturally arise on the doctrine of Karma 
and transmigration. One of them is discussed by the bhasya of 
Vyasa on Yogastitra II.13, In Yogasiitra II. 3 five 2408 
(hindrances) such as avidy@ (nescienca) are enumerated and it 
is stated (II. 13) that these Aiegas lead on to fruition of actions 
by way of birth, life (long or short ), kind of experience. Actions 
(Karma) are of four sorts according to Yogasitra (1V. 7) vis, 
kersna (dark found in wicked people), (2) suklakrana (white- 
dark) that are accomplished by external means in which there 
is some injury fo or benefit of others; (3) Sukla (white) 
belonging to those who engage in tapas, svidhyiya (study of 
the sacred texts) and contemplation; because this kind of deed 
depends on the mind alone and does not depend on external 
means and does not involve injury fo others; (4) Asuhlakrsna 
(neither white nor dark), which is found in sannydsins (ascetic 
saints ) whose hindrances (avidyé &c) have dwindled and whose 
bodies are the last (they will have). Of these four kinds, the 
yogin alone has non-white karma since he has renounced the 
fruit of all actions (even of good ones) and he has ajftrsna since 
he will never resort to dark actions. Tha bhisya on Yogasitra 
If, 18 states four questions, (1) whether one Karma is the cause 
of one birth, or (2) whether one Karma is the cause of more 
births than one; (3) whether more than one Karma brings 
about more births than one; (4) whether more than one Karma 
brings about one birth. The bhasya raines objections to the first 
three and states that the fourth alternative alone is acceptable. 
Vide p. 1417 note 2325 for the bext of the Yogabhasya on these 
four alternatives. The Santiparva (chap. 273. 33-34 of cr. od, 
=chap 280, 33-34 of ch, ed.) mentions individual souls as of six 
colours viz. krsna (dark), dhiima (grey), nila (blue), sakta (rod), 
haridra (yellow) and sukla (white ) in an ascending order, 
the dark being the lowest and éukla being the highest and 
verses 36-46 describe these six in detail.

Buddha and the doctrine of Karma 1577 


idea of transmigration as described in the Upanisads had become 
universal in India at the time of Buddha, Buddha rejected the 
reality of a permanent ego or self as an entity. He was nota 
metaphysical philosopher, but wanted tolay down a way or 
method by which mankind could be freed from ignorance and 
suffering and liberation could be achieved. Therefore, while 
rejecting a permanent ego he accepted the doctrine of rebirth. 


A side issue has been very much debated by some eminent 
scholars, viz whether the cherishers of the Vedanta thoughts 
were originally the Ksatriyas and not the Brahmanas, The 
present author dealt with that question in a brief compass in 
म. of Dh. vol. IZ. pp. 105-107 and note 222. Deussen in ‘Das 
System des Vedanta’ (1883 pp. 18-19) and Ph. Up. (tr. by 
Geden pp. 18-19} and Dr. R ©. Bhandarkar in ‘ Vaisnavism and 
Saivism ’ 9 hold the view that the ksatriyas were the original 
possesseors of Vedanta doctrines Deussen relies mainly on six 
passages and Dr. Bhandarkar on two only (Chan. V. 3 and 11 ) 
and besides Deussen (in Ph. Up. p 19) admits that his conclu- 
sion is not absolute certainty but has a high degree of 
probability. Barth in ‘Religions of India’ p. 65, Hopking in 
‘ Wthics of India’ (1924) p. 63, ‘ Vedic India’ by Macdonell and 
Keith (vol, I, p, 206), and Tuxen on ‘The religions of India’ 
(Copenhagen, 1949, ए. 88} do not subscribe to this view. 
Denssen went so far as to aver (ए 19) ‘this teaching with regard 
to the man was studiously withheld from them { the brabmanas), 
that it was transmitted mm a narrow circle among the ksatriyas 
to the exclusion of the brahmanas’. The present author had 
not set out the passages on which reliance was placed by Deussen 
aud those who followed him. They will be seb out here and will 
be examined as to the context in which they appear and tha 
subject with which they deal But it must first ba emphasized 
that the most important doctrines of the main and ancient 
Upanisads are two, viz, ' non-difference of the individual self 
from the Supreme Self, and (2) transmigration of the self 
depending on his deeds and conduct, Both these doctrines ara 
expounded by Yajiiavalkya to king Janaka j 
the Upanisads 8 &. in Br. Up IV. 4. 4-7 and following passages, 
Deussen regards this part of the instr 


chion as deepest, troeat 
and noblest (Ph. Up. p, 348-quoted above on p 1547) and this 
passage is (acc, to him } the leading passage on the doctrine of 


transmigration and on what accompanies the self in its trans- 


migration (Ph. Up ए. 287 ). Besides, the words of Yajilavalkya 
प, 9, 185 


1608 Efstory of Dharmuéastra {See, IX, Ch. Xxxv 


in Br. Up. IL, 2, 13 ‘He who does good is born good’ and inIV. 4, 
5 ‘He who does good is born good, he who does evil is born evil, he 
becomes righteous by righteous works &o.’ are declared by Deussen 
himself (Ph. Up. p. 410) as ‘the oldest in which > doctrine of 
transmigration is found’, Therefore, according to Daeussen 
himself, the original possessor of these two fundamental doctrines 
of the Upanisads is the brabmana Yajfiavalicya who in the sama 
Upanisad (Br. Up- IL 4, 4-14) propounds to his wife Maitreyl 
the identity of the self and elements and everything 958 with 
brahme (idam sarvam yadeyamaétma). Not only so, there are 
other brabmana teachers of these. For example, Uddalaka Arani 
expounds at great length to hisson Svetakelu the doctrine of 
identity in the famous words ‘ tat-tvamasi' (Chan. Up. VI. 8-16), 


Now the examples on which Deussen (Ph. Up. pp. 17-19) 
bases his couclusions must be cited and examined, Chan. Up, 
(V. 1L. 1) telis the story of five (named } wealthy householders 
and great students of Veda who came together and disonssed the 
queation ‘what is our atman, what is brahma’. They proposed

deeds and conduct determined the character of his succeeding 
existences, But from some passages in the Upanisads themselves 
it appears that they recognised some exceptions One exception

these two do not overwhelm, whether he says that he did evil for 
Some reason or that he did a good deed for some reason; he

Long before MacNicol wrote and since his days numerous 
‘Western scholars brought up in Christian surroundings have 
expressed their view that the ancient Indian doctrine as 
regards man’s destiny after death is far mora preferable to 
Biblical ideas on the same subject. It is enough to refer to only 
two or three authors, Arberry in his ‘ Asiatic Jones’ quotes 
(p. 37) from Sir William Jones’ letter to Earl Spencer tha 
following passage ‘I am no Hindu, but I hold the doctrine of the 
Hindus concerning a future state to be incomparably more 
rational, more pious and more likely to deter men from vice, 
than the horrid opinions inculcated by Christians on punishments 
without end’. Lowes Dickinson in ‘ Religion and Immortality’ 
(Dent and Sons, 1911) observes (on 2, 74) ‘it is really a consoling 
idea that our present capacities are determined by our previous 
actions and that our present actions again will determine our 
future character’. Owen Rutter, author of ‘the scales of Karma’ 
(London, 1925) says that Christianity has failed to solve the 
intellectual and moral problems which beset those who live in 
the complexities of the modern world, that he began to study 
the doctrine of Karma and reincarnation seven years before he 
wrote the book, which is a personal statement rather than an 
essay on Karma (pp. 12-13). Many who have written against 
this doctrine, while conceding that the Upanisadic doctrine is an 
ancient and serious attempt to solve the problem of injustice 
and evil in the world, call it a weak one and beseé with 
difficulties. One should like to ask, what systems of religion and 
philosophy are not beset with difficulties? Ono may take the

Some of the objections raised by Western thinkers and 
writers against the doctrine of Karma and re-incarnation will 
now be mentioned and briefly dealt with. One or two prelimin- 
ary matters have fo be emphasized. Many in the West regard 
our life after the death of the bodies as certain, but hardly any- 
one of them regards our life before our present bodies as a 08" 
sibility. The explanation of this attitude of many Westers 
thinkers lies in the fact that in modern Western thought the 
great support of the belief in immortality of the soul has tee 
the Christian religion, which is supposed not to recognize 8 
pre-oxistence of the soul. Besides, Christian writers Lt 
Augustine onwards firmly believed that religious truths ers 
the revelation in the Bible as interpreted by them were a a 
of the devil. McTaggart in ‘Some Dogmas of religion’ ( tence 
1930) attacks this attitude. He holds (ए, 113 ) that any ove vad 
which will prove immortality will also prove pre-exis ne with 
that there is nothing in pre-existence that is incomps omental 
any of the dogmas that are generally accepted as fun

Unwin, London, 1952, pp. 10-11} holds the same opinion (at the 
age of 92) as MceTaggart’s. Wordsworth in his famous 048 
appears to agree that the present life is preceded by another 
existence when he says ‘Our birth is but asleep and a forgetting, 
the soul that rises with us, our life’s star, had elsewhere its 
netting and cometh from afar’ LL. P. Jacks in the work men- 
tioned above remarks (on p 9) that an endless punishment is not, 
strictly speaking, a punishment at all but an exercise of cruslty 
or vengeance and that the same is trues of an endless reward, 


The first objection raised against the doctrine of Karma by 
Pringle-Pattison in ‘Idea of immortality’ ( Oxford, 1922) is that 
absenca of memory of the pre-existence is fatal to it (p. 112) 
and that immortality without recollection is quite useless. 
Miss Lily Dougall in ‘ Immortality’ by Canon Streeter and others 
raiees a similar objection (p. 29). This objection can be 
answered in various ways Does any one remember anything 
of what one did during the first two years of his life? It is alao 
well-known that men do not correctly remember in old age even 
the names of their grand-children nor does a man remember 
what he did exactly ten yeats ago during his present life, It is 
rather merciful that there is no memory of past lives. I¢ all the 
multifarious memories of many lives were to crowd on us in the 
present life, our minds would be confused and matters in the 
present life would be very much complicated. Karma is a 
cosmic law like the law of gravitation. The latter was not 
recognized by humanity for thousands of years but all the same 
it existed and worked, Several people claim to remember their 
past lives, The story of Santideyi was published ag a 6888 of 
re-incarnation by Lala Deshbhandhu Gupta, Pandit Nekiram 
Sharma, and Tarachand Mathur. The ‘Theosophist Monthly’ 
for January 1925 mentions concrete instances of the memory 
of past lives ‘The lives of Aleyone’ ( Adyar, 1924 ) is a work 
in two volumes by Mrg Besant and Mr Leadbsater in which 
48 lives are traced from 70000 BC to624 4.7 with photographs 
of somie of them as they must have appeared in the Tespective 
incarnations, The present author does not go into that question 
here In the Fssays on Immottality edited by B H. Streeter it ig 
said {on p 297} that lack of conscious continuity between two 
Yncarnatious of a sou] negatives the doctrine. One May ask: 
what grounds are thers to hald or to Prove that the reprabate 
criminal who will be awarded a judgment of eternal punigh-

Vide ‘Some Dogmas &c,’ 0. 130. Further, science holds that

into other forms, Why should one regard it ag absurd if one 
were fo hold that the soul (fo which post-existence is granted

The continuity of the soul in past and future existences is 
merely a metaphysical question and cannot be affected by the 
loss of memory, The latter occurs in one life of many years as 
to numerous happenings and at least in that one life the soul 
is admittedly one throughout 


Another objection is on the ground of heredity. We often 
find a strong likeness batween parents and children in body and 
sometimes in mental faculties also. How are we to explain 
this? One answer may be that by some law not yet discovered 
the soul that has to undergo rebirth is born to parents suited 
to hia condition. Besides, children are not exactly like their 
parents, some resemble in several physical features the mother 
or the father, buf nof in all and children of the same parents 
differ among themselves even as regards physical features, As 
regards mental qualities, children do not very often resemble 
their parents, What sori of mental equipment was possessed 
by the parents of such men of genius as Shakespeare, Newton, 
Ramanujan, Hinstein? Karma does not express what a man 
inherits from his ancestors, but it expresses that which he 
inherits from himself in some previous state or states of 
existence,

Another objection is sometimes raised as follows. The

sélyes that were masquerading as beasts now appear as human 
beings, because their Karma that reduced them to the state of 
beasts has been exhausted,

It is necessary to gather together the threads scattered over

roueé cultivate regard for spiritual values, love of righteousness

Hinduism is a combination of many systems and religious 
ideologies including ‘Vedic rituelism, Voedantic thought, 
Vaisnavism, Saiviem, Shaktism and primeval cults, adapted to 
the requirements of different types of men and communities with 
great disparities of intellectual and spiritual attainments, There 
were only a few matters that would be said to have bound most 
of the Hindus to each other, viz the doctrine of Karma and 
Punarjanma, the unifying influence of the vast and venerated 
Sanskri¢ literature that gradually enriched the regional langu- 
ages, the veneration in which the Vedas were held by all 
Hindus as the final authority in religious matters, though only 
asmall minority could learn and understand them, the feogra~ 
phical unity of the country from the Himalaya to Cape Comorin 
emphasized by the Purdnas and by the pilgrimages to holy 
placea from Manasa lake and Badrinath to Ramegvara These 
few elements, however, were not enough to neutralize the causes 
that militated against effective unity amongst all Hindus, Most 
of the Gciiryas and saints laid too much emphasis on other.

conclusion that the individual self is non-different from the 
one Essence, that all manifoldness is only apparent, that 
even fishermen, slaves, gamblers and the inanimate world 
are non-different from it This Vedanta doctrine is one of 
the most characteristic features of Hinduism and is India’s 
great contribution to the spiritual development of man, though 
there are sporadic instances of this doctrine having been 
held by some ancient philosophers in otherlands This idea 
of one in the many and many in one is the very core or centra 
of Vedanta. This has been dealt with above ( vide pp. 1499-1500 
notes 2451-52 and pp. 1509-10), In Europe the study of philo- 
sophy isan end in itself. In ancient India this idea of the 
unity in diversity was made the basis of education and 
sociology and it was held that the realization of this unity in 
one’s life was the highest freedom { moksa). 


The Upanisadic teaching is a universal doctrine in which all

IV. From very ancient Vedic times ono of the fundamental 
conceptions of our Indian culture has been the idea of three 
spiritual and religious debts owed by a person to the sages, gods 
and 71६75, which he paid off by the study of the ancient lore, by 
sacrifices, and by having a son or sons respectively Thia 
subject has been dealt with at length in the H. of Dh, Vol. II pp, 
270, 425, 560-61, 676, Vol. LIT p, 416 and above, p. 1818 note 2168, 
To these three debts the Mahabharata added a fourth viz. the debt 
owed to all men-paid off by goodness ( vide H. of Dh. Vol. III p. 416 
आ, 675). Sabara on Jaimini VI. 2.31 explains that this doctrine 
is not confined to brahmanas but to all members of the three 
classes, the word ‘brahmana’ used in the Tai S, and other 
Vedic texts being only illustrative

When reforms are suggested in these days, conservative 
people put forward the plea that ours is ‘ sandtana- dharma * 2612 
nd so no changes should be introduced. But the words ‘sanafana 
dharma’ do nof mean that Dharma always stands still or is 
immutable; all that those words mean is that our culture is very 
ancient and has a long tradition behind it but they do not mean 
shat Dharma permits nochange. Asa matter of fact funda- 
mental changes in conceptions, beliefs and practices have been 
made from aucient times to the medieval times by means of 
various devices, Attention may be drawn foafew Veda was 
all in all in very ancient times but in the Upanisads this was 
changed, the Mundaka I. 1.5 designating the four Vedas as 
inferior knowledge (apara vidya) and the knowledge of the 
immutable brahman as the higher vidya; in the Chan. Up. VIL 1.4, 
the four Vedas and several other branches of knowledge are called 
by Sanatkumara (whom Narada approached for instruction | 
mere name (nama), Yajfias were the most important religious 
practice in theearly Vedic period, but the Mundaka Up, 1.2.7 
designates them as leaky boats and regards those who hold them 
as the best thing to be fools. Vide above pp. 1265-72 about 
changes in the views on anuloma marriages, on the topic of 
whose food may be partaken even by a brahmana, the abrogation 
of many Vedic practices by the doctrine of Kalivariya ( matters 
forbidden in Kali age) &c. Manu, Yaj ,Visnudharmasitra, 
Visnu and other puranas expressly provide that one should not 
observe but give up what was once Dhamna, if it has come to be 
hateful to the people and if it would end in unhappiness ( vide 
p. 1270 71. 2071 above ). The Santiparva’6!? expressly states that 
what was adiarma (in one age) may become dharma in another

Dharma is divided into different classes from different 
standpoints. One classification is into sraufa (based on the 
Vedas ) and Sima ta ( basad on Smrtis ), There was another and a 
more comprehensive classification of Dharma into six 0198898 
vis. varnadharma ( duties and rights of varnas ), agramadharma 
Crules about the dSramas ), varndsramadharma (rules enjoined 
because the person belongs fo a certain classand was alsoin a 
certain dgrama (6, &, the rule that a brahmana brahmacarl 
should carry a staff of palasu tree), gunadharma (rules for one 
who holds or occupies a certain position, 28 in the case ofa 
king ), naimittikadharma (rules that have to be observed only 
on certain occasions such as bath on an eclipse, expiation for a 
lapse and lastly simanyadharma ( duties common to all (such 
as those described in pp. 10-11 of the H. of Dh, Vol. IT). This 
Jeads on to the next important characteristic of Hindu culture 
and society, viz. varnas and castes. 


V1, Varna and caste. The subjech of the origin of 
varna classification, the caste system and the duties, privi- 
leges and disabilities of the four varnas hava been dealt 
with at length in the History of Dharmaéastra Vol. IL. pp. 
19-164, It has been shown that the word ‘varna’ (colour) 
has been applied to Avyas and ddsas in the Reveda, that these 
two (dryas and 08888 } were opposite camps, that brahmanas 
and ksatriyas are mentioned in the Rgveda, but the word 
varna has not been expressly connected with them. The 
words Vaigya and Sidra do not occur in the Reveda except in 
the Purusasikta (Re X. 90.12) but even im that hymn the 
word varna’ is not employed with reference to them, That 
hymn is held to be comparatively a late one by most modern 
scholars. 16 7185 be conceded that at the time when the

The ideas underlying the original varna system made the nearest 
approach towards a society in which there was n0 attempt to 
secure a competitive equality but in which the interest of all 
groups were regarded as identical. In Vedic times there were only 
classes and vot castes in the modern sense. Even in the smrtis 
when many castes had arisen the greatest emphasis was laid 
on duijes rather than on privileges and on high moral character 
and the value of the effort made by a man. It is therefore

created on the basis of quality (or on the basis of saétza, rajas 
and éamas ) and actions and (in XVII 42-44) it specifies the

serenity of mind, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance,

atened to beat untouchables that wanted to draw water from

(XI) Vast Sanskrit literature, 


India produced 8 vast amount of Sanskrit literature of 
& most varied character for at least three thousand years. There 
is no country in the world that can exhibit continuous creation 
of several departments of Hterature for such a long period. 
Sanskrit literature penetrated to countries like Tibet, China, 
Java and others, Itg literature influenced the Moslem world and 
European world by means of the decimal place yalue system, 
its fable literature and system of Vedanta, Vide Winternite's 
‘Some problems of Indian Literature’ ( the Readership Leotures 
in Caleutta University} pp. 59-81 for a brief but instructive 
treatment of the Influence of Sanskrit Literature in the West. 
1४8 study by Europeans at the end of the 18th century and in 
the 19th century laid the foundation of several sciences, such 28 
the science of language, of comparative religion, of thought and 
of mythology. There exist several Histories of Sanskrit Litera- 
ture by several scholars such as Weber, Maz Muller, Winternitz, 
Keith, M. Krishnamachariar, which will give an ‘idea to any 
reader of the variety and vastness of Sanalkrié literature,

Vast Sanskrit Literature 1651 


India has preserved for itself and for the world @ vast literature 
in the best part of which the principal theme is to ask men 
never to cease in their efforts to control the senses and to reach 
higher and higher heights of morality and spirituality. H. त. 
Gowen in‘ A History of Indian Literature’ (1931 ) observe (on 
p. 8) ‘Indian literature has an intrinsic value which no 
remoteness avails to destroy. For sacredness, variety and 
continuity, scarcely any other may compare with it, cettainly 
none surpasses it. As for sacredness no other scripture, not 
even our Bible, may compete with the Veda in its continuity or 
in the matter of general acceptance’, He dilates also on the 
variety and remarkable continuity of Indian literature, Classical 
Sanskrit first blossoned at least before 500 B, C, Panini names at

XII. Yoga: Yogahas bean treated of above { pp. 1385- 
1462). In the whole world there exists hardly any well thought 
out and comprehensive system of psychical and moral discipline 
like Yoga. Mercea Eliade observes (on p. 359) in‘ Yoga, 
Immortality and Freedom’ (tr. by Willard R. Trask, 1958) 
‘ Yoga constitutes a characteristic dimension of the Indian mind, 
is marked by reaction againsh metaphysical speculations and 
the excasses of a fossilized ritualism’. Western minds having 
experienced a surfeit of economic prosperity, but worried by the 
tensions and crises of these times are turning more and more to 
Yoga and to Indian philosophy such as the Vedanta. In recent 
years numerous books are being published that deal with 
‘perennial philosophy’, Yoga (including Tibetan Yoga ), 
meditation, concentration, mystical experience &c. Many of 
these books are written by honest people after reading a good 
deal of literature on these subjects but they are wanting in any 
personal yogic or mystic experience, There ara some books that 
are written by persoss who want to take advantage of the popular 
craze for Yoga and similar mystical practices for the sake of wealth 
and fame. In'Vedantafor the Western World’ edited by Christopher 
Isherwood (Allen and Unwin, London, 1948) the famous writer 
Mr, Aldous Huxley sounds a note of-.warning against the plethora 
of books on mysticism and Yoga in the market (p 376 म).

that for real philosophy great’ moral preparation 38 necossary, 

that reason has to be extensively used in arriving at the truth, 

that tradition and authority have to be accepted and not 

neglected, Almost all darganas ( except that of Garvika) are 

concerned with Liberation ( variously called Moksa, Kaivalya, 
Nirvana, Amrtatva, Nihéreyasa, Apavarga) and all (except 
Carvaka) are agreed on the doctrine of Karma and Punarjanma. 

It is nob necessary fo say more on Indian Philosophy in this 
Chapter.

CHAPTER XXXVII 
Future Trends 


After the battle of Plassey in 1757 the civil government of 
the three large provinces of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa came under 
British rule from 1765. From 1818 when the last Peshwa 
Bajirao II was defeated and became a, pensioner, the British 
were In control over the whole of India except Punjab, which 
was subdued in 1845, The British left India in 1947. Thare- 
fore, they were rulers over a large part of India for 180 years, 
over the whole of it except Punjab for about 130 years and over 
Punjab just about 100 years. The impact of British occupation 
during these periods on Hindu society was tremendous in al) 
spheres, physical, mental and moral. The changes effected 
during these years of British rule were of such magnitude that 
they far exceeded the changes that occurred in hundreds of years 
before the coming of the British With the advent of British 
rule came a new system of Government on an all India basis, 
establishment of courts of justice on Western patterns, laws 
that applied to all Indians without distinction, modern indivi- 
dualistic liberty, Western pattern of living at least in towns 
and cities, an educational system placing all Indians on the 
same level, newspapers, better means of transport, study of 
modern science, English literature and arts &c. 


The present author has no intention of writing anything 
on the all round changes that have taken place in India under 
British rule, All thathe proposes to do inthis chapter is to indicate 
briefly the effects that are likely to be produced on Hindu 
society, its ancient ideals and values in the near future, on 
account of science and modern ideas, the Constitution framed 
for Indian democracy, the idea of a secular State, socialistic 
pattern of society, economical planning, legislation, growth of 
population and means fo check it. 

But before he deals with the above subjects, it is necessary 
to give a rapid review of the state of things before Independons 
was achieved. Lord Ripon as Viceroy of India in 1882 star’ 6 1 
a scheme of local self-government by means of munioipe 
corporations in the cities and district and local Boards ish 
rural areas, Thus after about 120 years from 1765 wien Bish 
rule was first established in a large part of India, the 


British colomal policy and its effects 1659 


thought fit to associate the conquered people in managing some 
of their own {unimportant and petty ) affairs Colonialism on 
the part of the British had reached its peak by that time, The 
British imported raw materials lke cotton from India, processed 
them in Manchester and exported the manufactured products 
back fo India's immense market. At the instance of British 
manufacturers laws were passed In Britain forbidding the 
import of Indian silk and cotton goods. India was drained of 
wealth by that policy for over a hundred years and India became 
one of the poorest countries in the world Dadabhai Naoroji in 
his ‘ Poverty and un-British rule in India’ (London, 1901, 675 
pages } demonstrated this very ably. The main elements of the 
colonial rule of Britain were thesa, complete political subjection 
existed, the main economic activity was in the hands of 
foreigners, if was foreign capital that was employed in India 
and substantial dividends or interest on fhe capital were 
guaranteed in some cases like tha Railways by the British 
tulers of India payable from the faxes imposed on Indian 
people, fhe control of large enterprises was in foreign hands and 
directed towards securing foreign interests, the land and people 
were used ag instruments of the purposes of Britain, India 
got peace and political unity at the cost of enormous poverty 
and distress and many of the economic problems that beset 
presené day India have to be traced back to the disastroug 
colonial policies of Britain,
